St. Johns Medical College, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) occurs more commonly among young adults. It is infrequent in older individuals and may differ in clinical presentations, risk factors, and outcome from CVT in young. Anticoagulation is pivotal in treatment, and preventing risk factors remains essential. Our aim was to study the clinical characteristics, risk factors, and outcomes of CVT in patients aged over 45 years.

Methodology: Case records of patients with CVT over the age of 45 years admitted in our hospital between 2009 and 2023 were studied retrospectively. Demographic details, clinical presentation, neuroimaging, laboratory profile, and treatment given were analyzed with appropriate descriptive statistics.

Results: During this period, 318 patients with CVT were treated, of which 60 were above 45 years of age. Among them, 43 were males (71%). Most common presentation was headache (73%), followed by seizures (41%) and motor deficits (33%). Risk factors included hyperhomocysteinemia (55%), anemia (hemoglobin [Hb] <12) (30%), and polycythemia (Hb >16) (25%). antiphospholipid antibody (APLA)/antinuclear antibody (ANA) was positive in 11 patients. Two patients had malignancy. In addition, 71% of patients had extensive thrombosis involving more than one sinus, with 61% having parenchymal hemorrhagic infarct. Nearly 70% had more than 7 days of hospital stay. Vitamin K antagonist (VKAs) were most commonly prescribed at discharge, while 15 patients were discharged on Non-Vitamin K Antagonist Oral Anticoagulant (NOACs).

Conclusions: CVT is a significant health concern among individuals over 45 years old, particularly males, due to extensive thrombosis and prolonged hospitalization. Identification of risk factors and implementation of better treatment options in older adults are crucial for improving outcomes.

Background and Aim: Optic neuritis (ON) refers to a group of conditions that involve inflammation of the optic nerve. Total number of patients was 50 (15 male, 35 female). Patients were examined for visual acuity and the fundus was also examined before admission and at the time of discharge and 2 weeks and 1 month after follow-up.

Results: Out of total 50 patients, 10 patients had toxic ON, one patient had high-altitude ON, and others had ON due to unknown causes. Mean age of the patients was 28 years. There was female predominance, and the visual acuity ranged at admission from perception of light to 6/9.

Conclusions: Seronegative ON spectrum is increasing day by day, so early recognition and treatment will lead to significant improvement.

Background and Aim: Mutations in the genes SLC52A2 and SLC52A3, which encode the riboflavin transporters RFVT2 and RFVT3, respectively, cause Brown–Vialetto–Van-Laere (BVVL) syndrome. Typically, patients present with sensorineural deafness and progressive pontobulbar palsy. Other features include sensorimotor axonal neuropathy, optic atrophy, and respiratory compromise. Here, we describe the clinical and genetic spectrum of eight genetically confirmed BVVL syndrome patients, which closely mimics the elusive Madras motor neuron disease (MMND).

Methodology: This was a retrospective observational study on eight patients with BVVL syndrome and corresponding genetic variants. Baseline demographic, clinical, and neurophysiology details were recorded, and genetic analysis was done by next generation sequencing.

Results: The mean age at disease onset was 11.25 (range: 7–16) years. All had varying illness durations, with a mean duration of 6.75 years (range: 3–12). All had severe sensorineural hearing loss, dysarthria and severe hypophonia, tongue atrophy and fasciculations, impaired tandem gait, and sensory ataxia. Weakness and atrophy of limb muscles were noted in five, facial weakness in four, sensory symptoms in three, and 9–11 cranial nerve palsy in five patients. In the eight patients, five novel variations (two homozygous and two heterozygous variants in the SLC52A3 gene and one heterozygous variant in the SLC52A2 gene) and previously reported one homozygous and one heterozygous variant in SLC52A3 were noted. Six of eight patients reported significant clinical improvement after 3–6 months of high-dose riboflavin therapy (600 mg/day).

Conclusions: This report highlights the importance of genetic confirmation of all patients suspected to have MMND/BVVL syndrome and not mislabel cases as MMND, for which still further advanced genetic testing is warranted.

Background and Aim: Embolic stroke of undetermined source (ESUS) is responsible for about 30% of ischemic stroke. Atrial fibrillation (AF) is an important cause of embolic stroke. Atrial cardiopathy predisposes to thrombus formation and thereby may be responsible for embolic stroke in the absence of AF. A link between atrial cardiopathy and ESUS, if proven, may support anticoagulant therapy in ESUS for secondary prevention. Our aims were to (1) classify various ischemic stroke types according to TOAST classification and to evaluate ESUS in the same subjects and (2) find the association of atrial cardiopathy in ESUS and compare it with non-ESUS group.

Methodology: This observational prospective study was conducted in Apollo Multispecialty Hospital, Kolkata from September 2022 to November 2023. Patients >60 years of age with ischemic stroke were selected for the study and were further classified according to Trial of ORG 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST)classification. Brain and neck vessel imaging, electrocardiogram, echocardiography, 24-h Holter, and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) test were done. Data was analyzed for atrial cardiopathy after excluding AF and other cardioembolic causes of stroke with appropriate statistical test of significance using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences 23.0 version software.

Results: Of the 225 eligible patients, 48 (21.3%) were classified as ESUS and 97 (43.1%) as non-ESUS. Atrial cardiopathy was significantly more prevalent in ESUS patients than non-ESUS patients, with NT-proBNP >250 pg/ml and P-wave terminal force in lead V1(PTFV1) >5000 mV ms as independent variables (P < 0.05).

Conclusions: Markers like NT-proBNP and PTFV1 may, therefore, be potential independent predictors of embolic stroke even in the absence of atrial fibrillation. Future research on the potential use of anticoagulants in ESUS should focus more on subsets of patients with the above markers of atrial cardiopathy.

Results: Eighty-eight patients each in E-MwA and NHC groups were studied (mean age 30.3 ± 8.8 and 31.4 ± 6.6 years, respectively; female:male ratio 3.4:1 and 1:1, respectively). Conclusions: Compared to non-headache controls, migraine patients had significant subjective and objective cognitive dysfunctions during a migraine attack.

National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences, Bengaluru (NIMHANS, Bengaluru), Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: The combination of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) with electroencephalogram (EEG) has opened new opportunities in epilepsy research, allowing direct investigation and modulation of cortical excitability and induction of epileptiform discharges (EDs) to enhance diagnostic and prognostic capabilities

Methodology: This prospective study analyzed 31 patients of genetic generalized epilepsy (GGE) and 31 matched healthy controls. EEG signals were recorded using a 32-channel TMS-compatible EEG amplifier. Magnetic stimuli were delivered using a figure-of-eight coil connected to a Magstim 200 stimulator. The motor cortex and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were localized through neuronavigational techniques. Optimal stimulus intensity was calculated based on resting motor threshold and paired-pulse TMS protocol. Each target received 300 stimuli of long-interval cortical inhibition (LICI), short-interval cortical inhibition (SICI), and motor threshold with a 5-s intertrial interval. Data was analyzed in MATLAB.

Results: In our study, discharges were evident in 51% (16 patients) on single-pulse stimulation, 41% (13 patients) by paired-pulse stimulation (SICI), and 39% (12 patients) with paired-pulse stimulation (LICI) over the motor cortex. In the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, 3% (one patient) showed discharges through single-pulse stimulation, 23% (seven patients) by paired-pulse stimulation (SICI), and 16% (five patients) by paired-pulse stimulation (LICI).

Conclusions: TMS-induced discharges have important implications in GGE, and further evaluation is needed to establish the role of TMS–EEG in understanding epileptogenesis and improving diagnosis and prognosis in GGE and epilepsy.

Sanjay Rao Kordcal, Debashish Chowdhury, Debashish Chowdhury, Rahul Nagane, Ashish Kumar Duggal

Kasturba Medical College, Manipal (KMC, Manipal), Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: ANODYNE 1 and II studies showed the effectiveness of greater occipital nerve block (GONB) with methylprednisolone and lignocaine as a transitional preventive treatment for episodic cluster headache compared to placebo. Here, we report the results of the patient-reported outcome (PROM) measures of the ANODYNE study. Our aim was to study the efficacy of GONB in improving PROM.

Methodology: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial included episodic cluster headache (ECH) patients, aged 18-65, diagnosed by International Classification of Headache Disorders third version criteria, with one or more attacks per 24 h for 7 days before randomization. ECH patients were randomized to receive active GONB (2 ml methylprednisolone [80 mg] and 2 ml lignocaine [2%]) and placebo (4 ml saline injections). PROM included headache impact, assessed by headache-impact-test-6, headache disability, assessed by headache disability inventory (HDI), and cluster headache quality of life (CHQOL). Efficacy analyses, that is, the changes in PROM scores from baseline to Week 4, were performed in a modified intention-to-treat population using a generalized linear model. The trial was registered with the Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI/2021/21/038397).

Results: Forty ECH patients were randomized. Thirty-nine patients (19 in the active group and 20 in the placebo group) were available for efficacy analysis. A significantly greater improvement in PROM in the active group compared to placebo was observed. The mean differences in these parameters between the two groups were -10.2 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -12.7 to -7.7; P < 0.001), -13.3 (95% CI: -9.6 to -7.0; P < 0.001), and -11.1 (95% CI: -16.6 to -5.6; P < 0.001) for HIT-6, HDI, and CHQOL, respectively, favoring active GONB. No serious adverse effects were reported.

Conclusions: ANODYNE study found that GONB injection with methylprednisolone and lignocaine, compared to a placebo, resulted in significant improvements in PROM.

Background and Aim: Paroxysmal nonepileptic events (PNEEs) are group of events with sudden paroxysmal changes in behaviors or consciousness, which resemble epilepsy but are not accompanied by electrophysiologic changes. We aimed to study the possible etiology and analyze clinical phenomenology of PNEE in children and identify differentiating pointers between PNEE and epilepsy.

Methodology: A prospective observational study was conducted over 10 months. Children with history of paroxysmal events characterized by abrupt changes in awareness, behavior, and movement were included. Children with strong family history of seizures, neurologic deficits, and static encephalopathy were excluded. Data of children was collected in a prefixed proforma, including demographic data, semiology of events, differentiating factors from epilepsy, history of stressors, and response to treatment. Children underwent video electroencephalogram (EEG) as per the protocol and details were noted. All the data were coded in Excel and analyzed statistically.

Results: Total number of subjects was 46, consisting of 23 boys and 23 girls. Their mean age was 9.95 years. Mean time lag from onset to diagnosis was 1.53 years. Most common semiology was mixed type (45%), which was followed by unexplained bizarre activity (19%). Most common differentiating features from epilepsy were abrupt onset and offset (97%), followed by occurrence in presence of caregivers (60%). Suggestibility was present in 41%. School absenteeism was very significant (32.6%, mean- 4.7 months). Significant stressors were present in many children. Also, 45.6% used antiseizure medications with the average duration being 1.03 years. Follow-up at 6 months was done, which showed improvement in 81% children.

Conclusions: Clear identification of PNEE helps in avoiding unnecessary treatment with antiseizure medications, thus helping child and family both socioeconomically and psychologically.

Background and Aim: N95 masks have become an essential tool in the daily working of health-care workers ever since the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. Our aim was to study the prevalence of and characteristics of headache in a group of health-care workers using N95 masks in our hospital.

Background and Aim: (1) We aimed to study the dietary habits of patients with dementia. (2) In addition, we attempted to compare the dietary habits of patients with cognitive decline to those with normal cognitive function.

Methodology: This was a case–control retrospective study. Demographic information and detailed medical history, including age at onset and duration of illness and medications, were noted. Background and Aim: Central nervous system (CNS) tuberculosis (Tb) is severe form of extrapulmonary Tb that can lead to significant morbidity and mortality if not promptly diagnosed and treated. This study highlights the spectrum of atypical CNS-Tb manifestations encountered in a single tertiary care center.

Methodology: A prospective study was conducted between May 2023 and May 2024 including 21 patients. We collected data on patient demographics, clinical presentation, diagnostic methods, radiologic findings, treatment regimens, and clinical outcomes.

Tirunelveli Medical College, North High ground Road, Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: The connection between sleep and epilepsy was first identified by ancient Greeks. Aristotle observed that both sleep and seizures involve altered states of consciousness and a separation of the soul from the body. This study investigates how nighttime sleep can trigger epileptic seizures, how nocturnal seizures disrupt sleep patterns, and how antiepileptic medications impact the sleep quality and seizure control. Recent advances in neurophysiology, neuropsychology, sleep medicine, and genetics offer promising opportunities to enhance our understanding of the relationship between sleep and epilepsy, leading to direct clinical benefits. This study aims to (1) examine the effect of sleep on epilepsy, (2) investigate how epilepsy affects sleep, (3) explore the impact of comorbid sleep disorders as a differential diagnosis of epilepsy, (4) assess the effect of antiepileptic medications on sleep and seizure control, and (5) evaluate whether the dose or timing of antiepileptic drugs can improve therapeutic outcomes.

Methodology: Two hundred epileptic patients attending the neurology outpatient department participated in this study. Comprehensive histories, clinical examinations, routine electroencephalograms, and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain epilepsy protocols were conducted. Detailed records of sleep disturbances during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) phases, as well as seizure occurrences during these periods, were maintained. The National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-sciences sleep disorder questionnaires, Children’s Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ), Epworth Sleepiness Scale, and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index were used to evaluate sleep disturbances.

Results: Postictal somnolence was observed in 8% of patients. Seizures disrupted sleep continuity in 43% of patients by increasing wakefulness after sleep onset and causing sleep fragmentation. Sleep was disturbed in 33% of patients during the immediate postictal and interictal periods. Increased sleep latency and frequent nocturnal awakenings (insomnia) were present in 52% of patients with epilepsy. Excessive daytime sleepiness was found in 44% of patients. Comorbid sleep disorders, such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSAS), were found in 13% of patients, exacerbating epilepsy symptoms and creating a vicious cycle.

Conclusions: In conclusion, this study highlights the critical interplay between sleep and epilepsy. Epilepsy significantly disrupts sleep, and addressing these sleep disturbances is vital for achieving optimal seizure control. By integrating sleep management into the treatment of epilepsy, clinicians can improve both sleep quality and seizure outcomes, ultimately enhancing the quality of life for patients with epilepsy. Future research should continue to explore the mechanisms underlying the sleep–epilepsy relationship and develop targeted interventions to address these challenges.

Background and Aim: Whether the serum calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) levels from peripheral blood during the interictal headache-free states can be used as a biomarker for migraine is still uncertain. Background and Aim: Carotid atherosclerosis is a well-known risk factor for ischemic stroke. However, screening of all patients by using computed tomography (CT)/magnetic resonance (MR) angiography is cumbersome and costly; hence, search for cost-effective methods is mandatory. Calf circumference is a marker of peripheral lean mass. We aimed to estimate the association between waist–to–calf ratio and carotid atherosclerosis in patients presenting with ischemic stroke.

Methodology: This was a prospective, cross-sectional, observational study from a single tertiary care center in western Maharashtra. Fifty-eight patients of ischemic stroke were included. A detailed history was taken, a clinical examination was conducted, and biochemical indices were measured. Anthropometric measurements were calculated as per standard and defined methods in the form of waist circumference, calf circumference, and waist–calf ratio. Carotid atherosclerosis was diagnosed on the basis of CT angiography or MR angiography of the brain and neck.

Results: The study includes 58 patients. Mean age of presentation was 57.19 ± 14.95 years and male to female ratio was 2.22. Vascular risk factors noted were: 21 (36.20%) patients were diabetic, 19 (32.75%) were hypertensive, eight (13.79%) had history of ischemic heart disease, six (10.34%) were smokers, 25 (43.10%) patients were tobacco chewers, and 12 (20.68%) patients had a history of alcohol consumption. There were 38 patients who had carotid atherosclerosis (waist–calf ratio was >2.5 in eight patients). We found an association between waist–calf ratio and carotid atherosclerosis with chi-square 3.62, degree of freedom 1, and P-value of 0.05, which was statistically significant.

Conclusions: Waist–calf ratio is an important anthropometric marker of carotid atherosclerosis and can be used in screening of high-risk patients. Studies on larger groups are suggested.

Background and Aim: Hyponatremia has been reported in Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), but its predictors and role in functional outcome have not been reported comprehensively. We report the occurrence of hyponatremia in GBS and its association with severity and neurophysiologic subtypes. We also evaluated its influence on disability and death.

Methodology: Five hundred and twenty-nine patients with GBS were evaluated retrospectively, and the data since 1998 was retrieved from our prospective GBS registry. The clinical and neurophysiologic subtypes were noted; clinical severity was graded on a 0–6 scale (Hughes). Results: We found that 193/529 (36.5%) patients had hyponatremia at admission: 132 (25%) had mild, 49 (9.3%) had moderate, and 12 (2.3%) had severe hyponatremia. The predictors of hyponatremia on univariate analysis included disease severity on admission (P < 0.001), facial palsy (P < 0.001), bulbar palsy (P < 0.001), autonomic involvement (P < 0.001), and respiratory involvement and assisted ventilation (P < 0.001). Occurrence of hyponatremia was not associated with age (P = 0.43), gender (P = 0.02), clinical subtype (P = 0.22), electrophysiologic subtype of GBS (P = 0.26) or intravenous immunoglobulin therapy (P = 0.58). Hyponatremia was associated with days of hospitalization (P < 0.001), 1-month outcome (P < 0.001), and 3-month outcome (P < 0.001). On multivariate analysis, the independent predictors of hyponatremia were facial palsy (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 1.82, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.16–2.83; P = 0.009) and autonomic dysfunction (AOR = 1.08, 95% CI 1.08-2.68; P = 0.02). Three (0.56%) patients died and two of them had hyponatremia. Hyponatremia was associated with poor outcome at 3 months (P = 0.03).

Conclusions: 36.5% patients with GBS may have hyponatremia, especially those with facial palsy and autonomic dysfunction. Occurrence of hyponatremia may suggest poor outcome at 3 months.

Background and Aim: This study was conducted with the aim of correlating electrophysiologic and neuroimaging findings with clinical progression to proximal limb involvement in patients with distal-predominant Hirayama disease (HD).

Background and Aim: Thrombolysis with intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator is the most widely used and approved form of reperfusion therapy in acute ischemic stroke (AIS), with post-thrombolysis hemorrhagic transformation being the most feared complication. Results: A total of 62 patients were included in study. Out of these, 42 (67.7%) were males and 20 (32.3%) were females. The patients’ mean age was 55.9 ± 13.64 years. Our study proves the same. Therefore, SEDAN score is a valid predictive tool for ICH post-thrombolysis in AIS.

Bharati Vidyapeeth Medical College, Pune, Maharashtra, India

Background and Aim: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) is a rare but serious neurologic condition characterized by thrombosis in the cerebral venous sinuses. This study aims to validate the prognostic cerebral venous thrombosis grading scale (CVT-GS) score in CVST patients, assessing its predictive value against the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at 30 days post-admission.

Methodology: This prospective single-center study was conducted at a university in western Maharashtra. All patients of CVST were studied, and detailed clinical history, risk factors, neurologic examination, laboratory and radiologic investigations, treatment, and outcomes were recorded. CVTGS score was assigned at presentation, which was categorized into mild (0–2), moderate (3–7), and severe (8–13), and patients were assessed using mRS on day 30.

Results: The study included 74 patients. Mean age of patients at presentation was 35.54 ± 12.47, and the male to female ratio was 1.55. Risk factors included smoking (31%), alcohol use (34%), and use of oral contraceptive pill (55%). Most common symptom on presentation was headache (59%), with 32% patients presenting with seizures. Transverse sinus (59%) was the most commonly involved sinus, followed by sigmoid sinus (49%) and superior sagittal sinus (37%). Thirteen percent of patients had poor functional outcome as measured by mRS >2. The Spearman correlation coefficient between CVT-GS scores and 30-day mRS scores was calculated, which revealed a significant positive correlation (r = 0.69, P < 0.01). Higher CVT-GS scores correlated with worse outcomes on the mRS scale.

Conclusions: The CVT-GS scale is a valuable prognostic tool for predicting 30-day outcomes in CVST patients. This study validates its use, providing a reliable method for early prognosis. Further studies with larger sample sizes are recommended to confirm these findings.

Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh (PGIMER Chandigarh), India

Background and Aim: Ethambutol (EMB)-induced optic neuropathy (EtON) is a well-known and potentially devasting adverse effect, but its exact etiopathogenesis is still unknown. Recent National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP) guidelines allow the prolonged (>8 months) use of EMB, increasing the cumulative drug exposure and hence the risk of EtON. It is prudent to identify population at risk for developing EtON for convenient and safe duration and dose adjustments of this important bacteriostatic anti-tuberculosis treatment (ATT). We assessed the role of genetics (mitochondrial and human leukocyte antigen [HLA] Class II profiling) in patients of EtON. Our aim was to evaluate the association of mitochondrial genes and HLA class II alleles in patients with EtON.

Methodology: This was prospective, observational, case–control study carried on 100 patients with EtON and 190 matched controls. Clinical, detailed neuro-ophthalmologic examination, serum and cerebrospinal fluid investigations, and detailed imaging were carried out in all patients. All possible risk factors of EtON were noted for subsequent multivariate analysis. Five milliliters of blood sample was stored in an ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid vial at -20°C for mitochondrial genetic assessment and HLA typing. DNA was isolated using Qiagen Mini kit. Isolated DNA was further processed for HLA typing using polymerase chain reaction - single specific prime (PCR-SSP) method. For mitochondrial mutations, REPLI-g Mitochondrial DNA Kit was used to amplify mitochondrial DNA and polymerase chain reaction - restriction fragment length polymorphism (PCR-RFLP) method was used to assess the mutations.

Most patients with EtON had severe vision loss (80%) and complete visual field loss (59%). Thickness of optic nerves and optic chiasma was reduced significantly in the EtON group (P ≤ 0.0001) compared to the normative data on imaging. All the patients were found to have wild mitochondrial mutations. The allele frequency of HLA-DQB1*05:01 allele was found to be significantly high compared to controls (P ≤ 0.0001). Similarly, the allele frequency of HLA-DQB1*03:01 (P = 0.03), HLA-DRB1*03:01 (P = 0.04), and HLA-DRB1*12:01 (P = 0.03) was found to be higher in cases compared to controls. The later three were significantly associated with good visual outcome at 6 months follow-up on multivariate analysis (R-1.00).

Conclusions: This is the first study highlighting the association of EtON with HLA Class II alleles. Our findings provide an insight into the role of HLA alleles in the etiopathogenesis of EtON.

Background and Aim: The advent of next generation sequencing (NGS) techniques allowed to identify a large number of novel variants and its use in clinical contexts are still challenging. A comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms of disease, as well as the structure, function, and biological network of the proteins involved in its pathogenesis, is required to device precision therapy. Background and Aim: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is the standard of care for patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD) experiencing motor complications in the mid-stages of the disease. DBS improves patients’ quality of life remarkably; its impact on long-term survival in patients from the developing world is unclear. We aimed to examine the long-term survival of patients with PD, who had undergone DBS of the subthalamic nucleus (STN) bilaterally, and the factors associated with mortality from our surgical cohort over a span of 25 years.

Methodology: The survival status of patients with PD who had undergone STN DBS in our center and with a minimum of 5 years of follow-up after surgery was examined. Families of patients who were not on follow-up were contacted over the telephone.

Background and Aim: The long-term efficacy and safety of greater occipital nerve block (GONB) for the preventive treatment of episodic cluster headaches (ECHs) remains unknown. This study aims to find the long-term efficacy and safety of GONB in patients with ECH, following a double-blind treatment phase (DBTP).

Methodology: Open-label treatment phase (OLTP) of ANODYNE trial included patients who opted out of DBTP and those with persistent attacks at the end of DBTP (Week 4). Background and Aim: There is limited data on the clinical profile of episodic cluster headache (ECH) in the Indian population. Herein, we report on the clinical profile of ECH patients.

Methodology: Demography and clinical characteristics of headaches were documented prospectively for consecutive ECH patients diagnosed by International Classification of Headache Disorders third version criteria and attending the Headache Clinic from December 2021 to January 2023. The mean MHD and MMD at baseline were 23.6 ± 3.9 and 18.5 ± 4.2, respectively. Following the combination treatment, at 6 months, MHD and MMD were significantly reduced compared to baseline (-13.3 ± 1.1 [confidence interval {CI}: -10.4 to -16.3; P < 0.001] and -11.5 ± 0.9 [CI: -9.0 to -13.9; P < 0.001], respectively). Fifty percent responder rate was 56.3%. Adverse effects were mild and transient that included pain and mild bleeding at the injection site. No serious adverse effects were reported.

Conclusions: This open-label, prospective study undertaken for the first time in the world showed good efficacy and tolerability of the combination treatment of BoT-A and GONB in patients with RM over 6 months.

Donti Ramakrishna Anusha

Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal (MAHE, Manipal), Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Geriatric epilepsy includes pre-elderly (60 years old) and new-onset epilepsy in elderly. Recognizing seizures in this population is challenging because of clinically subtle presentation of seizures in most cases. This study aims to demonstrate the role of electroencephalogram (EEG) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in late-onset seizures and epilepsy.

Methodology: Consecutive patients with late-onset seizures and epilepsy attending the neurology services were enrolled in the study after obtaining their informed consent and applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria. All the patients were stratified into late-onset seizures and late-onset epilepsy groups. EEG and MRI were done in all patients.

Results: One hundred and nine elderly patients presented with seizures, with males constituting 62 of them. Of the 109 patients, 67 were in seizures group and 42 were in epilepsy group. In the seizures group, MRI findings were normal in 61.1% and abnormal in 39.9%. In the epilepsy group, all patients had abnormal MRI. In the seizures group, 68.6% and 31.4% of patients had normal and abnormal EEG, respectively. Of them, generalized slowing (25.3%) was the most common finding, followed by focal slowing (5.9%), focal spikes (2.9%), and generalized spikes (1.4%). In the late-onset epilepsy group, 47.6% and 52.4% of patients had normal and abnormal EEG, respectively. Focal slowing (30.9%) was the most common finding in them, followed by generalized slowing (21.4%), focal spikes (7.1%), focal electrographic seizures (7.1%), generalized spikes (2.3%), and generalized electrographic seizures (2.3%). EEG changes were statistically significant favoring normal EEG in the seizures group (P = 0.0287) and focal slowing and focal electrographic seizures favoring the epilepsy group (P = 0.0008).

Conclusions: The yield of abnormal EEG was low in elderly. If abnormal, generalized slowing was the most common abnormality. Patients with abnormal MRI tended to have epilepsy rather than unprovoked seizures.

Devavrata Sahu, B. K. Bajaj, Jyoti Garg, Ashish Kumar Duggal

ABVIMS and Dr RML Hospital, New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Studies on non-invasive brain stimulation techniques such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) have shown positive results in rehabilitating chronic aphasia after a stroke. However, their effects on acute ischemic stroke patients with aphasia have not been well studied.

Methodology: This was a prospective, double-blinded, randomized trial. Using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 28 patients were enrolled and randomized into two 14-patient groups. One group received 5 days of anodal tDCS to the Broca’s area, whereas the other received sham stimulation. The outcomes were a change in the Accuracy, Reaction Time, and Picture Naming Test (PNT) scores on the Indian Council of Medical Research PNT at 4 weeks after the last session of anodal tDCS.

Results: Both groups had similar baseline characteristics. Naming Accuracy results at 4 weeks after tDCS compared to baseline were statistically significant in the anodal tDCS group (Friedman test, P = 0.002). Reaction time results at 4 weeks after tDCS compared to baseline were statistically significant in the anodal tDCS group (Friedman test, P = 0.001). PNT score results at 4 weeks after tDCS compared to baseline were statistically significant in the anodal tDCS group (Friedman test, P = 0.002). No such results were obtained in the sham stimulation group (P = 0.992). A mixed analysis of variance comparing the anodal tDCS and sham stimulation groups showed a significant effect of both time and stimulation on both groups, eliminating time as a confounding factor (F (4, 104) = 4.27, P = 0.003 for Accuracy, F (4, 104) = 4.47869, P = 0.004 for Reaction Time, and F (4, 104) = 4.42, P = 0.002 for PNT scores).

Conclusions: Transcranial direct current stimulation is helpful in patients with aphasia after acute stroke, but larger studies are needed to confirm these findings.

Sir Gangaram Hospital, New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Autoimmune encephalitis has a subacute presentation with an estimated prevalence of 0.7–12.6 per 100,000 people. However, the diagnosis is hindered by a lack of appropriate investigations. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET–CT) scans can predict the effect of treatment, recurrence, and progression of the disease, with detection of associated neoplasms. Hence, this test is a biomarker of autoimmune encephalitis. The aims of this study were to compare two groups of hospitalized patients: group 1 with PET–CT scans and group 2 with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scans. The clinical spectrum, hospital course, abnormal antibody assay, abnormal imaging, rehabilitation, outcome, and the quality of life after treatment were studied.

Methodology: Two cohorts of 30 hospitalized patients with and without PET–CT scans were included in a retrospective study that spanned 5 years from 2018 to 2023. PET–CT scans were not done in the second group due to delayed presentation, lack of awareness, or lack of resources for PET–CT.

Results: The clinical features, hospital course, and outcome were severe in those whose diagnosis was delayed due to lack of fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)–CT scans (P < 0.001). The sequels were higher in the patient group without PET–CT scans (P < 0.009). Recovery was better in the PET–CT group (P < 0.010). In patients who were not investigated by PET–CT, the clinical features were severe with refractory seizures, behavioral and personality changes, impaired memory, and automatisms.

Conclusions: FDG PET–CT scans are cost-effective imaging modalities which can identify different forms of encephalitis based on specific imaging patterns. This test enables early diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of complications of this dreaded condition.

Guwahati Medical College and Hospital, Bhangagarh, Guwahati, Assam, India

Background and Aim: Myasthenia gravis is a relatively uncommon autoimmune disorder characterized by antibodies targeting the neuromuscular junction. This condition can manifest with drooping eyelids to paralysis of respiratory muscles. In the context of this disease, we only have access to very few studies of myasthenia patients from India. This study aimed to identify the detailed clinical presentation, age of symptom onset, gender distribution, antibody status, thymus abnormalities, and myasthenic crisis in myasthenia patients.

Methodology: An observational, cross-sectional study of myasthenia gravis patients was conducted from May 2022 to April 2024.

Results: Sixty-nine patients with acquired myasthenia were included in the study (37 females and 32 males). The youngest patient was 4 years old and the eldest was 72 years old. Sixty-six (95%) patients had positive neostigmine test. Thirty-six (52%) had generalized myasthenia, 29 (42%) had bulbar symptoms, and 18 patients (26%) had only ocular symptoms. Conclusions: Despite its serious nature, myasthenia gravis responds well to treatment when promptly addressed. The increasing incidence of anti-MUSK antibodies is changing the treatment landscape, with a shift toward the primary use of rituximab. Subasree Ramakrishnan, Suhail A T, Vinod A Prasad

National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences, Bengaluru (NIMHANS, Bengaluru), Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: The burden of cognitive impairment is increasing worldwide. Neurofeedback training (NFT) is emerging as a promising nonpharmacologic intervention for enhancing cognition in healthy and cognitively impaired patients. In this study, we aimed to examine the efficacy of a real-time neurofeedback game using a four-channel consumer-grade electroencephalography (EEG) system on enhancing overt and covert attention skills in stroke and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) patients.

Methodology: The proposed NFT was conducted across 15 patients, which included seven stroke and eight mild cognitive impairment subjects. The game was based on the navigation of a car in a Graphical Use Interface on a computer screen, with the car’s speed proportional to the player’s attention. Sample entropy of EEG signals was the metric for computing attention score. The attention level of the player was computed from EEG signals streamed in real time and was displayed in the form of a progress bar, which acted as feedback to the player. The efficacy of the proposed neurofeedback game was evaluated using different performance measures. Data acquisition, signal processing, attention score computation, and car navigation took place in a synchronized mode as a closed-loop system.

Results: The attention score significantly improved from the first session to the final session by 1.25%–12.55% in the stroke group and 1.84%–44.14% in the MCI group. The cognitive performance and attentional resource index (BATR) also increased in nine subjects from session 1 to session 3.

Conclusions: To our knowledge, this is the first EEG–brain computer interface study for enhancing overt and covert attention in the cross-sectional stroke–MCI patients.

Background and Aim: Peripheral nerve hyperexcitability (PNH) syndromes are an uncommon group of conditions characterized by spontaneous discharges from motor nerve fibers. Government K.A.P Medical College, Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Our aim is to compare the transcranial Doppler (TCD) results with magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) findings in diagnosing intracranial artery stenosis in patients with ischemic stroke involving the anterior circulation.

Methodology: As a prospective study, TCD and MRA were done in 52 patients with ischemic stroke involving the anterior circulation and admitted in neurology department, KAPV Government Medical College for past 6 months. MRA was done by 1.5-T TOF (time-of-flight) method. TCD was done with EMS 9U Shenzen Delica medical equipment, M Mode, 2 MHz probe. Both magnetic resonance imaging and TCD were done on the same day. Kappa coefficient was used to compare the results of TCD and MRA. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were calculated, and MRA was considered as a comparator.

The stenotic vessel identification ability of TCD was sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%, PPV 92.3%, and NPV 57%.

Conclusions: TCD is one of the noninvasive methods to assess intracranial artery stenosis. TCD and MRA have substantial agreement in diagnosing acute ischemic stroke involving the anterior circulation. TCD can be used as a noninvasive diagnostic test to assess intracranial artery stenosis in ischemic stroke involving the anterior circulation.

Background and Aim: A wide range of tasks have investigated the treatment of word-finding difficulties in aphasia. Many researchers have incorporated technology to facilitate self-practice of traditional therapy tasks. However, some therapy tasks are less easily adapted for self-practice by people with aphasia, even with technology. For example, while repetition in the presence of picture (RIPP) can be relatively easily implemented as self-practice, semantic feature analysis is more challenging due to the need for feedback and adaptation depending on the participant’s response. We examined a plausible model for clinical service delivery using two modes of service delivery with two different therapy approaches: a smartphone-based home program using RIPP and clinician-delivered therapy using Semantic Feature Analysis (SFA).

Methodology: We used a single case methodology with six people with chronic aphasia who had a predominant difficulty in picture naming. Participants were given a set of 300 pictures for naming. We had three treatment orders with two participants per order: clinician-delivered treatment (using SFA) followed by smartphone-delivered treatment (using RIPP), smartphone-delivered treatment followed by clinician-delivered treatment, and simultaneous provision of both treatment modes. We analyzed the picture naming results using weighted statistics.

Results: Of the six participants, four showed significant item-specific improvements in naming following smartphone-delivered treatment with three of these participants also showing improvement with the clinician-delivered treatment. There was no significant difference between the tasks for any participant.

Conclusions: This study reinforces the potential for technology-based home practice to improve word retrieval through the use of simple tasks. Such technology-based interventions have advantages over pen and paper “homework” as they allow for (remote) monitoring by clinicians.

The long-term outcomes observed were ongoing epilepsy (73/96), unfavorable motor status (77/96), moderate to severe socio-adaptive deficits (68/96), autism spectrum disorder (47/96), attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (39/96), impaired QoL (78/96), and moderate to severe caregiver burden (79/96). Interictal sleep electroencephalogram showing generalized paroxysmal fast activity was associated with ongoing epilepsy in the last follow-up (P = 0.01). Epilepsy control correlated with motor and cognitive outcomes.

Conclusions: With the increasing survival of children and adolescents with this severe chronic epilepsy, improvement in epilepsy control can translate into better long-term neurocognitive outcomes and improvement in QoL with less caregiver burden.

Background and Aim: Brainstem glioma is a highly devastating disease, and any mass-like lesion in the brainstem can raise suspicion of this diagnosis. Rajarshi Chakraborty, Rajesh Verma

King George’s Medical University, Lucknow (KGMU Lucknow), Uttar Pradesh, India

Background and Aim: Guillain–Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute acquired autoimmune inflammatory disorder of peripheral nerves and roots. The clinical subtype of GBS include acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP), acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN), acute motor sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN), and variants. Respiratory insufficiency is an important predictor of poor prognosis in GBS. We aimed to perform phrenic nerve conduction study (NCS) to predict respiratory involvement and outcome in GBS.

Methodology: A total of 75 patients (including nine coronavirus disease 2019 [COVID-19] +ve patients) of GBS admitted to our hospital over 2 years were thoroughly evaluated with clinical examination, blood tests done in the laboratory, and NCS including phrenic nerve study.

Results: The median age of patients was 31 years (range 1–75 years) with a male:female ratio of 2:1. Subtype analysis showed AIDP (10.67%), AMAN (38.66%), and AMSAN (50.67%). The mean Erasmus Guillain- Barre Syndrome Respiratory Insufficiency Score (EGRIS) score at admission was 3.8 ± 0.17 days and mean Medical Research Council (MRC) score at admission was 30.35 ± 1.80, with the need for ventilatory assistance observed in 24 (32%) patients with a mean duration of ventilatory stay of 23.83 ± 3.50 days. It reduced to 16 ± 3.89 days in COVID-19 patients with GBS due to increased early deaths. Phrenic nerve study corroborated with future requirement of ventilatory support and this was statistically significant. Mortality was observed in eight (10.67%) patients, which increased to two (22.22%) patients in COVID-19 illness, with ventilatory deaths occurring in eight (33.33%) patients that increased to two (50%) in COVID-19 illness.

Conclusions: Respiratory insufficiency and subsequent ventilatory requirement is an important predictor of poor outcome in GBS. Phrenic NCS can be incorporated in routine NCS protocol to provide information about impending requirement of ventilatory support.

Background and Aim: We aimed to assess the clinical profile and precipitating factors in patients presenting with breakthrough seizures in a tertiary care center in northern India.

Methodology: We conducted a cross-sectional observational study in a tertiary referral hospital and research center in northern India involving patients >14 years of age, diagnosed as a case of epilepsy and in remission for at least 3 months and presenting with breakthrough seizures. Results: T2-weighted brain magnetic resonance imaging showed multiple linear hypointensities in the pontine parenchyma. Superoanterior vermian and superior cerebellar peduncle atrophy, as well as mild atrophy of the cervical spinal cord were noted. Nerve conduction studies showed sensorimotor demyelinating polyneuropathy. Genetic testing showed a homozygous, pathogenic variant, c.7504C>T p.Arg2502Ter (73X/74X), on chromosome 13 in the SACS gene.

Conclusions: ARSACS must be suspected in early-onset cerebellar ataxia combined with spasticity and peripheral neuropathy. Typical radiologic features such as superior cerebellar vermian atrophy and linear pontine hypointensities greatly enhance the diagnosis. Ultimately, the diagnosis is confirmed by genetic studies.

Background and Aim: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most prevalent and lethal of the inherited dystrophies. Globally, the incidence is reported at 1 in 3500 live male births. Tirunelveli Medical College, Palayamkottai, Tirunelveli, India

Background and Aim: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and myasthenia gravis (MG) are two autoimmune diseases that have a relapsing–remitting course and positive antinuclear antibodies. SLE can precede or follow the development of MG. Coexistence of SLE and MG is a rare phenomenon.

Case Report: A 33-year-old female patient developed mononeuritis multiplex and was diagnosed with SLE 10 years back. Serum antinuclear antibodies and anti-ds DNA were positive. Anti-cardiolipin and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative. She was treated with six cycles of cyclophosphamide and was put on maintenance therapy with azathioprine, chloroquine, and steroids. She was admitted with slurring of speech, drooping of eyelids, difficulty in swallowing, and difficulty in walking. She had diurnal variations in her symptoms. On examination, she had proximal muscle weakness and signs of fatigability. Oral hydroxychloroquine (HCQS) was stopped, and there was no improvement even after 1 week of discontinuing this drug. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and chest X-ray were normal. Serum creatinine kinase was normal. Nerve conduction studies showed a decremental response of more than 20%.

Discussion: The findings were consistent with neuromuscular junction disorder. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody was positive. She was treated with oral pyridostigmine 60 mg twice daily. Clinical improvement was seen within 48 h.

Conclusions: In conclusion, the association between SLE and MG is complex. In MG patients who had undergone thymectomy, any clinical and serological suspicion of SLE should be carefully evaluated. In lupus patients complaining of decreased muscle strength and fatiguability, the possibility of MG should be ruled out.

Background and Aim: CNS vasculitis is a rare complication of rheumatoid arthritis that is usually seen in advanced burnt-out stages of the disease. Patients may present with strokes, infarcts and hemorrhages with characteristically low CRP and ESR without active joint inflammation.

Background and Aim: Neurocysticercosis is one of the most common parasitic infections of the central nervous system and is caused by the larvae of the tapeworm Taenia solium. Spinal cysticercosis is a rare manifestation of neurocysticercosis, accounting for 0.7 to 5.85% of all cases. Isolated intramedullary spinal neurocysticercosis (NCC) can create challenges in terms of diagnosis and management.

Case Report: A 26-year-old male presented with complaints of backache for 2 months and insidious onset and progressive weakness of bilateral lower limbs for 2 weeks with early involvement of bowel and bladder. Upon neurological examination, the patient exhibited paraplegia with the lower limb muscle power of MRC grade 1 and a sensory level located at T6. Spinal imaging revealed a well-defined cystic lesion, hyperintense on T2 images and complete suppression on FLAIR. The patient was managed medically with oral steroids and anthelminthic drugs, and intensive physiotherapy was advised. The patient showed significant improvement and was able to walk independently within 2-3 weeks. The oral steroid was tapered slowly, and antihelminthics were continued for a period of 6 weeks. The patient improved completely over a period of 3 months.

Discussion and Conclusions: Intramedullary spinal neurocysticercosis is a rare but treatable clinical entity. The treatment includes both medical and/or surgical management. Steroids should be given along with medical therapy as they reduce therapy-associated inflammatory reactions. Surgical therapy is required when patients present with severe and progressive neurological deficits, which do not improve on medical therapy.

Background and Aim: Accidental or intentional ingestion of organophosphate is common in South India, mainly in agricultural community. It can present as acute cholinergic crisis, intermediate syndrome and organophosphate-induced delayed neuropathy (OPIDN). Neuropathy target esterase is thought to be the target of OPIDN initiation. It is characterized by distal degeneration of some axons of both the peripheral and central nervous systems occurring 1-4 weeks after exposures. Here, we describe the case of a 19-yr-old female presenting with OPIDN.

Case Report: A 19-yr-old girl, without significant family history, present with chronic progressive, spastic paraparesis, pure motor with wasting hypertonia hyperreflexia, without sensory, bowel and bladder or other cranial nerves, cerebellar or higher mental function involvement. The total duration of illness is 6 months, preceded by organophosphorus poisoning, with requirement of ventilator support and prolonged intensive care support 6 months prior to the symptom onset.

Discussion: Common etiologies for myeloneuropathy like B12, vitamin E and copper deficiency were ruled out, infectious etiologies like HIV HTLV 1 and Lyme CMV were ruled out, and whole exosome for inherited causes was also reported normal.

Conclusions: It has been proposed that OPIDN is caused by the covalent inhibition of neuropathy target esterase (NTE). For instance, the administration of potent NTE inhibitors in animals causes neuropathy, and mutations of the NTE gene are associated with slowly developing motor neuron disorders similar to OPIDN. The inhibition of the NTE activity by organophosphate may perturb the metabolism of important membrane phospholipids, potentially leading to neuropathy.

Rohan R Mahale, Anudeep Davaluri

National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences, Bengaluru (NIMHANS, Bengaluru), Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Primary hemifacial spasm (HFS) is due to neurovascular conflict (NVC) at root entry zone of the facial nerve. Whether reduction of posterior cranial fossa (PCF) cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volume is a risk factor for HFS is not clear. The study aims at the radiological assessment of PCF CSF volume and its clinical correlation.

Methodology: 50 cases of primary HFS and 50 age- and sex-matched controls were recruited. PCF CSF volume was quantified in 3-T brain MRI (3D-DRIVE seq) using 3D Slicer software version 5.0.3 r30893/7ea0f43. Space between outline of brainstem/cerebellum (inner boundary) and posterior fossa endocranium (outer boundary) was PCF CSF volume.

Results: The mean age at presentation of cases was 50.7 ± 10.7 years (42-69 years), and controls were 52.4 ± 8.7 years (45-68 years). The mean duration of symptoms was 3.5 ± 1.3 years (1.5 to 8 years). About 52% of patients had grade 2 (mild) severity of HFS. The mean PCF CSF volume of patients was 13725.1 ± 909.5 mm3, and controls were 14458.5 ± 973.5 mm3 (p < 0.001). The mean PCF CSF volume of females with HFS was 13714.8 ± 852.5 mm3, and female controls was 14521.8 ± 973.5 mm3 (p = 0.006). PCF CSF volume was significantly associated with the presence of HFS (p = 0.007), the severity of HFS (p < 0.001) and the presence of NVC (p = 0.02).

Conclusions: PCF CSF volume was lesser in HFS patients and was associated with the presence of HFS, the severity of HFS and the presence of NVC. Females with HFS had smaller PCF CSF volume. Small PCF CSF volume is a risk factor for HFS particularly in females with HFS.

Ruchika Tandon Tandon, Ajay Chavan, Varsha Ambwani, Anupama Kaul, Vimal Paliwal

Sanjay Gandhi Post Graduate Institute of Medical Sciences, Lucknow (SGPGI Lucknow), Uttar Pradesh, India

Background and Aim: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) in renal failure patients is bothersome, and there is a limited data on the utility of pregabalin and gabapentin in these patients with comorbid anxiety and depression. Hence, we compared the effect of gabapentin and pregabalin in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients on maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) with restless legs syndrome with regard to anxiety and depression.

Methodology: We classified 100 RLS patients on MHD into anxiety- and depression-based categories and gave them either pregabalin or gabapentin and compared treatment response in them at 3 months using t tests.

Results: Patients on both pregabalin and gabapentin improved significantly at 3 months, and there was no significant difference in between gabapentin and pregabalin. However, the anxiety group improved more at 3 months and gabapentin was better than pregabalin at three months in those with anxiety. Also, there was no significant difference between different age and sex groups with regard to their response to these two drugs at 3 months.

Conclusions: Hence, we concluded that both pregabalin and gabapentin may be equally effective in treating RLS in MHD patients. Gabapentin may be a better choice in the anxious patients.

Rahul Naik, Samhita Panda, Anka Arora, Gopal Krishna Bohra

All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Jodhpur (AIIMS, Jodhpur), Rajasthan, India

Background and Aim: Post-COVID-19 condition, a constellation of cognitive decline, neuropsychiatric manifestations and fatigue has been observed in individuals who have recovered from COVID-19. The extent of affected population and progression of the disorder have been areas of interest.

Methodology: We conducted a prospective observational study at a tertiary care hospital on patients who had COVID-19 infection at least 6 months prior. Cognitive functions, anxiety, depression and fatigue were assessed. P300 was performed, and the same set of tests were repeated after 6 months.

Results: Among 102 patients with history of COVID-19 infection >6 months prior, 38.2%at baseline and 43.84% at 6 months were cognitively impaired. A high incidence of anxiety (80.4%) and depression (69.6%) was found. 46.1% experienced significant fatigue at baseline. 48%at baseline and 61.64% at 6 months had prolonged P300 latency. All scales including frontal assessment battery (FAB), Hamilton anxiety scale (HAM-A), Hamilton depression rating scale (HDRS) and fatigue severity scale (FSS) were found to be more significantly affected in cognitively impaired group (<0.05).

Conclusions: The study underscores those long-term neuropsychiatric implications of COVID-19, including cognitive decline, anxiety, depression and fatigue can present even years after infection and may also worsen progressively. Anxiety was more prevalent in our patients than in previous studies, while depression and fatigue were observed to increase with time in the post-COVID-19 condition. Interestingly, abnormality in P300 latency and amplitude was found even in patients in whom cognitive decline was not found clinically with additional worsening with time.

DR. S N Medical college, Jodhpur, Rajasthan, India

Background and Aim: N-hexane, a volatile organic chemical, is notorious for its neurotoxicity in occupational settings. The early recognition of n-hexane toxicity manifestations is essential to prevent its harmful effects in persons dealing with the substance. We present four patients of polyneuropathy after exposure to hexane by inhalation.

Methodology: Three males and one female, aged between 32 and 45 years, are working in a needle manufacturing factory for the past 10 years. In September 2023, due to malfunctioning of exhaust of furnace burners due to which gas particles of mixture (N-hexane, silicone and isopropylene) could not be burnt out, patient was exposed to gas through inhalation. Results: We found that all patients presented with painful slowly progressive weakness and numbness for 1 month. Cerebrospinal fluid showed albumino-cytological dissociation. Excluding the other possible treatable underlying pathologies, the diagnosis of n-hexane neuropathy was kept based on the occupational history and toxic substance exposure. Patients were managed with symptomatic treatment and had marked clinical and electrophysiological improvement on 6-month follow-up.

Conclusions: N-hexane neuropathy should be considered in a patient with subacute or chronic neuropathy if there is history of prolonged to this chemical in a poorly ventilated workplace.

Background and Aim: Motor neuron disease (MND) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder involving motor neurons. Methodology: This study enrolled 22 patients diagnosed with MND along with 22 healthy controls. Evaluation using the non-motor symptoms score (NMSS) was conducted, and relevant statistical analyses were performed to derive various results.

Conclusions: The higher prevalence of NMSs in the disease group compared to the control group supports the hypothesis that MND may be characterized as a “multisystem disease.” This explains the importance of integrating the evaluation and management of NMSs into a comprehensive and contemporary healthcare approach for individuals with MND.

Background and Aim: Background: Parkinsonism is defined as a clinical syndrome characterized by tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability. Aim: To assess visual, auditory and somatosensory evoked potential in patients with Parkinsonism.

Methodology: This study enrolled 30 patients diagnosed with parkinsonism based on history and clinical examination and 28 healthy controls. All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Bhubaneswar (AIIMS, Bhubaneswar), Odisha, India

Background and Aim: Background: Organophosphorus (OP) compound poisoning clinically presents with acute cholinergic symptoms, intermediate syndrome, and rarely as OP-induced delayed neuropathy and myeloneuropathy. The thoracic cord is predominantly affected. The pathogenesis of this myeloneuropathy in humans is still not well perceived. Aim of Study: To determine the clinical features and predictors of the development of delayed myeloneuropathy in patients with OP poisoning.

Methodology: Patients of OP ingestion with delayed myeloneuropathy, presented to the neurology OPD, were evaluated with detail poisoning history, clinical examination, MR imaging, nerve conduction, electromyography studies, visual, auditory, somatosensory and motor evoked potentials to elicit the pattern of disease manifestation and progression.

Results: Among the 19 patients who were included, 10 (52.6%) patients had consumed chlorpyrifos and permethrin composition. Eleven (57.8%) patients had undergone gastric lavage. Methodology: This was a prospective, double-blind, randomized controlled trial carried out on 34 patients of IIH in a tertiary care center. EEG at onset captured interictal epileptiform discharges and background slowing in 88% and 68%. After treatment with anti-seizure medications (ASM), 44% responded with single ASM, and 28% developed drug-refractory epilepsy required keto diet. EEG was normal in 68% of patients in 1 year of treatment. Outcome was poor in tonic, recurrent non-convulsive status epilepticus. Frequent generalized spike and waves and the presence of generalized paroxysmal fast activity (GPFA) were the EEG features suggestive of a poor outcome.

Conclusions: EMAS-childhood-onset epileptic encephalopathy with polymorphic seizures is often underdiagnosed. Failure to start the early treatment adversely affects developmental outcome. The presence of poor prognostic factors warrants the need for aggressive treatment with appropriate antiseizure drugs and early initiation of keto diet.

SCTIMST, Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, India

Background and Aim: To estimate the prevalence of personality disorders in persons with idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) and to compare it with the general population.

Methodology: The study was conducted in a tertiary epilepsy care center in South India. Study population included 57 normal controls and 57 cases (18 years of age, confirmed cases of IGE). Exclusion criteria included history of any psychiatric disorder or family history of any psychiatric illness. Self-administered questionnaire was used for study data collection. IPDE-ICD10 screening questionnaire was applied to investigate personality traits, and Bear-Fedio inventory (BFI) was used to study different behavior traits in patients with IGE and controls. To compare the prevalence of personality disorders in cases and controls, we applied chi-square test. For ascertaining the relation between different demographic variables with the presence of personality disorders, Pearson’s chi-square test and Fischer exact test were applied. Mann–Whitney U test was used to analyze the significant difference of Bear-Fedio inventory (BFI) scores between cases and controls.

Results: Compared to controls, a higher prevalence of personality disorders was noted among IGE patients (87.72% in cases versus 36.84% in controls). Personality traits like borderline (p = 0.000), anankastic (p = 0.000), anxious (p = 0.000), histrionic (p = 0.000), paranoid (p = 0.098) and impulsive (p = 0.002) were considerably higher in cases with IGE. This was comparatively higher among females (p = 0.034) than males. In BFI also, significantly higher scores were found among cases in all behavioral traits except hypermoralism, altered sexual and aggression.

Conclusions: Personality disorders were significantly higher in cases with IGE. An early intervention in the form of counselling may be considered to improve their quality of life, in addition to drugs, since a majority of them need life-long treatment.

KIMS Hospital, Hyderabad (KIMS, Hyderabad), Telangana, India

Background and Aim: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is known to improve the outcomes of patients experiencing an acute ischemic stroke (AIS) due to large vessel occlusion (LVO). However, despite an endovascular reperfusion rate close to 90%, only half of the patients are functionally independent at 90-day follow-up. Identification of factors influencing clinical outcomes of LVO strokes who undergo MT is essential. This study was aimed to investigate the clinical, radiological and procedural factors that may influence clinical outcomes of LVO strokes treated with MT.

Methodology: In this bispective observational study, 52 AISs with LVO patients who underwent MT were included. IV thrombolysis was done in eligible patients. Patients were divided into good or poor outcome groups according to modified Rankin Score (mRS), good outcome: mRS 0-3, poor outcome: mRS 4-6. Statistical comparison of the clinical (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale [NIHSS score]), radiological (occlusion site, Alberta stroke program early CT score [ASPECTS score]) and procedural factors (IV thrombolysis, time to intervention, thrombolysis in cerebral infarction [TICI score], post-procedure symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage [sICH]) between two groups was done.

Results: Of the 52 patients, 35 (67.3%) had good outcome. Patients with lower NIHSS score (p < 0.04), higher ASPECTS score (p < 0.001) and no post-procedure sICH (P < 0.05) had good outcome. Factors like age, gender, IV thrombolysis, time to intervention and TICI score did not have statistically significant correlation with outcome at 90-day follow-up.

Conclusions: Mechanical thrombectomy had absolute benefit in LVO stroke. Lower NIHSS score, higher ASPECTS score and the absence of post-procedure sICH were reliable predictors of good outcome at 90-day follow-up.

Fortis Hospital, Mulund, Mumbai, India

Background and Aim: AIM: To study the utility of vessel wall imaging in ischemic strokes. BACKGROUND: Conventional imaging techniques are limited to evaluating changes in the vessel wall lumen. High-resolution magnetic resonance vessel wall imaging (MRVWI) can allow visualization of the vessel wall and help differentiating atherosclerotic stenosis from primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS).

Methodology: This was a prospective study in a tertiary care center over 6 months from October 2023 till now. Ten consecutive patients presenting to the emergency room with acute ischemic stroke due to intracranial stenosis were enrolled. Their symptoms, demographic characteristics, comorbidities and relevant investigations (including workup for systemic vasculitis) were noted. MR VWI was done in all patients. All patients were treated according to the standard of care. A follow-up MRI was done on all patients after 3 months.

Results: Seven elderly with focal neurodeficits with comorbidities had eccentric enhancement of luminal stenosis. These patients were diagnosed with atherosclerotic stenosis and treated with antiplatelets, statins and correction of their risk factors. Three young patients had recurrent symptoms without any vascular risk factors and had concentric, homogenous vessel wall enhancement. These were treated as primary CNS angiitis (with systemic steroids/immunosuppressants) and had complete recovery after treatment.

Conclusions: MRVWI should be considered in all patients presenting with ischemic strokes due to intracranial stenosis. It helps to differentiate between vasculitis (concentric) and atherosclerosis (eccentric) stenosis. MR-vessel wall imaging can also be used to monitor the disease activity in the case of primary CNS angiitis.

Background and Aim: Ischemic stroke is a significant health issue worldwide leading to serious long-term disability and is one of the leading causes of mortality. Acute management of stroke is restricted to causative recanalization and restoration of cerebral blood flow. This study was done with an aim to compare the efficacy and outcomes in patients who were given Sovateltide and aspirin with patients given aspirin alone within 24 hours of acute ischemic stroke.

Methodology: A hospital-based prospective study with a sample of 100 patients of 40-90 years was considered, who presented to the hospital within 24 hours of stroke onset. Patients who were given Sovateltide and aspirin were named group S, and patients who were given aspirin alone were named group A. Both groups of patients were assessed using NIHSS, MRS, Barthel’s index at the time of admission, discharge, 1-month and 3-month follow-up, and the scores were then compared.

Conclusions: This study concludes that a combination of Sovateltide and aspirin is a better choice than giving aspirin alone with better reductions in stroke indices in patients presenting within 24 hours of acute ischemic stroke.

ABVIMS and DR RMLH, Baba Kharag Singh Marg, New Delhi- 111

Background and Aim: Alberta Stroke Program Early Computed Tomography Score (ASPECTS) is a noncontrast computed tomography (NCCT)-based topographic scoring system that provides quantitative measure of early ischemic changes. The score was initially developed for evaluating candidacy for stroke thrombolysis, but currently also predicts functional and cognitive outcomes of stroke. The aim of the study is to assess if ASPECTS score at presentation can predict the clinical severity of stroke at presentation and also its functional and cognitive outcome at 90 days after the event.

Methodology: Thirty-five patients with acute ischemic stroke presenting within 48 h of onset were included in the study. National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was ascertained at presentation, and ASPECTS score was calculated (less than 6 and 6 or greater). On presentation, NIHSS score and length of hospital stay were considered to be markers of early severity, and modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores were assessed at 90 days. Patients with MoCA less than 26 were considered to be having post-stroke cognitive impairment.

Results: Correlation between ASPECTS and NIHSS, stay length, 90-day mRS and MoCA were -0.452, -0.632, -0.778, and 0.618, respectively. ASPECTS of less than 6 by univariate analysis was seen to be a risk factor for more severe strokes in acute setting with greater morbidity and cognitive decline at 90 days. Cardioembolic strokes also tended to have greater post-stroke cognitive decline.

Conclusions: ASPECTS score is a surrogate marker of early and long-term stroke severity and its impacts.

Background and Aim: Early initiation and maintenance of anticoagulation appears to be the mainstay of treatment of cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) but the evidence supporting the intensity and duration of anticoagulation is limited.

Methodology: We retrospectively collected data of patients admitted with CVT over a 5-year period, who had a minimum of 6 months of clinical follow-up and three or more prothrombin time international normalized ratio (PT INR) values spread over 6 months. Data collected included demographic, clinical and radiological parameters, anticoagulation status during the follow-up, complications and clinical status at the last follow-up.

Results: We identified 204 patients, and the mean age was 34.4 ± 11.1 years. The majority had a provoked etiology (194, 95.1%) for CVT. Background and Aim: The accessory deep peroneal nerve (ADPN) is an often-overlooked anomalous nerve of the lower limb. Background and Aim: Accidental or intentional ingestion of organophosphate (OP) is common in South India, mainly in agricultural community. Here, we describe the case series of two patients presenting with delayed OPC-induced myeloneuropathy.

Case Report: We are presenting a case series with two patients, a 19-yr old female and 28-yr old male, both the patients with a significant history of OPC consumption and hospitalization in intensive care, with delayed presentation of chronic symmetric progressive bilateral lower limb pure motor paraparesis, with weakness, wasting, hypertonia and hyperreflexia with other CNS examination being normal.

MRI spine in the patients was also not suggestive of structural etiology for myelopathy.

Conclusions: It has been proposed that OPIDN is caused by the covalent inhibition of neuropathy target esterase. Karthika Valaparambil, Sruthi S. Nair, Soumya Sundaram

SCTIMST, Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, India

Background and Aim: Hirayama disease (HD) is a rare disease characterized by asymmetric weakness and amyotrophy of the upper limbs with no objective sensory involvement. Our study aimed to describe the clinical, radiological and electrophysiological characteristics of patients with HD.

Methodology: This is a retrospective observational study of patients satisfying the Haushan criteria of HD registered between January 2013 to December 2023. Data collection included clinical details along with electrophysiological and radiological parameters.

Results: We identified 71 patients, among whom all but one were males. The mean age of patients was 19.1 (±3.86) years. The median duration of illness at diagnosis was 2 (0.3-14) years. The most common clinical presentation in our study cohort was bilateral asymmetric upper limb involvement. Polyminimyoclonus was the most frequently detected clinical examination finding in our cohort. Atypical findings of proximal upper limb involvement and hypereflexia of the limbs were noted. The most frequent electrophysiological abnormality was the reduced CMAP in ulnar nerve. The electrophysiological correlate of the reversed split hand index was observed in 52 (73.2%) patients. The most recurring radiological abnormality in our cohort was thinning of the cord.

Conclusions: Revisiting the atypicalities of this rare disease assumes importance in this era of newer modalities of treatment.

Sri Sai Venkata Haritha Putrevu, Gopi Seepana

Andhra Medical College Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, India

Background and Aim: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive degenerative disorder involving motor neurons in motor cortex, brainstem and spinal cord. In recent times, ALS is known to involve other systems in addition to motor system resulting in non-motor symptoms Aim: (a) To compare the incidence of these non-motor symptoms between limb onset and bulbar onset patients ALS and (b) To explore the burden of Non-Motor Symptoms on quality of life in patients with ALS

Methodology: Patients admitted to neurology department, fulfilling the criteria of ALS, were included. Every patient was asked to report non-motor symptoms during the disease course. Non-motor symptoms were considered significant based on standard scales like hospital anxiety and depression scale for anxiety and depression, Epworth sleepiness scale for daytime sleepiness, numeric pain scale for pain, ALSAQ 5 scores for quality of life. Individuals were subjected to relevant investigations like nerve conduction studies, electromyography, MRI of spine and brain

Results: In total of 18 patients, 15 were male (84%), and 3 (16%) were female. Most had onset in fifth decade (7 patients) with a mean age of onset 50.77. Mean disease duration was 10.7 months. Five patients had bulbar onset, and 13 patients had spinal onset. Itching was reported in one patient with bulbar onset ALS. Tingling was seen in 4 patients and numbness in 2 patients of spinal onset ALS. Executive dysfunction was seen in 6 patients (23% in spinal and 60% in bulbar). Depression was seen in 3 patients of spinal onset and none in bulbar onset.

Conclusions: Varied and few non-motor symptoms are present in each patient. Larger sample is required to define association of non-motor symptoms with severity of disease and any differences between bulbar and spinal onset ALS.

All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Bhubaneswar (AIIMS, Bhubaneswar), Odisha, India

Background and Aim: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune disease affecting neuromuscular junction. 40-60% was associated with sleep disorder breathing (SDB) and restless leg syndrome. Till date, study is sparse regarding relationship between myasthenia gravis quality of life (MGQOL) and polysomnography (PSG) detected sleep disorders. Aim is to evaluate relationship of sleep disorder, sleep parameters with quality of life (QOL) in myasthenia gravis patients. Secondary objective is to know prevalence of metabolic abnormality and its correlation with QOL in MG patients.

Methodology: A total of 21 stable myasthenia patients were included in this prospective study. Basic clinical parameters, demographic profile, thymus status, subjective sleep score (ESS, PSQI), MGQOL, metabolic parameters, PSG detected sleep parameters were evaluated. At 2-month follow-up, subjective sleep score was documented

Results: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) was found in 5 (23.80%) patients and apnea hypopnea index (AHI) (>5/hour) in 6 (28.57%) patients. Periodic limb movement (>5/hour) was found in 6 (28.57%) patients. ESS > 10 was seen in 11 (52.38%) patients, with PSQI > 5 in 14 (66.67%) patients. In MGQOL 15 r score, mean was 7.52 ± 2.73 with highest scoring item “frustration by MG.” In PSG parameters, MG patients are found to be early and light sleepers with reduced REM. Metabolic syndrome was found in 5 (23.80%) patients, but no correlation was found between QOL and subjective sleep score.

Conclusions: Sleep abnormality in the form of decreased sleep latency and REM sleep duration was found in this study. The presence of OSA and AHI >5 positively correlated with poor QOL in stable MG patient. Metabolic syndrome was seen in one-fourth of the MG patients. Metabolic profiles did not correlate with MGQOL score.

Taniya Upadhyaya, Kaavya Rao, Neetu Ramrakhiani

Fortis Hospital Jaipur, India

Background and Aim: To describe the varied clinical presentation, diagnostic modalities and treatment of psoas abscess, a potentially serious condition.

Methodology: We conducted a retrospective analysis of medical records for a series of patients with confirmed psoas abscess who were treated at our institution between October 2020 and May 2024. Demographic data, clinical presentation, diagnostic methods, treatment options and outcomes were analyzed and summarized.

Results: Eight patients were included in the study. The mean age was 55.62 years, and males and females were equally affected. Common symptoms included severe backache not responsive to standard analgesics and diagnostic methods included basic blood workup, ultrasound of local area, MRI of spine/CECT of abdomen. Most patients were treated with IV antibiotics, both empirical and as per culture sensitivity, or ATT as per etiology, drainage of pus collection in most patients and the majority showed improvement after treatment. However, two patients experienced complications during the course of treatment and succumbed.

Conclusions: Psoas abscess is a rare but important clinical entity that requires early recognition and appropriate treatment. Our case series provides valuable information on the clinical presentation, diagnosis and treatment of psoas abscess, which may aid in the management of this condition in clinical practice.

This study aims to assess the role of TNF alfa in diabetic neuropathy patients and how the levels of TNF alfa levels vary with severity of neuropathy in Indian type 2 diabetic subjects.

Patients having neuropathy due to nutritional deficiency, chemotherapy, hypothyroidism and patients with malignancy, pregnancy and autoimmune disease were excluded from the study. 94 included subjects divided into Group 1 (healthy controls, n = 36), Group2 (diabetes without neuropathy, n = 28), Group 3 (diabetes with neuropathy, n = 30).
