TNF alfa levels were measured by using ELISA done in standard kits adapted to Lisa scan (Evolis twin plus, Biorad). All collected data were analyzed statistically by keeping p value of <0.05 as significant.

TNF alfa levels (r= 0.218, p = 0.015). Serum TNF alfa levels are significantly increasing with the progression of diabetic neuropathy indicating the extent of peripheral nerve damage (p value 0.008).

Conclusions: TNF alfa is positively correlated with severity of diabetes. S. TNF alfa level increased in diabetic neuropathy, and it is significantly high in severe DPN patients

ABVIMS & DR RML HOSPITAL, New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute, frequently severe and fulminant autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy. Incidence ranges between 10 and 20 cases per million annually, and cranial nerve involvement ranges from 50% to 75% of patients with GBS. Facial paralysis was reported at a frequency of up to 50%, usually bilateral, and is a poor prognostic indicator. Aim: To assess the incidence of facial paralysis caused by GBS with the clinical and electrophysiological features and outcomes of patients in our study.

Methodology: In a prospective observational study done between November 2022 and April 2024 of a total of 33 adult patients who fulfilled the NINCDS criteria for GBS, clinical and electrophysiological data, including facial NCS, EGRIS score at the time of admission, Hugh GBS disability score and MRC sum score, done on admission and at discharge and finally outcome were recorded.

Results: Cranial nerve dysfunction occurred in 63% of patients. The facial nerve was most commonly involved, followed by bulbar dysfunction, and 3 patients had ophthalmoparesis. Autonomic dysfunction occurred in 6 patients (18.18%). Respiratory difficulty was noted in 7 cases (21.21%), and 4 patients required mechanical ventilation. Facial nerve conduction study was abnormal in 11 (33%) cases), and bilateral, symmetric involvement was present in all cases.

Conclusions: The simplicity of the technique and the information yield is adequate justifications for routine determination of facial nerve conduction in GBS, which can predict impending respiratory insufficiency, higher disability and outcome.

Topiwala National Medical College and BYL Nair Charitable Hospital, Mumbai (TNMC, Mumbai), Maharashtra, India

Background and Aim: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is most common autoimmune disorder that affects the neuromuscular junction. MG is largely treatable disease but can result in significant morbidity and mortality. This can usually be prevented with timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment. Herein presenting the clinical profile and long-term follow-up of MG patients on combination therapy with oral Azathioprine and prednisolone presented to our hospital.

Methodology: Hospital is a tertiary care hospital in Mumbai. In last 5 years, total of 61 MG patients was followed up in immunology OPD. These 61 Patients with acquired MG confirming inclusion criteria were included in study. Variable studied were: age, sex, MG subgroup, MGFA class at onset, peak and last follow-up and treatment details with follow-up of patients on combination therapy with oral azathioprine and prednisolone.

Results: The analysis included 61 (31 males and 30 females) patients. Mean age at onset was 39.6 years. Fifteen (27%) patients were in successful pharmacological remission with prednisolone 0.05 mg/kg/day and azathioprine 1 mg/kg/day 5 (9.25%) patients were in complete stable remission after stopping azathioprine and prednisolone. Background and Aim: Hirayama disease (HD) is typically a progressive focal amyotrophy and weakness of the distal upper limb (s) typically involving C7, C8 and T1 segmental myotomes with sparing of muscles innervated by C5 – 6 myotomes. Epidural venous congestion was noted in all (100%). Maximum detachment was seen at the level of C5, C6, C7

Conclusions: Till date, MRI abnormalities have been described to exist only in the cervical spine. We have now documented that the dural detachment could documented that the dural detachment could involve the entire length of the cord.

Soaham Desai, Devangi Desai

Shree Krishna Hospital, Pramukhswami Medical College, Karamsad, Anand, Gujarat, India

Background and Aim: Pain is a prevalent and disabling symptom in Parkinson’s disease (PD), yet our understanding of its diverse manifestations and underlying pathophysiology remains limited. This scoping review aimed to comprehensively characterize the types of pain experienced in PD and elucidate potential pathological processes driving its manifestation.

Methodology: Adhering to the PRISMA scoping review guidelines, a systematic literature search was conducted across Embase, MEDLINE and Scopus databases. Rigorous screening, data charting and descriptive thematic analysis were performed on the included studies.

Results: The review identified five distinct pain phenotypes in PD: musculoskeletal, dystonic, neuropathic, akathetic and central pain. While the overall mean prevalence of pain was 53.2%, substantial variability (19-83%) existed, influenced by assessment methodologies. Proposed pathological mechanisms centered on central sensitization, peripheral rigidity/dystonia and neuroinflammation. However, a paucity of studies validating these mechanisms through pathology or imaging highlighted significant evidence gaps. Moreover, the delineation between central and peripheral mediators remained elusive, and detailed characterization of non-neurologic comorbidities contributing to pain was lacking.

Conclusions: This review highlights critical knowledge gaps hampering targeted pain management in Parkinson’s disease.

Vignesh Kumar, Rajagambheeran Venugopal

Madras Medical College, Chennai (MMC, Chennai), Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Leukoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter (LVWM) is a disease inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Ovarioleukodystrophy refers to LVWM in females who exhibit signs or symptoms of progressive ovarian failure. We describe LVWM with secondary amenorrhea and infertility in two sisters.

Methodology: Patient 1, a 25/F presented with a 5-year history of difficulty in walking and stiffness of all four limbs. She also had secondary amenorrhea for the last three years. Patient 2, 29/F also had similar complaints from the same age.

Results: On examination, both patients had normal cognitive function. Both of them had spasticity in all four limbs. Power was 4/5 in all four limbs. All deep tendon reflexes were grossly exaggerated. Ankle clonus was present bilaterally. Babinski’s reflex was positive bilaterally. There was mild difficulty in finger nose test and finger finger nose test. Spastic gait was noted. Sensory, autonomic and extrapyramidal examination was normal. Routine blood investigations, TSH was normal. FSH and LH were increased and estrogen and progesterone were decreased. USG’s abdomen showed atrophic uterus and small ovaries. MRI Brain showed diffuse T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving bilateral subcortical, central and deep white matter along frontal and occipital horn of lateral ventricles. Genetic analysis in patient 1 showed homozygous missense mutation in exon 13 of EIF2B4 gene on chromosome 2:g.27364531A>G, with substitution of proline for serine at codon 481.

Conclusions: The possibility of VWMD needs to be considered in adult patients who present with features of leukodystrophy and associated premature ovarian failure.

Pratibha Prasad

All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Patna (AIIMS, Patna), Bihar, India

Background and Aim: Breakthrough seizures are an essential aspect to consider while treating epilepsy. No study has been done on the precipitating factors for breakthrough seizures in the tribal area of Jharkhand. Hence, awareness regarding the possible precipitating factors of breakthrough seizures is vital to prevent their occurrence. AIM: To identify the frequency and precipitating factors for breakthrough seizures in epilepsy.

Methodology: This cross-sectional study was conducted between July 2022 and October 2023 at AIIMS Deoghar, Jharkhand Centre of Excellence for the tribal area in Jharkhand. The study included epileptic patients who had been receiving anti-epileptic drugs for at least six months before the survey.

Results: 300 patients with epilepsy were included. 46% of epileptic patients had breakthrough seizures. Non-adherence to anti-epileptic drugs (p < 0.0001); the number of anti-epileptic drugs (AED) (p < 0.0006), duration of treatment (p < 0.05), level of education (p < 0.04), awareness of triggering factors (p < 0.05) and sleep deprivation (p < 0.05) carried the significant association with breakthrough seizures. In contrast, no association was found with gender, occupation and stress.

Conclusions: Breakthrough seizures are preventable. Hence, there is a need to create awareness of this issue to prevent its occurrence.

Calcutta National Medical College and Hospital Kolkata, West Bengal, India

Background and Aim: The clinical presentation and etiology behind vision loss due to anterior visual pathway dysfunction are numerous and varied. The mode of onset, associated clinical symptoms and neuroophthalmic examination play a critical role in diagnosis. There are ancillary investigations that can support the diagnosis. Literature has scanty data on this topic from eastern India. Hence, this study was taken up with the objective to evaluate the various neurological causes of visual impairment affecting anterior visual pathway and their clinical profile presenting to a tertiary institute in eastern India.

Methodology: INCLUSION CRITERIA: Patients with clinical evidence of anterior visual pathway dysfunction. EXCLUSION CRITERIA: Patients with local ophthalmological causes or posterior visual pathway dysfunction contributing to visual impairment will be excluded from the study. STUDY DESIGN: Institution-based observational cross-sectional study

Results: A total of 56 patients of anterior visual pathway dysfunction were included in our study. Demyelinating optic neuritis (ON) was the most common etiology, observed in 57% of patients followed by AION in 14% and toxic amblyopia in 9% of patients. IIH, infectious neuropathy, non-infectious granulomatous disease, LHON, trauma and CVST were the other observed causes. In the ON cohort majority were idiopathic.

Conclusions: The majority of patients having anterior visual pathway dysfunction had demyelinating diseases. The other important causes were AION followed by toxic and infective optic neuropathy.

Archita Makharia, Divyani Garg, Ayush Agarwal, Ajay Garg, Achal Kumar Srivastava

All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi (AIIMS, New Delhi), India

Background and Aim: SSPE has an expected survival of 3-4 years post-symptom onset. We introduce the term “elite survivors” for individuals with SSPE surviving beyond ten years.

Methodology: We analyzed symptomatology, EEG, anti-measles antibody index, and neuroimaging of “elite survivors” of SSPE at our center, comparing them with ten previously documented cases, to discern patterns in disease progression and treatment response.

Results: We included four patients (male: female = 3:1). Age at presentation ranged from 9 years and at enrolment ranged from 10 to 26 years. The female patient represents the only female “elite survivor.” None had a history of measles infection. Three were unvaccinated against measles. Treatment strategies included combinational intrathecal Interferon alpha and Isoprinosine (two patients), and Interferon alpha alone (two patients). Survival ranged from 10 to 17 years; the 17-year survival is the second longest reported in the literature. All patients demonstrated clinical stabilization with resolution of myoclonus albeit with neurobehavioral issues. Follow-up EEGs were normal for two. CSF analysis showed low titers of persistent measles antibodies in one patient and negative in another. Repeat neuroimaging indicated ongoing white matter changes and brain atrophy in all patients.

Conclusions: This study enriches SSPE literature by examining factors influencing disease progression through the lens of “elite survivors.”

Harpreet Kaur, Sudesh Prabhakar, Kiran Pal Singh, Hardeep Singh, Chasham Mitra

Fortis Hospital, Mohali, Punjab, India

Background and Aim: Cognitive dysfunction and depression are frequently underdiagnosed in type 2 DM patients. Literature suggests that their relation with diabetes control has been insufficiently explored. This study aimed to compare the prevalence of cognitive dysfunction and the prevalence and severity of depression in different groups of patients with type 2 DM, categorized by their HbA1c levels.

Methodology: This observational cross-sectional comparative study included 90 patients with type 2 DM with at least a high school education and proficiency in English. Participants were evenly distributed into three groups based on HbA1c levels (6.5% to 7.0%, 7.1%-9%, >9%). Cognitive function was evaluated using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), where scores < 26 indicated dysfunction. Depression was assessed using DSM-5 criteria and the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) for severity.

Results: The study found that cognitive dysfunction was most prevalent in poorly controlled diabetics (>9% HbA1c), followed by those moderately controlled (7.1%-9% HbA1c), and least prevalent in well-controlled patients (?7% HbA1c). Depression rates were 10% in well-controlled patients, 30% in moderately controlled patients, and 53.3% in poorly controlled patients, with significant differences observed among the groups. Moderate depression was significantly higher in poorly controlled patients compared to others.

Conclusions: Effective glycemic control is crucial in managing type 2 DM and its associated conditions. Regular screening for cognitive dysfunction and depression in these patients is vital for early intervention. The findings highlight the need for interdisciplinary care with early involvement of neurologists and psychiatrists thus improving overall health outcomes in patients with type 2 DM.

Mitul Kasundra

S.M.S. Medical College, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India

Background and Aim: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a chronic encephalitis occurring due to persistent mutant measles virus affecting children and adolescents and manifestations in form of psychiatric, cognitive decline, seizures and movement disorders are prominent. Subsequently, myoclonic seizures usually lead to a final stage of akinetic mutism. Aim: To highlight atypical presentation of SSPE and to create high index of awareness about phenotypic spectrum of the disease especially in developing countries.

Methodology: In this case series, we enrolled five children with subacute sclerosing panencephalitis whose presenting features were less common movement disorders like chorea, parkinsonism and unilateral myoclonus. All children had fulfilled the diagnosis as per modified Dyken criteria and were examined for movement disorders. We also assessed their clinical profile and disease severity via Jabbour staging

Results: out of five children 1 child had chorea, 2 children had parkinsonism and 2 children had unilateral myoclonus. MRI brain of all 4 patients showed T2 hyperintensities in subcortical white matter. EEG revealed periodic high amplitude (200-500MV) complexes in 4-10 seconds interval, nonspecific generalized slowing, frontal rhythmic delta activities. All the 4 patients were subjected to various investigations including viral markers, urinary copper and autoimmune profile. There were no significant differences in laboratory features among children with different movement disorders.

Conclusions: Movement disorders were frequent in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Hyperkinetic disorders were dominant. Movement disorders may manifest even in earlier stages of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis and may be the heralding feature. SSPE is a great mimicker and index of suspicion should be high in appropriate clinical setting.

Arvind Visweshwar, P. K. Murugan, Venkateswaran, Justin

Madurai Medical College, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: We present a case of a pregnant woman who presented with symptoms suggestive of acute CIDP (Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy) but was diagnosed with nodopathy, highlighting the diagnostic challenges and management considerations in pregnant patients presenting with neurological symptoms resembling CIDP.

Case Report: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester developed progressive weakness, numbness and tingling in all limbs over four weeks, consistent with demyelinating polyneuropathy, potentially AIDP. Due to pregnancy, concerns arose about immunomodulatory therapy safety. She received IVIG and supportive care, improving on GBS disability scale. A month later, she relapsed, managed with IVIG again, showing partial improvement. Post-delivery, she presented with acute quadriparesis, neck weakness and hand/leg wasting. NCS indicated nodopathy, not CIDP. MRI showed no significant pathology. Treated with IV rituximab, she significantly improved, regaining full function and 6 months post-therapy she is currently symptom-free and fully mobile

Discussion: Initially, NCS indicated demyelinating polyradiculopathy with prolonged latency and absent F wave. After IVIG, conduction velocity and latency improved. In the second episode, NCS revealed reduced CMAP amplitude and prolonged latency. Postpartum, NCS showed reduced CMAP amplitude with conduction block, suggesting nodopathy. EMG showed fibrillation potentials. CSF was normal, autoimmune profile negative.

Conclusions: This case highlights nodopathy as a differential diagnosis in pregnant patients with CIDP-like symptoms. Tailored diagnostics and therapies are crucial for maternal and fetal well-being. Further research is needed to understand nodopathy’s pathophysiology and optimal management during pregnancy.

Background and Aim: Craniovertebral junction is the most important interface between the skull and the spine, comprising various bony and soft tissue structures. Anomalies of these regions can lead to diverse neurological presentations. Prompt identification and treatment are needed to avoid unnecessary complications. Here, we are presenting a series of patients presented with various neurological complaints and diagnosed to have CVJ anomalies.

Methodology: In the period of 6 months, patients attended to neurology out-patients department were examined thoroughly, and necessary neuroimaging was done. Of these, 7 patients were diagnosed as CVJ anomalies and all of them had different presentations with varied pathology.

Results: Over the period of 6 months, 7 patients were diagnosed to have CVJ anomalies by clinical and neuroimaging. Of these, 2 patients presented with chronic headache, who were being treated as migraine, one patient presented as transient flaccid quadriparesis which spontaneously improved, another with chronic spastic quadriparesis with chronic neck pain, one patient being treated with AED for drop attacks and one patient with multiple cranial nerve palsy. All these patients were initially evaluated for respective common causes and finally diagnosed as CVJ anomalies. These patients were managed with surgery according to need and improved.

Conclusions: CVJ, a distinct ligamento-osseous craniospinal axis structures, possesses unique embryological origins and specific biomechanical requirements. Diagnosing complexities in this region poses a challenge for imaging specialists and neurophysicians.

Vaishakh Anand, Amol Kumar Jadhav

Amrita School of Medicine, Kochi, Kerala, India

Background and Aim: Hereditary spastic paraplegias (HSP) are a group of genetically and clinically diverse inherited neurological disorders characterized by progressive weakness and spasticity in the lower limbs. It can be associated with other neurological or non-neurological symptoms (complicated forms, cHSP) or occur in relative isolation (pure forms, pHSP). HSP is usually reported in adults, and pediatric-onset forms have rarely been investigated in isolation. Our study aimed to explore the clinical, radiological and genetic spectrum of pediatric-onset HSPs in South Indian children.

Methodology: This retrospective chart review was conducted at a tertiary care center between January 2019 and December 2023 in children aged < 18 years with either pHSP or cHSP.

Results: 45 children (62% boys) with HSP were investigated, and genetic causes were identified in 18 children. Mean (SD) age at symptom onset was 3.5 years (1.2 years). Clinical features included: gait difficulty (31/45), delayed motor milestones (20/45), ataxia (6/45), cognitive impairment (5/45), and urge incontinence (6/45). MRI showed white matter changes in 10/45 (22%) and thinning of the corpus callosum in one child. All of them had gradual worsening spasticity, despite treatment. The majority of children had recessive form of HSP with positive family history in 13/45 (29%). SPG11 and KIF were the most frequent autosomal recessive and dominant HSPs respectively. Complicated phenotype was seen in almost half of study cohort.

Conclusions: Our study highlighted the clinico-radiological and genetic heterogeneity of pediatric HSP. High index of clinical suspicion with knowledge of genetic heterogeneity can lead to early diagnosis and timely institution of neurorehabilitative services thereby improving the quality of life in an otherwise degenerative disease.

Thanjavur Medical College, Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Osmotic demyelination syndrome is a rare cause of secondary demyelination. It includes both central pontine and extrapontine myelinosis. Case reports of ODS were reported in the settings of rapid correction of serum osmolality or serum sodium. Here, we are reporting a series of patients diagnosed with ODS with varied pathogenesis and clinical presentations.

Methodology: After obtaining informed written consent, a detailed history and thorough examination were done. Relevant investigations were done. Neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies were carried out.

Results: ODS usually occurs in the setting of rapid correction of serum sodium. In our series of patients, all of them had normal serum sodium at the time of presentation and without prior history of correction. Two patients were alcoholics, one presented as subacute ataxia and dysarthria, and another with acute locked-in state mimicking vascular etiology. One was female, who was non-alcoholic with long-standing poor glycemic control, presented with chronic quadriparesis with dysarthria. All of them were evaluated and diagnosed as ODS based on clinical and neuroimaging and managed conservatively and improved

Conclusions: ODS is rare preventable complication of rapid fluctuations of serum sodium and osmolality. This potentially irreversible complication can be prevented by frequent monitoring of electrolytes. Hence ODS should be suspected in the setting of other precipitating factors like malnutrition and hyperglycemic state, with clinical features of intra-axial involvement.

Background and Aim: This case report highlights a rare and perplexing clinical presentation in a 55-year-old female who presented with a 1.5-year history of progressive weakness in her lower limbs, leading to walking difficulty. Upon examination, the patient displayed spastic quadriparesis, a magnetic gait, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes (DTR) in all four limbs, and extensor plantar responses. MRI brain and spine revealed non-communicating hydrocephalus accompanied by a cystic lesion located at the foramen magnum along with arachnoid webs, adhesions, and arachnoiditis, with associated mild compression of the upper cervical cord. The patient then underwent ventriculo-peritoneal (VP) shunt decompression along with cyst. The cyst excision biopsy report was suggestive of neurocysticercosis. Patient was then started on anthelmintic and steroids, following which patient had significant clinical improvement.

Methodology: Observational study of uncommon presentation of common disease.

Results: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis displayed an unremarkable profile.

Conclusions: This case serves as a compelling illustration of the diagnostic challenges that clinicians may encounter when presented with a rare neurological presentation. Early recognition and treatment of neurocysticercosis are crucial to prevent complications such as seizures and neurological deficits. This case underscores the significance of a multidisciplinary approach involving neurologists, radiologists, pathologist, and infectious disease specialists to accurately diagnose and manage patients with complex presentations.

Ranjot Kaur, Ayush Agarwal, Divyani Garg, Pooja Sharma, Mohd. Wasiq, Roopa Rajan, Ajay Garg, Mohd. Faruq, Achal K. Srivastava

All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi (AIIMS, New Delhi), India

Background and Aim: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is a rare, progressive neurodegenerative disorder with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. It is characterized by six cardinal features: ataxia, epilepsy, cognitive impairment, myoclonus, chorea, and psychiatric abnormalities. The diagnosis is established in the presence of clinical features and heterozygous pathogenic CAG trinucleotide repeats in the ATN1 gene. The onset varies from childhood to old age and is inversely proportional to the number of CAG repeats. Individuals presenting before the age of 20 years typically present with epilepsy, myoclonus, and cognitive impairment, whereas later presentation is associated with ataxia, chorea, and neuropsychiatric symptoms.

Methodology: We present a series of three cases from successive generations in an Indian family.

Results: A 46-year-old gentleman presented with progressively increasing pancerebellar syndrome and seizures (unknown onset to bilateral tonic-clonic) for the past eight years. The seizures were refractory to anti-seizure medications. He had become increasingly forgetful and withdrawn for the past 2–3 years. His father had developed similar complains at the age of 70 years. The patient’s son was suffering from progressively increasing intellectual impairment, behavioral abnormalities, and seizures since the age of 10 years. An MRI brain revealed severe cerebellar atrophy and genetic testing revealed pathogenic heterozygous CAG trinucleotide repeats (CAG repeats – 58; normal: 6–35) on the ATN1 gene. Testing in his father (CAG repeats – 50) and son (CAG repeats – 69) revealed similar findings with increasing number of repeats in successive generations.

Conclusions: A wider gain in understanding is required for such rare neurodegenerative disease.

Believers Church Medical College Hospital, Thiruvalla, Kerala, India

Background and Aim: We report the case of a 63-year-old gentleman k/c/O T2DM, hypertension, who presented initially with imbalance while walking, heaviness of head and numbness for two days. On examination, he had mild gait ataxia and minimal right hand dysmetria. An MRI brain stroke protocol with MRA was normal. Considering a diagnosis of MRI-negative stroke, he was started on dual antiplatelets and statins and sent home. During follow-up, he had persisting heaviness and numbness of head.

Methodology: One month later, he again presented with giddiness and multiple episodes of vomiting. On examination, his GCS was full. An MRI brain with MRA showed acute right pontine infarct and focal moderate stenosis of mid basilar artery.

Results: He was incidentally detected to have syphilis (VDRL+, TPHA+) in October 2023. Retaking history, he was found to have MSM contact history. He was treated with IV penicillin, and antiplatelets were continued. Follow-up VDRL at 6 weeks was negative. APLA remained positive.

Conclusions: APLA should be performed in all syphilis positive patient as it warrants lifelong anticoagulation.

Anupama Gupta, Alka Arya, Arun EV, Gautam Sharma

All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi (AIIMS, New Delhi), India

Background and Aim: Autonomic imbalance associated with increased sympathetic activity and reduced vagal tone has been strongly implicated in the pathophysiology of myocardial infarction and sudden cardiac death. In post-MI patients, reduced heart rate variability (HRV) is a marker for autonomic dysfunction and a strong predictor of increased mortality. Yoga Nidra (YN) modifies the autonomic balance on favorable side through complex interplay between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system. The aim of current study is to explore how autonomic variation on HRV during YN is different from sleep and wake states in post-MI patients.

Methodology: Male patients with coronary artery disease, who were ongoing 24 h Holter recording, were given with YN sessions in the morning hours between 10–12 AM. These sessions were given by a trained yoga therapist, and duration and time for various sections of YN session was noted manually. Sleep was marked on Holter recording according to patient’s sleep log and baseline shift of heart rate. The day time HRV was measured from end of YN session to the sleep onset. HRV parameters during YN, sleep, and wake state were compared.

Results: A total of nine sessions with six male patients with coronary artery disease were recorded during Holter recordings. The mean age of participants was 56.88 ± 7.81 years. Autonomic profile during YN is similar to sleep state, except for a significant reduced in TINN during YN (306.43 ± 108.51 vs. 184.98 ± 107.67, P = 0.041). The percentage of HF is significantly higher during YN sessions compared to wake state (19.67 ± 11.27 vs. 8.45 ± 5.27, P = 0.024).

Conclusions: “Yoga Nidra” effectively modulates autonomic nervous system, and percentages of HF power were significantly increased during YN sessions.

Soaham Desai, Manthan Dave, Sachin Udwani

Shree Krishna Hospital Pramukhswami Medical College, Anand, Gujarat, India

Background and Aim: The thalamus plays a critical role in integrating sensory information. Damage to this region can disrupt normal sensory processing, leading to vivid sensory hallucinations, a phenomenon known as “experiential hallucinosis.” This case report presents an unusual manifestation of this condition, where the patient exhibited self-biting behavior at the onset of a thalamic stroke.

Methodology: A 64-year-old male farmer was brought in after suddenly biting his right hand twice during sleep. According to witnesses, the patient seemed to be in a dream-like state but was alert upon awakening, with no signs of a seizure. The patient reported feeling heaviness in the right half of his body and a sensation of being forcefully held and unable to free himself. He claimed to have bitten his hand in an attempt to free himself from what he perceived as a thief who had entered his room and muzzled him.

Results: Physical examination revealed right-sided sensorimotor deficits. An MRI brain confirmed a left thalamic hemorrhage. Toxicology screening and electroencephalography were unremarkable, and a psychiatric evaluation did not reveal any significant findings.

Conclusions: This case represents an unusual presentation of a thalamic stroke, with self-biting behavior likely triggered by vivid experiential hallucinations. It highlights the potential for thalamic strokes to manifest with complex neuropsychiatric symptoms distinct from typical lacunar syndromes and expands our understanding of the symptomatic presentations associated with disruptions in sensory processing.

Background and Aim: Neurological disorders contribute significantly to maternal morbidity and mortality during pregnancy and the postpartum period, accounting for approximately 20% of maternal deaths. Objectives: To determine the prevalence of neurological disorders among pregnant and postpartum women (up to 6 weeks) and evaluate their association with maternal and fetal outcomes.

Methodology: A prospective cross-sectional observational study was conducted at Shree Krishna Hospital, Karamsad, Anand, Gujarat, India, between September 2022 and April 2024. Background and Aim: We present a rare case of a 65-year-old female who initially presented with ocular symptoms suggestive of myasthenia gravis (MG) but was incidentally diagnosed with papillary carcinoma of the thyroid during diagnostic workup. This case highlights the importance of comprehensive evaluation and interdisciplinary collaboration in managing patients with autoimmune disorders, as well as the significance of considering concurrent pathologies in atypical clinical presentations.

Methodology: A 65-year-old female presented to our neurology clinic with a three-month history of intermittent diplopia and ptosis, particularly worsening with prolonged periods of near vision and alleviating with rest. She denied any difficulty in swallowing, voice changes, or limb weakness. Neurological examination revealed bilateral ptosis, more pronounced on sustained upgaze, and mild limitation of extraocular movements, consistent with ocular onset MG. Acetylcholine receptor antibody testing was positive, confirming the diagnosis.

Results: Given the coexistence of autoimmune MG and the patient’s age, a thorough evaluation for associated autoimmune conditions was initiated. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits, but ultrasound of the neck revealed a 1.5 cm hypoechoic nodule in the right thyroid lobe. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) of the nodule was performed, and histopathological examination revealed features suggestive of papillary carcinoma. Subsequent thyroid imaging demonstrated no evidence of regional or distant metastasis, and the patient was referred to the endocrine surgery team for further management.

Conclusions: Interdisciplinary collaboration and early detection are vital for managing concurrent MG and papillary carcinoma of the thyroid.

Background and Aim: Nasu-Hakola disease, also known as polycystic lipomembranous osteodysplasia with sclerosing leukoencephalopathy (PLOSL), is a rare genetic disorder. It primarily affects the Finnish and Japanese populations. The disease is characterized by early-onset dementia and multifocal bone cysts caused by mutations in the genes TREM2 and TYROBP.

Methodology: We report a case of young onset dementia who turned out to be Nasu-Hakola disease.

Results: A 45-year-old male security guard presented with progressive behavioral changes for 4 years, urinary incontinence for 3 years, and gait disturbances for 2 years. Symptoms included inappropriate smiling, apathy, impulsive behavior, repetitive speech, distractibility, and difficulty recalling recent events. He developed socially unaware urinary incontinence and a dragging foot, stiff-legged gait. Born of a consanguineous marriage, with no family history of dementia or neuropsychiatric disorders, he was conscious but disoriented to time and place, with alopecia, short stature (160 cm), and a MOCA score of 7/30. MRI showed diffuse cerebral atrophy with periventricular T2 white matter hyperintensity and basal ganglia calcification. X-rays revealed fractures and osteoporosis. Whole exome sequencing identified a homozygous TREM2 mutation, diagnosing him with Nasu-Hakola disease. He is being treated with donepezil, memantine, baclofen, physiotherapy, and orthopedic care, with genetic counseling provided to his family.

Conclusions: This case serves as a reminder to clinicians to consider this rare form of dementia in patients presenting with early-onset dementia accompanied by fracture and bony cysts.

Background and Aim: Stroke, an acute neurological syndrome of cerebral vascular origin lasting over 24 h, can stem from either ischemia or hemorrhage. We present three varied presentations of medullary stroke syndromes

Conclusions: Stroke mechanisms in medullary infarction differ between lateral and medial medullary syndromes. Clinical and radiological characteristics, especially perfusion weighted MRI features, are helpful in discriminating the etiologies of stroke in these patients.

Background and Aim: AD and VaD are two common types of dementia in the elderly, with overlapping presentation, and clinical course may lead to diagnostic confusion and prognostic difference. Preclinical studies have shown evidence of several peripheral biomarkers which needs extensive validation in clinical samples in diverse race and ethnicity.

Methodology: In the current cross-sectional study, patients diagnosed with AD and VaD as per standard diagnostic criteria recruited along with age- and sex-matched controls without cognitive impairment were selected from the neurology outpatient department. (microtubule associated protein Tau/ phosphorylated Tau) protein levels from their respective serum samples. The protein levels were measured using Kit based ELISA technique (Elabsciences, China).

Prem Vaijwade

Bharati Vidyapeeth Medical College, Pune, Maharashtra, India

Background and Aim: Post-stroke subjects are likely to have autonomic dysfunction which may predispose them to falls and delay their recovery. If diagnosed appropriate interventions can be provided. To study the prevalence and pattern of autonomic dysfunction (sympathetic and parasympathetic) among patients admitted with acute stroke.

Methodology: A prospective, cross-sectional observational study of acute stroke patients (ischemic and hemorrhagic) was conducted in a tertiary care medical college in Maharashtra from January 2023 to May 2024. Patients were tested at three months follow-up after acute stroke. Patients with recurrent stroke, NIHSS >24, and parkinsonism were excluded. Both arms of autonomic dysfunction were tested – sympathetic (six deep breath tests, standing test, and Valsalva test) and parasympathetic (handgrip test and cold immersion test).

Results: In our study of 43 cases of acute stroke, 72.1% were males. Mean age was 57.12 years. Risk factors were diabetes mellitus (46.5%), hypertension (39.5%), alcohol (32.6%), ischemic heart disease (16.3%), and smoking (14%). Sympathetic dysfunction was observed in 6 (14%), parasympathetic dysfunction was observed in 4 (9.3%), and 4 (9.3%) had both. Cold immersion test and Valsalva tests were the most sensitive tests in diagnosis autonomic dysfunction. Among those with autonomic dysfunction, four out of six (66%) were diabetics, and 1 (16%) had IHD and was not on any alpha blockers nor diuretics.

Conclusions: In our study, the prevalence of post-stroke autonomic dysfunction was found to be 14%. This study highlights the problem of autonomic dysfunction among patients with acute stroke. Further studies need to be conducted to establish post-stroke dysautonomia.

Nischal Yedla, Naveen Kumar Venigalla, Sudheer Penchala Puttiboyina, Krishnaveni Vanapala, Ananya Krosuri

Kamineni health care, Poranki, Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh

Background and Aim: The incidence of stroke in India ranged from 105 to 152 per lakh persons per year over the past 20 years. Sodium and potassium concentration disorders are common electrolyte abnormalities in CVA, potentially leading to mortality if not corrected in time. Data on the prevalence of electrolyte disturbances in stroke patients, particularly in developing countries, is insufficient. This study aims to determine the frequency of electrolyte imbalance in patients presenting with acute stroke at a tertiary care hospital.

Methodology: This retrospective cross-sectional study was carried out in the neurology department at a tertiary care hospital in India from December 2023 to April 2024. A total of 107 patients, aged between 30 and 70 years, diagnosed with either ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke via CT scan or MRI of the brain were enrolled. The biochemical analysis of the stroke patients was conducted as routine.

Results: Out of 107 participants, 61 (57.0%) were in the ischemic stroke group, while 46 (43.0%) were in the hemorrhagic stroke group. The mean sodium level was significantly lower in the ischemic group compared to the hemorrhagic group (128.12 ± 4.30 mEq/L vs.137.45 ± 6.15 mEq/L; P value < 0.0001). Potassium levels were significantly higher in the hemorrhagic group compared to the ischemic group (4.65 ± 1.05 mEq/L vs. 4.02 ± 0.6 mEq/L; P value < 0.0001).

Conclusions: Patients arriving at the emergency department with stroke should be screened for electrolyte imbalance as part of routine investigations. Early detection of serum electrolyte imbalances may facilitate prompt intervention and improved outcomes. Monitoring electrolyte imbalances is crucial to prevent complications and improve prognosis.

U.P. University of Medical Science Saifai, Etawah-26 13

Background and Aim: Drug-induced hepatitis (DIH) following anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) in patients with central nervous system tuberculosis (CNS-TB) remains poorly studied. This research aimed to assess the frequency, spectrum, and predictors of DIH in CNS-TB patients.

Methodology: A prospective study enrolled 104 CNS-TB patients without prior liver disease. Clinical, laboratory, and MRI data were collected. DIH was diagnosed based on transaminase elevation after ATT initiation. Predictors of DIH and its impact on outcomes were evaluated.

Early recognition and management of DIH are crucial for optimizing CNS-TB treatment outcomes.

Shivani Jasti, Sadeesh Kumar V, Shobana N, Socrates M, Sadeeshkumar V, Selvakumar C. J.

Coimbatore Medical College Hospital, 1619 A, Trichy Rd, Gopalapuram, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: NMOSD is a relapsing autoimmune disorder of CNS characterized by core clinical features of myelitis, optic neuritis, area postrema, or symptomatic brainstem syndrome. Despite its recognition as a relapsing disease, the choice of relapse prevention immunotherapy in NMOSD remains controversial. This study aims to analyze the effectiveness of rituximab versus oral immunosuppressive agents (azathioprine and mycophenolate-mofetil) for relapse prevention in a cohort of NMOSD patients.

Methodology: Ten NMOSD patients fulfilling Wingerchuck criteria were analyzed for demographic information, clinical presentations, and the various treatment strategies employed. All the patients were started on steroids as initial therapy and either rituximab or oral immunosuppressive agents as maintenance therapy. Clinical improvement was determined by EDSS scale, and the patients were followed up for development of relapse.

Results: Our cohort consisted of 10 NMOSD patients with mean age of 36 years with 90% females. The initial clinical presentation was myelitis in 40%, optic neuritis in 30%, and area postrema syndrome in 30%. Relapsing disease was present in 60%, and the mean number of relapses was 2. Among steroid sparing maintenance therapies tried, rituximab was used in 80%, azathioprine in 30%, and mycophenolate-mofetil in 30%. One out of eight patients (12.5%) receiving rituximab experienced a relapse within the first three years of treatment vs three out of 3 (100%) patients receiving azathioprine and two out of three patients (66.6%) receiving mycophenolate-mofetil. All the patients on azathioprine and one out of three patients on mycophenolate-mofetil who experienced a relapse were eventually started on rituximab therapy, none of whom developed a further relapse.

Conclusions: Rituximab significantly lowered NMOSD-relapses when used as initial therapy as well as rescue therapy in individuals who failed to respond to oral immunosuppressive agents.

Methodology: A total of 429 consecutive patients were included in the study who underwent DSA for any indication by a single neurologist with expertise in stroke and neurointervention. Patients with incomplete imaging, total occlusion of vessel, severe vasospasm, and moyamoya disease were excluded from the study. DSA images were acquired via transfemoral approach with a 5 Fr catheter in a fully equipped DSA unit.

Results: Normal and variation pattern of arteries were found in 45.69% and 54.31% of the subjects, respectively. Fetal PCA was observed in 82 (21%) subjects, and 23% of these subjects had bilateral fetal PCA. Hypoplastic and aplastic ACA was observed in 11.93% and 5.1% subjects, respectively. Azygous and accessory ACA were only observed in 4 and 2 subjects, respectively. MCA trifurcation was observed in 41 subjects (10.4%), among these only four subjects had bilateral MCA trifurcation. Fenestrations were observed in seven subjects (1.77%), most commonly seen in BA (3 subjects). Dolico-ectasia of BA was observed in five subjects. Infundibular PCOM was reported among 3.05% of the subjects.

Conclusions: Fetal PCA, hypoplasia, or aplasia of proximal anterior cerebral artery (A1) were the most common anatomical variations.

Background and Aim: There is paucity of randomized controlled trials comparing the outcome benefit of beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker in acute stroke. We compare the effect of metoprolol and amlodipine in reducing mortality, disability, and infections in acute stroke.

Methodology: This is an open-labeled randomized controlled trial conducted in a single institution. CT/MRI confirmed stroke patients within three days of onset were included whose age was 18 to 75 years. The patients with secondary intracerebral hemorrhage, organ failure, pregnancy, malignancy, immunosuppressant or already receiving beta-blocker/amlodipine were excluded. Stroke risk factors, Glasgow Coma scale (GCS) score, National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score, and CT/ MRI findings were noted. The patients with a blood pressure of >160/90 mm of Hg were randomized using 1:1 randomization to metoprolol (25 mg on day 1, 50 mg from next day) or amlodipine (2.5 mg day 1, 5 mg on day 2, subsequent increase was optional). Other standard treatment was continued. Primary outcome was in-hospital death, and secondary outcomes were in-hospital gastrointestinal hemorrhage, pneumonia, sepsis, and three months functional outcome based on modified Rankin scale (mRS). Side effects were noted.

Results: A total of 18 (14%) patients died; 6 (9.8%) in metoprolol and 12 (14%) in amlodipine (P = 0.20) group. At three months, 45 (80.4%) in metoprolol and 21 (43.3%) in amlodipine group had good outcome (P < 0.001). The other secondary outcomes were comparable between the two groups. Metoprolol was withdrawn in six patients due to bradycardia and amlodipine in one due to allergic reaction.

Conclusions: Metoprolol is associated with disability benefit in acute stroke compared to amlodipine.

KIMS Hospital, Hyderabad (KIMS, Hyderabad), Telangana, India

Background and Aim: Advancements in robotics are expected to have broad and important implications in neuro-rehabilitation. However, these advancements will be accompanied by ethical implications like – anonymization to safeguard patient data and privacy. Ethical frameworks may ensure accountability from healthcare institutions and professionals thus making the process transparent to patient. Aim: To understand the expectation of robotic rehabilitation from the stake holders of rehabilitation – Patient, therapists, and physicians.

Methodology: A survey of professionals in area of rehabilitation about their point-of-view on ethics in rehabilitation and assistance robotics was conducted at a tertiary referral center in South India. An electronic survey was designed using Google Forms and in-person interview. One-hundred and seventeen responses were received. The average age of the respondents was 43.72 ± 34 (23–64) years. The respondents included 42 patient/caregivers, 38 rehabilitation therapists, 24 physicians, and 13 device manufacturing companies.

Results: The most frequent reported lacunae in ethical considerations from the various sub-groups of respondents were as follows: • Patients – Lack of sufficient patient education about factors like contraindications and cautions to be taken (78.2%) and concerns about cost (71.3%). • Rehabilitation therapists – Lack of well-defined aims and objectives for rehabilitation robotics (88.7%). • Device manufacturers – limited understanding of requirements (software and safety) to implement ethical guidelines (100.0%). • Healthcare providers/Physicians – staffing issues as robotics require specialist training (64.3%), followed by logistical issues like data security and adaptability (58.2%).

Conclusions: Current survey highlights on position of various stake holders of rehabilitation toward robotics in rehabilitation. While patients report lack of awareness, healthcare providers state logistics and ambiguous objectives as lacunae in ethics.

This study aims to determine the prognostic value of serum albumin levels in acute ischemic stroke by co-relating its levels with clinical outcome.

Methodology: This study has been conducted in a tertiary medical college, western Maharashtra. It is an observational study conducted for 12 months. The patients of acute anterior circulation ischemic stroke were evaluated. NIHSS at admission was calculated and serum albumin levels were measured within 24 h of admission. The functional outcome was evaluated using modified Rankin scale (mRS) at day 30 and day 90.

Results: There were total of 90 patients with the mean age 55.4 + 14.21 years. There were 61 males (67.78%). The comorbidities associated were hypertension (50%), DM (46.67%), ischemic heart disease (18.89%), and smoking (45.56%). The mean albumin was found to be 4.007 ± 0.5524 (range from1.8 to 5.0 mg/dL). Pearson’s correlation test of albumin and mRS at one month was −0.162, and P value was 0.128; correlation of mRS at three months was −0.198, and P value was 0.061.

Conclusions: Our study was a prospective observational study which showed that low albumin levels are associated with poor functional outcome, and better outcome was observed in higher serum albumin levels.

Background and Aim: Hirayama disease (HD) is a rare disease predominantly causing distal atrophy of the upper limbs. It mainly affects the male in their second or third decade. Mary Iype, Anitha Ayyappan, Bineej B. Jayan, Suresh A. Poovathinal, Ismail Thanseem

Government Medical College Trivandrum, Kerala, India

Background and Aim: The genetic architecture of epilepsy is highly complicated. Specific EEG abnormalities have been observed in epilepsy. Photoparoxysmal response (PPR), often observed in epileptic disorders, is an abnormal cortical response to photic stimulation manifesting as specific EEG changes and is highly heritable. PPR is a potential endophenotype for the mapping of epilepsy genes. Here, we have conducted a whole exome sequencing (WES) study of epilepsy patients with PPR in a South Indian population, in an attempt to identify the genetic causes of PPR.

Methodology: The study design was exploratory and descriptive. Twenty-eight patients with epilepsy, exhibiting Grade-4-PPR, were recruited for the study. WES was performed for all the participants.

Results: Eleven children with primary generalized epilepsy-PPR, 15 with epilepsy with eyelid myoclonia-PPR, and two with focal epilepsy and PPR participated in the study. Among the genes in the cohort that harbored rare and pathogenic variants (n = 1628), 190 genes have been reported previously in epilepsy. Among the protein products of the candidate genes, IGSF3 is known to bring about hyperexcitability of neurons, CTDSP2 regulates the development of neural progenitor cells, and SETD8 is involved in neural stem reactivation. The PPR candidate genes were enriched in pathways involved in extracellular-matrix-receptor (ECM-receptor) interaction and focal adhesion. The “epilepsy genes,” in particular, were enriched in pathways involved in neurodevelopment and biological processes related to ion transport. The expression of these gene products is also abundant in brain and retina. Apart from epilepsy database, the candidate genes are also enriched in gene-databases associated with intellectual disability, global developmental delay, cognitive delay, and autism spectrum disorder.

Conclusions: This genetic analysis of PPR should trigger studies that finally unravel the genetic etiology of primary generalized epilepsy.

Background and Aim: Epilepsy is one of the most common neurologic disorders faced by neurologists worldwide. Aim: This study aims to compare the occurrence and localization of interictal and ictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) and epileptic seizure patterns (ESPs) in suspected focal epilepsy with the localization of MRI lesions.

Methodology: After informed consent, detailed medical history will be noted. All EEG recordings were performed with electrode placement according to the 10–20 system. Results: In patients with temporal lesions, the localization of interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) was most congruent, with 60% of patients showing IEDs exclusively over the lesional lobe. Background and Aim: Primary progressive aphasias (PPAs) are a group of neurodegenerative diseases with early and prominent speech and language impairment, with relative preservation of cognition and without behavioral abnormality. PPA is viewed as a part of fronto-temporal dementia. It consists of three variants – nonfluent/agrammatic variant (naPPA), logopenic variant (lvPPA), and semantic variant (svPPA).

Methodology: We prospectively identified three patients with PPA and report their history, clinical examination, and radiological data.

The patients with naPPA presented with difficulty in speaking with effortful and halting speech, suggestive of apraxia of speech. Patients with lvPPA presented with word-finding difficulties with preserved single-word comprehension. Detailed higher mental function supported the diagnosis of predominant impairment in the language domain with relative preservation of other cognitive domains. Apraxia battery test was conducted in one patient with naPPA which suggested buccofacial apraxia. Brain imaging was suggestive of cortical atrophy predominantly in the fronto-temporal lobe in all three patients. PET-CT of one patient with naPPA showed bilateral fronto-temporal hypometabolism. Histopathological evidence or genetic testing of known pathogenic mutation was unavailable for any patient. All three patients were managed conservatively, including referral for speech therapy.

Conclusions: A high degree of suspicion is required for diagnosis which is based on history and clinical examination, including a detailed higher mental function examination. Patients with PPA should be managed with speech and occupational therapy to enable them to carry out activities of daily living.

Background and Aim: ANODYNE study showed that the greater occipital nerve block (GONB) for episodic cluster headache (ECH) was effective. Here, we report the results of the secondary outcome measures. Objective: To study the efficacy of GONB in improving the pre-specified secondary outcome measures.

Methodology: ANODYNE was a randomized, double-blind, and placebo-controlled trial in ECH patients diagnosed by ICHD-3 criteria who received active GONB (2 mL methylprednisolone [80 mg] and 2 mL lignocaine [2%]) or placebo (4 mL saline injections). The secondary outcome measures included mean change in attack duration, severity, requirement of repeat GONB, verapamil dose, changes in cranial autonomic symptoms (CAS), and severity of restlessness. Efficacy analyzes were performed at week 4 in a modified intention-to-treat population using a generalized linear model. The trial was registered with the Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI/2021/21/038397).

Results: Thirty-nine (19 in the active group and 20 in the placebo group) were available for efficacy analysis. The change in attack duration and severity was −18.8 (95% CI: −29.7 to −7.9; P = 0.001) and −2.3 (95% CI: −4.1 to −0.4; P = 0.019), Respectively, favoring the active group. The mean verapamil dose was lower in the active group (−96·6; 95% CI: −191·5 to −1·8; P = 0.046). Five patients receiving placebo and none receiving active GONB required a repeat injection (27.8% vs. 0%; P = 0.022). The mean CAS/attack duration was lower in the active group compared with placebo (−32.8 vs −22.3; −10·5 (95% CI: −15·9 to −5·1); P = 0.001). The active group had fewer attacks between Day 1–3 and Day 1–28 (−0·9 and −11 attacks, respectively) and a significant reduction in the severity of restlessness (−0·4; 95% CI: −0·7 to −0·03; P = 0.036).

Conclusions: GONB resulted in significant improvements in multiple secondary outcomes for ECH patients.

Methodology: This was a single-center study where adults between the age groups of 12 and 80 years who had neurologic symptoms and pachymeningeal enhancement on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain/spinal cord retrospectively, over the past 2–3 years, from the electronic database of the institute from the department of neurology, and followed for 5 years from when they were diagnosed. The characteristics of patients, including demographics, clinical features, laboratory data, radiological features, risk factors, and response to treatment were analyzed.

Results: Headache, cranial nerve palsies, and seizures were common symptoms. Cases of hypertrophic pachymeningitis mimicking spinal meningiomatosis, cavernous sinus syndrome, Tolosa–Hunt syndrome, jugular foramen syndrome, meningioma, and hyperostosis are presented.

Conclusions: Ours is an attempt to alert the treating physicians and surgeons about atypical presentations of hypertrophic pachymeningitis in clinical practice to avoid undue complications. In patients with chronic headaches who do not respond to conventional treatment, neuroimaging should be conducted to rule out pachymeningitis.

Background and Aim: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) occurs due to abrupt spontaneous leakage of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) outside of its anatomical space (vascular/extradural). It is commonly due to disc disease causing rent in the meninges or a fistula formation, leading to the draining of the CSF in the venous network. SIH is an extremely rare presentation that is characterized by orthostatic headache, diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), with magnetic resonance (MR) myelography identifying CSF leak in most cases.

Case Report: A 49-year-old diabetic hypertensive male patient presented with acute-onset severe dull aching pain in the occipital region radiating to the neck that appeared on the erect posture and disappeared in the supine position. On examination, no neurological deficiency was present. An extensive workup was inconclusive, except for a diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement in the MRI brain and mild sagging. By the second week of presentation, the patient had developed tinnitus and aural fullness.

Discussion: MR myelography of the whole spine was conducted that revealed an epidural CSF collection at 4th to 6th cervical vertebral levels with a focal collection in the posterior paraspinal muscles due to a possible dural defect. The patient was then treated with an epidural blood patch repair that resolved his symptoms and he was discharged without any complications.

Conclusions: SIH is a rare but possible cause of orthostatic headache that may be lethal if early intervention is not done.

Background and Aim: Leukodystrophies are a rare heterogenous group of disorders characterized by central nervous system white matter degeneration. Background and Aim: Multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN) is an immune-mediated disease entity, characterized by progressive asymmetrical weakness and atrophy without sensory involvement. Chebolu Harshika, Randhi Venkata Narayana, Puvvada Srikar, Amarapu Sravanthi

Sevenhills Hospital, Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, India

Background and Aim: Stroke contributes to a significant proportion of mortality and disability globally. There is an increasing need to identify better prognostic indicators. Our study aims to determine the predictive value of the Inflammatory Prognostic Index (IPI) and Atherogenic coefficient (AC) as prognostic indicators in acute ischemic stroke, and correlate these indices with outcomes.

Methodology: A retrospective analysis of 254 patients admitted with acute ischemic stroke between January 2023 and January 2024 was performed. Data including comorbidities, NIHSS score at admission, lipid profile, blood counts, C-reactive protein (CRP), serum albumin, and modified Rankin Score (mRS) at discharge were obtained. IPI= CRP * neutrophil–lymphocyte ratio/serum albumin level. AC = (serum total cholesterol–serum HDL cholesterol)/serum HDL cholesterol. Patients were classified into mild stroke (NIHSS score-5).

Results: Of the 254 patients, 39% had a mild stroke and 96.2% of patients had comorbidities. The IPI and AC values were significantly higher in the moderate-to-severe group (P-value < 0.05) as compared to the mild stroke group (median values of IPI [1.72 vs. 1.14] and AC [2.5 vs 2.01]). Higher IPI values were shown to be associated with prolonged duration of hospital stay and poor outcomes, whereas AC values did not show such a correlation.

Conclusions: IPI and AC are easily accessible blood parameters, without subjective bias. Including these indices in routine practice helps in risk quantification and prognosis assessment in patients with stroke.

Background and Aim: Pregnancy increases the risk of acute ischemic stroke (AIS) among young women and is responsible for maternal deaths and significant disability. Background and Aim: Young stroke is an emerging problem in India, where the increase in standards of living is leading to an ocean of lifestyle-related disorders. Background and Aim: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) is the most recently defined inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (CNS). The clinical spectrum of MOGAD is expanding with case series and reports. This study aimed to report the clinical profiles, imaging characteristics, and treatment outcomes of MOGAD in our center.

Background and Aim: Vasculitic neuropathies are a heterogeneous group of peripheral nerve disorders that can be either systemic or non-systemic. Most patients present with mononeuritis multiplex, requiring high clinical suspicion for proper diagnosis and management.

Case Report: This case series details five patients diagnosed with vasculitic neuropathy. Two patients presented with burning pain in the ankles, palms, and feet, along with walking difficulty and trouble holding slippers for 2 months. Examination showed hip power of 5/5, knee power of 4/5, and ankle power of 1/5, with absent knee and ankle jerks. Sensory examination indicated reduced pain perception. NCS revealed bilateral sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy. Elevated CRP and ESR were noted; ANA and ANCA were negative. A nerve biopsy confirmed vasculitic neuropathy. Two patients presented with numbness in the left foot, extending to the ankle, and later the right foot. They experienced difficulty holding objects and walking. Examination showed 4+ power in the upper limbs with finger clawing, and 4-/5 in the hip and knee, and 0/5 in the ankle. NCS showed bilateral sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy. Elevated CRP and ESR; ANA IF and anti-CCP were positive. A 65-year-old male patient reported numbness and weakness in his hands and feet over several months. Examination showed 4+ power in the upper limbs and 4-/5 in the hip and knee, with absent ankle jerks. NCS indicated bilateral sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy. Elevated CRP and ESR; pANCA was positive. A nerve biopsy confirmed vasculitic neuropathy.

Discussion: All five patients underwent extensive blood panels, autoimmune and serological tests, and NCS. Four patients had biopsy-proven vasculitic neuropathy.

Conclusions: Vasculitic neuropathy should be suspected in patients presenting with mononeuritis multiplex over weeks to months. High clinical suspicion is essential for the diagnosis and management to prevent complications and morbidity.

Pradeep Kumar, Manyata Srivastava, Annu Gulia

All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi (AIIMS, New Delhi), India

Background and Aim: Atrial fibrillation (AF) poses an increased risk of stroke, prompting the emergence of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) as a treatment option for stroke prevention. We aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy of different DOACs compared to vitamin K antagonist (VKA) in preventing strokes among patients with AF through a network meta-analysis.

Methodology: A thorough search on PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane databases up to March 31, 2024, for published randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing the risks of stroke and systemic embolism among different DOACs with VKA was conducted. A pooled risk ratio (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) was calculated using a frequentist network meta-analysis.

Results: A total of 22 RCTs that compared the efficacy of various DOACs with VKA in preventing strokes among patients diagnosed with AF were included. No significant variations in major bleeding were observed between each DOAC and VKA (RR = 1.05, 95% CI; 0.97 to 1.13). Dabigatran (RR = 0.78, 95% CI; 0.68 to 0.89), apixaban (RR = 0.81, 95% CI; 0.71 to 0.92), and edoxaban (RR = 0.79, 95% CI; 0.69 to 0.90) exhibited significantly lower risks of intracranial hemorrhage compared to VKA (RR = 1.15, 95% CI; 1.03 to 1.29) and rivaroxaban (RR = 1.13, 95% CI; 1.01 to 1.27) showed similar risks. High-dose regimens were associated with reduced risks of stroke or systemic embolism compared to VKA and low-dose regimens, with both dosage levels presenting similar bleeding risks.

Conclusions: Our findings underscore the potential benefits of DOACs over traditional VKA therapy in the management of AF, particularly in reducing the risk of intracranial hemorrhage. However, individual patient factors and preferences should be considered when selecting the most appropriate anticoagulant therapy.

Background and Aim: Central nervous system complications of dengue include encephalopathy, meningoencephalitis, and intracranial hemorrhage. However, the involvement of the spinal cord is uncommon. Institute of Post Graduate Medical Education and Research, Kolkata (IPGMER Kolkata), West Bengal, India

Background and Aim: Cognitive dysfunction and mental health problems have been frequently reported in research investigating the long-term effects of COVID-19. However, standardized cognitive tests are often not sensitive to subtle cognitive changes, creating a hurdle for early detection of cognitive decline. In this work, we paired standardized tests with higher-order cognitive tests focusing on pragmatic processing.

Methodology: A total of 376 COVID-19 patients were interviewed via telephone. In-person interviews with 99 COVID-19 patients and 31 matched controls were conducted as part of a more thorough examination. Participants were administered regular standardized tests and higher-order cognitive tests. Voxel-based morphometry and vertex analyses were conducted using the FSL software.

Results: In all, 64.89%, 44.95%, and 41.49% of COVID-19 patients reported a deterioration in physical functioning, mental health, and cognitive abilities, respectively. They had an increased risk of depression, anxiety, stress, and insomnia. COVID-19 patients who had depression and anxiety were 8.6 and 19.4 times more likely to have cognitive decline, respectively. Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had reduced gray matter volumes in the frontal mid-orbital R (P =0.015), frontal superior orbital R (P = 0.018), rectus R (P = 0.015), rectus L (P = 0.025), and right amygdala (P = 0.047). Most patients who had difficulty in figurative language processing (P < 0.05) despite scoring above the cut-off on the standardized cognitive tests, reported a considerable decline in their cognitive abilities after a gap of 1 year.

Conclusions: Higher-order cognitive tests might be a marker of early cognitive decline. Incorporating these tests into the dementia assessment protocol might help identify patients who may go unnoticed if we depend too much on standard screening measures.

Background and Aim: The aim of the study was to determine whether primary headaches such as migraine with or without aura and trigeminal autonomic cephalgia (TAC) have altered anterior and posterior circulation cerebrovascular hemodynamics and reactivity changes compared with the control group as assessed by transcranial Doppler (TCD) during an interictal period.

Methodology: A total of 25 patients (17 females, 8 males) with a mean age of 34 ± 10 were evaluated during an interictal period: migraine without aura 12 (48%), migraine with aura 10 (40%), and TAC 3 (12%). They were compared with 25 age- and sex-matched controls. Each participant was examined with a 2 MHz probe power mode B TCD of the middle, anterior, and posterior cerebral and vertebral arteries and basilar artery during the interictal period. The indices measured were mean flow velocity, peak systolic velocity, Pulsality Index, and Breath Holding Index.

Results: A significant difference was present between bilateral anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral and vertebral arteries, basilar artery mean flow velocities and peak systolic velocity, Pulsality Index between migraine with or without aura and in patients with a trigeminal autonomic cephalgia versus normal controls (P < 0.05). There was also a significant increase in vertebral, basilar artery cerebral blood flow velocities relative to controls and migraine with or without aura versus in patients with trigeminal autonomic cephalgia (P < 0.05).

Conclusions: The possibility of cerebrovascular changes is confirmed in the present study in patients with primary headaches versus healthy controls during the interictal period. The hypothesis of pathophysiology of primary headache with vascular hemodynamics changes was correlated with the non-invasive transcranial Doppler with this study.

All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi (AIIMS, New Delhi), India

Background and Aim: Cerebral nocardiosis is a rare entity characterized by brain abscesses with non-specific symptoms that often elude timely diagnosis, leading to a high mortality rate.

Case Report: We report the case of a 69-year-old non-diabetic male patient presenting with persistent headache and right eyelid pain, swelling, and proptosis over 4 years, without visual disturbances or a history of an immunocompromised state. Initial fine-needle aspiration cytology suggested nodular fasciitis; however, as symptoms worsened a repeat biopsy was conducted that suggested pseudo papillomatosis hyperplasia of the epidermis. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed an inflammatory lesion encompassing the bilateral orbital apex and surrounding sinuses, raising the possibility of IgG4 disease. However, as IgG4 was within normal limits, he did not receive steroids as the diagnosis was doubtful. A year later, another biopsy of the right orbit showed brownish-black refractile material, suggesting a fungal pathology. Despite the administration of voriconazole, the patient’s condition deteriorated. He returned 8 months later with reduced verbal output, altered sensorium, and pus discharge from eyes and was found to have extensive subdural empyema with a right temporal abscess. He underwent decompressive craniectomy and expansion duroplasty, wherein intraoperative samples confirmed nocardiosis. He subsequently developed hydrocephalus, for which an external ventricular drain was inserted. Despite management with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), imipenem, and supportive care, the patient succumbed to his illness.

Discussion and Conclusions: Nocardiosis, although rare, should be considered in progressive rhinosinusitis unresponsive to treatment. Differentiating nocardiosis from other pathologies is critical, as each requires distinct management. Employing meticulous microbiological techniques, including acid-fast staining, is crucial for timely and accurate diagnosis, given the high mortality associated with cerebral nocardiosis.

Prion-associated rapidly progressive dementia was observed in two (6.6%) patients. The most commonly associated additional symptoms were seizures (40%), followed by psychiatry manifestations (33%). Radiology abnormality (MRI + PET) was observed in 26 (86%) patients, which helped with the diagnosis. The mean age of presentation was 45.6667 ± 11. 476 years. There was equal sex predilection with 15 males and 15 females.

Conclusions: Rapidly progressive dementia is an emergency in cognitive neurology. We feel that many patients have treatable or reversible causes. Ajaya Biswal, S. Saravanan, Birla Pavalam, Sankar Narayanan

Tirunelveli Medical College Hospital, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: The potential role of hypertriglyceridemia as an independent risk factor for ischemic stroke remains controversial. However, accumulating evidence has shown that hypertriglyceridemia is associated with pathophysiological processes such as endothelial dysfunction, atherosclerosis, and the production of a prothrombotic state, which could contribute to ischemic stroke. Our aim is to assess early in hospital recovery patterns of patients of acute ischemic stroke in relation to triglyceride level.

Methodology: This cross-sectional analytical study was conducted in 110 cases of acute ischemic stroke on patients in the age group 18 to 80 years between August 2023 and March 2024. The severity of stroke was assessed by the NIHSS score, GCS, and clinical neurological examination at the time of admission. Baseline information was collected. All risk factors for ischemic stroke such as hypertension, DM, chronic alcohol intake, and smoking were recorded. Fasting triglyceride (TG) level was conducted on the next day. Hypertriglyceridemia was defined as having a TG level >150 mg/dL. Patients were classified according to TG levels as 1) <150 mg/dL, 2) 150–250 mg/dL, 3) 250–350 mg/dL, and 4) >350 mg/dL. Patients’ neurofunctional status was assessed at the time of discharge using the MRS scale and their relationship with different ranges of TG level was studied by regression analysis.

Results: In all, 110 patients were included with a mean age of 71 years in this study. Also, 69% of patients had hypertriglyceridemia. In the bivariate analysis, an unfavorable outcome was more frequent in older patients, with higher admission NIHSS score, and serum triglyceride levels of more than 250 mg/dL. Unfavorable outcome at discharge was independently associated with NIHSS score (P < 0.05), age (P < 0.05), and high serum triglyceride levels (P < 0.05).

Conclusions: Hypertriglyceridemia is an important modifiable risk factor that negatively affects the recovery in patients with acute ischemic stroke.

Background and Aim: Guillain–Barre Syndrome (GBS) subtypes can be classified as acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) and acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) based on the results of electrodiagnostic studies. Here, we report three such cases of AMAN with reversible conduction failure. AIM: Serial nerve conduction studies were conducted on patients with GBS presenting with AMAN to evaluate the occurrence of reversible conduction failure.

Methodology: We prospectively studied all patients with GBS admitted to our hospital between June 2022 and December 2023. Clinical outcomes and serial NCS were analyzed in all patients. Motor NCSs were performed on bilateral median, ulnar, tibial, fibular nerves with F waves, and sensory NCS conducted on median, ulnar, and sural nerves at the time of admission, within 2 to 3 weeks of the first NCS, and at 8 to 12 weeks interval.

Results: Total GBS cases: 33. Of these, the initial nerve conduction study showed severe amplitude reduction in distal CMAP with conduction blocks in non-compression sites with normal sensory conduction –observed in three cases. Serial nerve conduction studies in all three cases showed an evolving pattern of improvement in proximal amplitude and disappearance of conduction blocks without prolongation of distal latencies or excessive temporal dispersion of CMAPs, suggestive of reversible conduction failure.

Conclusions: Reversible conduction failure has been documented in AMAN and is considered a sign of nodopathy and has a favorable prognosis.

Conclusions: Elderly age, poor GCS on admission, and hematoma expansion are the most consistent predictors of death and poor outcomes.

Anil Behera, Vikram Kumar Huded, Tanaya Mishra, Anush S. Rangrajan

Narayana Health City Bangalore, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: As highlighted in the BRAT study, the outcome of treatment modalities depends strongly on the location of the aneurysm. The sustained advantage of endovascular treatment in posterior circulation aneurysms is well-proven. Regrowth and remnant of aneurysm lead to re-rupture, which is associated with significantly higher morbidity and mortality. The rate of de novo aneurysm appearance in previously clipped ruptured aneurysm could be 0.09%. Young individuals and patients with multiple aneurysms are more prone to de novo aneurysm formation during the follow-up. In this study, various characteristics of aneurysms were analyzed, which underwent clipping. An effort was made to understand the importance of angiographic follow-up of aneurysm after clipping.

Methodology: In this single-center retrospective study, we included patients whose intracranial aneurysms were initially treated surgically, identified to have re-growth, remnants, or de novo aneurysm on follow-up and subsequently addressed by endovascular treatment at our center between 2014 January and 2024 January. The study protocol was approved and consent was waivered by the institution review board. Data were entered in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM-SPSS. Continuous variables are summarized as mean with standard deviation and median and interquartile ranges based on data distribution. The Chi-square test was used to analyze categorical and t-test for continuous variables. A P-value less than 0.05 was considered significant.

Results: Eleven patients underwent endovascular treatment after post-clipping re-growth/remnant. The mean age was 44.55 ± 8.64 years. Five females and six males were included The time interval between clipping and check DSA ranged from 1 to 75 months with a mean of 9.77 ± 21.89 months. Only one patient underwent check DSA after re-rupture. Almost all de novo aneurysms were treated endovascularly along with the re-grown aneurysms in view of anatomical proximity between de novo and re-grown aneurysms. Flow diverter (FD) stenting was conducted in eight patients. Stent-assisted coiling was performed in two patients.

Conclusions: Interval angiographic follow-up of aneurysms after clipping is necessary to prevent a fatal outcome of rupture. Difficult-to-clip aneurysms need short interval follow-ups, that is, 1 week to 1 month to identify residual aneurysm, which can be treated endovascularly. Awareness among the patients must be raised regarding angiographic follow-up as re-rupture is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. De novo aneurysms can arise during the follow-up, which need to be treated based on size and morphology.
