All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi (AIIMS, New Delhi), India

Background and Aim: Autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy (ADNFLE) is a genetic epilepsy syndrome, characterized by clusters of nocturnal motor seizures. This condition is linked to heterozygous pathogenic variants in genes encoding subunits of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, such as CHRNA2, CHRNA4, CHRNB2, CABP4, DEPDC5, CRH, and KCNT1. Mutations in the CHRNB2 gene, encoding the beta-2 subunit, are extremely rare. This case report presents the first documented instance of ADNFLE with a CHRNB2 mutation in an Indian family.

Case Report: We describe an Indian family with two siblings (brother and sister) diagnosed with ADNFLE and identified with a pathogenic variant in CHRNB2. Both siblings had normal birth and developmental milestones without a previous seizure history. Seizure onset occurred at the age of 12 years in the brother and age 14 years in the sister, characterized by sudden nocturnal awakenings 1.5 to 2 h into sleep, exhibiting confused speech, and bilateral tonic–clonic seizures lasting 30 s to 1 min. They experienced three to four such episodes during sleep, including daytime naps, with no neurological deficits and preserved cognition.

Discussion: Video EEG recorded seizures originating during sleep, with a head turn to the left and bilateral tonic–clonic activity accompanied by focal slow waves in FP2. MRI brain epilepsy protocol results were normal. MEG localized seizure activity to the right posterior frontal and right mid-frontal regions. PET imaging revealed hypometabolism in the right inferior frontal region.

Conclusions: We report the first Indian family diagnosed with ADNFLE harboring a rare pathogenic mutation in the CHRNB2 gene, contributing to the understanding of this rare genetic epilepsy and highlighting the importance of genetic testing in diagnosis and management.

Raiz Iqbal, Sriramakrishnan V, Jason Ambrose

Tiruvannamalai Medical College, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: In posterior circulation stroke, the DWI lesion detection rate is significantly lower than in anterior circulation stroke. It is unclear whether DWI provides clinically useful information about stroke etiology or prognosis in patients with infratentorial strokes. The aim is to study the association between DWI characteristics and stroke etiology, stroke severity, and functional outcome in patients with infratentorial strokes.

Methodology: Study population: All patients with infratentorial stroke who attended the Neurology Department, TVMCH, from June 2023 to May 2024. Study design: Cross-sectional study, sample size: n = 100. All patients received standard stroke treatment. We used blinded comparison of DWI features (number, distribution, and volume of lesions) with clinical characteristics, namely, stroke etiology ([TOAST] classification), severity (NIH Stroke Scale [NIHSS]), length of stay [LOS], and functional outcome using modified Rankin Scale and Barthel Index.

Results: The number of DWI lesions was correlated with underlying stroke etiology, which showed cardio-embolic strokes had more DWI lesions (P < 0.001). No significant correlations were detected between the number of DWI lesions and other clinical characteristics. The distribution of DWI lesions showed a correlation with stroke etiology. Cardioembolic stroke had clinically silent, acute DWI lesions in the anterior circulation in addition to their infratentorial lesions (P < 0.001). DWI lesion volume did not show a correlation with clinical characteristics (P > 0.05).

Conclusions: DWI is a more reliable imaging method than MRI in detecting lesions in infratentorial strokes. The positive correlations between stroke etiology and the number and distribution of DWI lesions require confirmation by future studies before these findings can be generalized.

Bharati Vidyapeeth Medical College, Pune, Maharashtra, India

Background and Aim: Cerebral collaterals of patients with acute anterior ischemic stroke are of prime importance as this holds the key to successful reperfusion of the injured brain. Determining associations between modifiable risk factors such as hypertension and cerebral collateral status to functional outcomes will help streamline stroke care. Aim: To estimate the prevalence of good functional outcomes in acute anterior ischemic stroke subjects using CT angiography scores of cerebral collaterals and assess if chronic hypertension provides robust cerebral collateral circulation in patients with acute anterior ischemic stroke.

Methodology: This was an observational analytical study of patients with acute anterior ischemic stroke who presented within 48 h of symptom onset. Cerebral collaterals were classified based on various scores to identify the best to predict functional outcome at 3 months of follow-up. We also assessed hypertension and its relation to cerebral collateral.

Results: A total of 121 patients of acute anterior ischemic stroke were enrolled. The mean age of patients was 55.88 ± 18 years, 70.2% being males. The average NIHSS of patients was 6.6 ± 3.6. Hypertension was the most common risk factor (57.0%), followed by diabetes mellitus (40.5%). There was no significant correlation between chronic hypertension and good cerebral collateral status (P-value = 0.68). Also, 19.8% of cases underwent IV thrombolysis and 5.8% endovascular thrombectomy. CT ASPECTS had the best sensitivity in predicting the functional outcome with an area under the curve of 0.918, followed by the MAAS collaterals scoring system with an area under the curve of 0.637. Good outcomes (modified Rankin Score at 3 months ≤ 2) were observed in 86% of cases.

Conclusions: Patients with poor collateral status had poor functional outcomes.

Background and Aim: Melioidosis, which is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, is predominantly a disease of tropical climates and is especially widespread in southeast Asia and northern Australia. Melioidosis affecting the central nervous system has a low incidence but a high mortality. A recent systematic review found 120 cases reported worldwide with only 16 cases from India. Only 1.5 to 5% of cases present with craniospinal manifestations. However, mortality in neuromelioidosis remains high. CNS melioidosis has varied manifestations, including encephalomyelitis, cerebral abscess, cranial nerve deficit, and isolated meningitis.

Case Report: We presented a case of a 38-year-old patient presenting with a fever with seizure with multiple cranial nerve palsies, diagnosed to have neuromeloidosis via pus culture through brain biopsy. Patient, a 38-year-old male patient, with nil comorbidities presented with complaints of subacute onset loss of dexterity in the right hand, which progressed to right-side hemiparesis. The patient was admitted to a local hospital for the evaluation of a stroke. The patient had high-grade fever with seizure with worsening of weakness and right UMN facial palsy with lateral gaze palsy with bulbar symptoms, dysphagia. MRI brain plain and contrast with vessel wall imaging showed foci of increased signal intensities on T2-weighted and FLAIR images involving the left fronto-parietal lobes, left ganglio-capsular region, thalamus and brainstem, with areas of patchy diffusion restriction in left fronto-parietal lobes, thalamus, and left cerebral peduncle, which was reported to have CNS infectious and neuro-melioidosis with less likely possibilities of CNS vasculitis.

Discussion: Neurosurgery consultation: Brain biopsy from the frontal region was taken and sent for tissue culture. Tissue culture showed Burkholderia pseudomallei, which was previously suspected and was susceptible to meropenem and cotrimoxazole. The patient was treated with inj. meropenem and inj. cotrimoxazole and other supportive medications.

Conclusions: There are very few case reports of neuromeliodosis in India, with some authors describing its presentation as cerebral abscesses. This case proves that in tropical countries such as India, a high index of suspicion along with knowledge of varied presentations and unique imaging findings are key to the management of neuromeliodosis.

Methodology: A total of 50 chronic migraine patients between the ages of 18 and 45 years who fulfilled the ICHD-3 criteria were evaluated at our outpatient clinic between January 2023 and April 2024. Results: All patients clinical and neurological examinations were normal. In all, 34 patients were women and 16 were men and their neuroimaging showed no significant abnormalities. Conclusions: Co-morbid conditions such as vitamin deficiency and abnormal accumulation of metabolic products should be identified and treated in migraine patients to get better relief of their symptoms.

Background and Aim: Ethambutol-induced toxic optic neuropathy (EON) is a well-known potential side effect of ethambutol. Methodology: A cross-sectional observational study including patients clinically diagnosed to have EON with a history of intake of anti-tubercular drugs including ethambutol within 1 year of symptom onset. Conclusions: Ethambutol toxicity may occur even with a standard dose and extended duration of ethambutol intake. All newly diagnosed TB patients must have a baseline ophthalmological examination and a periodic evaluation thereafter. The prescribing doctor and patient need to be well aware of EON.

Background and Aim: TB meningitis accounts for 1–2% of all tuberculosis (TB) cases in immunocompetent individuals with a mortality as high as 30%. Case Report: This 29-year-old female patient in the postpartum period presented with subacute onset progressive and improving neurological illness in the form of altered sensorium with low-grade fever, weight loss, and secondary headache with visual disturbances, which improved with medications briefly followed by worsening that improved after the correction of communicating hydrocephalus with a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt. Discussion: Routine blood investigations revealed anemia, elevated ESR, and hyponatremia. Computed tomography (CT) brain showed diffuse cerebral edema with hydrocephalus. Initial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain with contrast showed leptomeningeal enhancement in the basal cisterns. Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences, New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Status epilepticus (SE) has potential wide-ranging after-effects, including cognitive dysfunction. The study aimed to assess the cognitive profile of patients after SE at three follow-up intervals, and also to identify the clinical predictors of cognitive functions in status epilepticus.

Methodology: A total number of 50 patients suffering from SE admitted to neurology were included in the study. Patients already having an additional alternative cause of cognitive impairment were excluded. They were evaluated 24 hours after the last seizure event, at 7 days, and 1 month. A set of cognitive tests including mini mental state examination (MMSE), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), frontal assessment battery (FAB) and others were used for assessment.

Results: The study is currently under process, interim analysis found cognitive dysfunction initially in all patients. All patients (100%) had impairment in attention, calculation, recall, set-shifting, cognitive flexibility, processing speed, and lexical fluency. The majority of patients (>70%) had disorientation, executive dysfunction, and poor abstract thinking. The language part of the test was preserved in most of the cases (>80%), and deficits if any were mild. In the follow-up assessment, the majority of patients (>95%) had complete improvement in orientation, attention, calculation, and recall and partial improvement in visuospatial skill deficits, lexical fluency, abstract thinking, set-shifting, and processing speed. A small proportion of patients (<5%), out of the super-refractory SE group had severe and persistent cognitive deficits.

Conclusions: Status epilepticus causes cognitive dysfunction. The deficits improve gradually in most of the cases, but some long-term deficits are present in a minority of them. In status epilepticus, such as in stroke and myocardial infarction (MI), time is of utmost importance.

Tintu Thomas, Prasanth C Varghese, Fiju Chacko

Jubilee Mission Medical College, Thrissur, Kerala, India

Background and Aim: Guillain–Barre syndrome (GBS) is an acute-onset immune-mediated monophasic polyneuropathy. Various prognostic models were needed to identify the patients with poor outcomes. The Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score (EGRIS) and the modified Erasmus GBS Outcome Score (mEGOS) are prognostic models used in the prediction of mechanical ventilation and functional outcome, respectively. The aim is to study the use of mEGOS in determining the poor functional outcome at 6 months and use of EGRIS in predicting the need for mechanical ventilation and to determine the various parameters predicting the outcome in GBS.

Methodology: This study was a prospective observational study in patients with GBS for determining the utility of prognostic models such as modified EGOS and EGRIS in determining the poor outcomes at a tertiary care hospital. In addition to the above, the clinical, demographic, investigational, and treatment parameters affecting the outcome were studied. All patients with a diagnosis of GBS fulfilled by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) criteria were admitted within 2 weeks of onset of weakness to the Department of Neurology within a period of 18 months from the date on which institutional ethics committee clearance was obtained. A total of 58 patients were enrolled in the study. All patients underwent complete neurological examination, including Medical Research Council (MRC) sum score, nerve conduction study, and CSF examination. Informed consent was taken for each subject. Outcome was assessed by Hughes disability Scale (HMS). HMS is a functional rating from 0-6 (0-asymptomatic, 1- mild signs and symptoms but able to run, 2- able to walk unaided for 5 meters, 3- able to walk with support, 4- bed ridden or wheel chair bound, 5- requiring ventilator assistance and 6- death). The mEGOS and the EGRIS were conducted for all patients at admission. The mEGOS predicted the risk of being unable to walk independently within the first 6 months of disease based on age, muscle strength, and preceding diarrhoea. The EGRIS corresponds to an estimated risk of respiratory failure within the first week based on the time from the onset to admission, MRC sum score, and the presence of facial/bulbar weakness. GBS outcome score is predicted as a good outcome when the score is less than or equal to 2 and a bad outcome when it is more than or equal to 3. Enrolled patients were followed up for 6 months. Statistical analysis was carried out using SPSS version 21.0. Descriptive analysis was reported as the mean and standard deviation of continuous variables. Independent sample t-test and chi-square test were used to establish the association, P < 0.05 was considered as significant.

Results: In all, 58 patients (43 males; 15 females; mean age of 47.1 ± 18.6 years) were enrolled. Amongst these, 4 (6.9%) patients died during their in-hospital stay. Antecedent infection was present in 21 (36%), areflexia in 54 (93.1%), autonomic dysfunction in 6 (10.3%), facial and bulbar weakness in 23 (39.7%), neck flexor weakness in 14 (24.1%), albuminocytological dissociation in 52 (89.7%), respiratory insufficiency/mechanical ventilation in 10 (17.2%) patients. The mean mEGOS at admission was 4.9 ± 3.1 and EGRIS was 3.1 ± 1.39. The mean MRC sums core at admission was 42.2 ± 10.4. 49 cases (84.5%) were demyelinating and 9 cases (15.5%) were axonal patterns. On analysis, predictors associated with poor outcome at 6 months were age (P = 0.001), female gender (P = 0.016), MRC sum score at admission (P = 0.021), autonomic dysfunction (P = 0.030), mechanical ventilation/respiratory insufficiency (P = 0.001), and demyelinating pattern (P = 0.007). Higher mEGOS at admission was a predictor of poor outcome (P = 0.035) and EGRIS at admission of 4.8 ± 0.7 predicted the need for ventilation (P = 0.001).

Conclusions: EGRIS and mEGOS are good prognostic models for determining the need for mechanical ventilation and functional outcome. Detailed evaluation of clinical and electrophysiological parameters may help in predicting the outcome.

Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute, Bengaluru (BMCRI Bengaluru), Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: In vasculitic neuropathy (VN), a 50% side-to-side difference in the amplitude of compound muscle action potentials has been proposed but the evidence is lacking. The aim of this study was to characterize electrodiagnostic features that best distinguish VN from other non-inflammatory axonal polyneuropathies.

Methodology: We conducted a retrospective observational study between September 2016 and April 2024. We reviewed the records of patients with VN who had bilateral nerve conduction studies (NCS) and evaluated different electrodiagnostic models to help distinguish VN from other non-inflammatory axonal polyneuropathies. Inclusion criteria: Cases- patients aged above 18 years with biopsy-proven VN. Controls- Polyneuropathy secondary to diabetes mellitus, ethanol, toxin-induced neuropathy, vitamin B12 deficiency with baseline nerve conduction study.

Results: We identified 25 cases and 25 controls with non-inflammatory axonal neuropathies. The amplitude percent difference Z score model did not show discriminatory capability between cases and controls. The conduction velocity (CV) percent difference Z score of posterior tibial nerve (PTN) showed the best discriminatory capability between cases and controls (area under the curve [AUC]: 0.789; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.606, 0.972). The CV absolute difference Z score of PTN showed the second-best discriminatory capability between cases and controls (AUC: 0.781; 95% CI: 0.595, 0.968).

Conclusions: As proposed by multiple studies, VN has a 50% difference in side-to-side amplitude. This study did not show any significant discriminatory capability between cases and controls for the proposed hypothesis.

In functional outcomes, no disability was observed in 18, minor in 62, major in 9, and 4 patients died.

Conclusions: Males were affected more and the age commonly involved was above 60 years. Hypertension, diabetes, and smoking contributed as the major risk factors. Giddiness was the commonest symptom. Most patients had cerebellum and brainstem lesions. The territory commonly involved was mid-brain, cerebellum, thalamus, and occipital and temporal lobes.

Background and Aim: Nearly 25–30% of patients with epilepsy are refractory to treatment due to various factors. Conclusions: Perampanel is tolerated well and reduces seizure frequency in adults with refractory epilepsy.

Background and Aim: Although acute movement disorders are often encountered, the literature is sparse, especially in our socio-demographic background. In this study, we describe 26 cases of movement disorder emergencies.

Case report: Patients attending the Medical College, Kolkata, with movement disorder as the sole or predominant presentation within 4 weeks of disease onset were enrolled in our study after taking proper consent. Detailed history, examination, and relevant investigations were obtained.

Discussion: Amongst 26 patients, 21 had hyperkinetic disorders, whereas there were only three cases of hypokinetic and two mixed movement disorders. Among the hyperkinetic group, phenomenologically, tremor was most common, followed by chorea, dystonia, and myoclonus. Conclusions: Movement disorder emergencies vary widely in phenomenology and etiology. Vascular and metabolic causes predominantly have hyperkinetic phenomenology, whereas neuropsychiatric causes have hypokinetic presentation. All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Raebareli (AIIMS, Raebareli), Uttar Pradesh, India

Background and Aim: There is evidence that has shown that carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels are increased in atherosclerosis. To the best of our knowledge, there is no published literature where it has been used to assess the correlation between the severity of acute ischemic stroke (AIS) with infarct volume on computed tomography (CT) scan and CEA level. The aim is to study the correlation between CEA levels and infarct volume and severity of AIS.

Methodology: We conducted a hospital-based, observational study, and all the consecutive patients of AIS (>18 years of age) presenting within 1 week were enrolled and detailed clinical examination, investigation, and CEA levels were done within 7 days. We had also done CEA in healthy subjects between 45 and 75 years of age with no chronic diseases.

Results: Fifty-seven consecutive AIS cases were recruited in the study. The age group of cases enrolled in the study ranged from 30 to 85 years with a mean age of 61.56 ± 13.17 years. Among them, 39 (80.6) cases were male. The mean infarct volume on CT scan was 15.73 ± 20.86 cm3. Baseline Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was good, GCS (13–15) in 28 (77.8) cases and the mean modified ranking scale (mRS) was 3.94 ± 0.583 and the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was 6.86 ± 4.89. No significant association was observed between CEA levels and NIHSS scores at admission, mRS, or with GCS. No significant association was observed between the infarct volume on CT scan and CEA levels.

Conclusions: The CEA levels are higher among AIS patients than in the normal population. However, no significant association was observed between CEA levels and NIHSS score at admission, mRS, or with GCS and infarct volume on CT scan.

Background and Aim: Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder resulting from neurohumoral and synaptic aberrations. Background and Aim: Recessive loss of function mutations in the HINT1 gene is associated with predominantly motor neuropathy with neuromyotonia (NMAN). Around 19 variations in the HINT1 gene are reported in around 100 patients worldwide.

A 17-year-old adolescent male presented with a 2-year history of progressive weakness of lower limbs, mainly involving the proximal muscles. He also reported muscle cramps. Vardhman Mahavir Medical College (VMMC), New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Epilepsy is one of the commonest neurological disorders affecting approximately 70 million people worldwide. The prevalence of epilepsy in India in 2020 was 4.7 per 1,000 population. The commonly used anti-seizure drugs are phenytoin, valproic acid, carbamazepine, and levetiracetam. This study investigates the risk of atherosclerosis in patients taking anti-seizure medications for over 2 years. Atherosclerosis is a potential side effect of these medications, and this study uses biochemical markers and carotid artery intima-medial thickness (CA-IMT) to assess this risk.

Methodology: The study was carried out in the Department of Neurology in collaboration with the Department of Radiology, Vardhman Mahavir Medical College, and Safdarjung Hospital. Fifty patients of epilepsy aged 12–40 years and on anti-seizure medications (ASM) and 50 healthy controls were recruited in the study. Detailed medical history and physical exams were conducted on both groups. Blood tests assessed general health and cholesterol levels. Ultrasound scans measured the thickness of the carotid artery walls, a marker of atherosclerosis risk.

Results: The mean age of patients and controls were 22.58 (±6.97) years and 23.5 (±5.79) years respectively (P = 0.475). In the patient group, 28% were females and 72% were males, whereas in the control group, these percentages were 34% and 66%, respectively. There was a significantly higher frequency of overweight individuals among the cases (P = 0.019). Patients had significantly higher levels of total cholesterol (P = 0.001), non-HDL cholesterol (P = 0.001), and LDL:total cholesterol (P = 0.001) compared to controls. There was no significant difference in triglyceride level, or LDL cholesterol between the patient group and the control group. The examination of carotid artery intima-media thickness (CA-IMT) among patients treated with various anti-seizure medications (levetiracetam, phenytoin, carbamazepine, and valproate) in comparison to the control group revealed significant differences (P = 0.0001). The mean±SD of CA-IMT was 0.65 ± 0.12 mm for levetiracetam, 0.61 ± 0.19 mm for eptoin, 0.68 ± 0.15 mm for carbamazepine, and 0.7 ± 0.15 mm for valproate.

Conclusions: We concluded that there is an increased risk of atherosclerosis in patients on ASM monotherapy for more than 2 years as compared to age- and sex-matched healthy controls of age 12 to 40 years as there was greater CA-IMT and dyslipidemia in the patient group as compared to the control group.

Naveen Ranga, Naveen Kumar Ranga, Surekha Dabla

Pt BD Sharma PGIMS, Rohtak, Haryana, India

Background and Aim: An overdose of dextromethorphan (DXM) can cause significant central nervous system issues, such as coma. This case study seeks to demonstrate how severe DXM poisoning is managed clinically, underscore the critical role of neurocritical care in enhancing patient recovery, and track the patient’s progress and functional improvement.

Case report: This report describes a 28-year-old male patient who ingested an entire bottle of DXM-containing antitussive and was found comatose at home. On admission, he exhibited poor respiratory effort and a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 3/15, necessitating immediate mechanical ventilation. Initial metabolic tests revealed severe metabolic acidosis and acute kidney injury, which required hemodialysis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans at admission were unremarkable, but toxicology confirmed opioid exposure. Despite remaining comatose and experiencing a seizure, the patient’s metabolic profile gradually improved with supportive care. Follow-up MRI a week later showed extensive bilateral symmetrical damage to the centrum semiovale and basal ganglia. By the second week, he was weaned off the ventilator, though he remained akinetic and mute. By the fourth week, he regained consciousness, displayed purposeful movements, and required minimal assistance for walking. This case underscores the critical role of neurocritical care in managing severe DXM poisoning.

Discussion: The focused, supportive care provided in a neurocritical setting significantly enhances recovery prospects and functional restoration in patients suffering from severe acute brain injury due to DXM overdose.

Conclusions: The focused, supportive care provided in a neurocritical setting significantly enhances recovery prospects and functional restoration in patients suffering from severe acute brain injury due to DXM overdose.

Background and Aim: Healthcare delivery in rural India faces significant challenges due to a shortage of specialists, particularly in managing acute conditions such as stroke. This study is part of an ongoing multi-centric SMART INDIA project, which aims to compare two innovative solutions: training physicians in district hospitals to manage stroke (“Stroke physician model”) versus using a low-cost Telestroke model. We evaluated the current stroke care standards at district hospitals and nodal centers using a 24-point stroke care bundle, with the objective of leveraging these data in the future to quantify the enhancements following the implementation of SMART INDIA training.

Methodology: The study is currently ongoing and the available patient data from eleven district hospitals and six nodal centers were analyzed. Two neurologists independently assessed the extent of stroke care bundle components administered before SMART INDIA training.

Results: Interim analysis revealed that of 268 records screened (nodal centers 201, district hospitals 67), the mean age of the cohort was 59.83 ± 14.94 years, with 164 males [61.19%] and ischemic stroke n = 183 [68.3%] as the major subtype. The mean percentage of stroke care bundle components administered overall was 37.12 ± 17.90%. Nodal centers performed better (42.14 ± 16.92%) than district hospitals (20.99 ± 11.26%), (P < 0.00001).

Conclusions: Preliminary results highlight the suboptimal acute stroke care delivery in rural district hospitals, with less than 50% adherence to standard care protocols, underscoring the stark gaps in rural healthcare, particularly in managing stroke. Background and Aim: We present a rare case with atypical presenting features of asymmetric bilateral chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) with a false positive acetylcholine receptor antibody test resulting in diagnostic delay. The case was treated initially for myasthenia gravis due to asymmetric ptosis and ophthalmoplegia.

Case report: A 26-year-old female patient presented with a 13-year history of slowly progressive extraocular motility restriction with ptosis in the right eye, followed by a 5-year history of similar presentation in the left eye with a 5-year history of diplopia. Clinical examination showed extraocular motility restriction in all gazes with asymmetric ptosis in the right eye more than the left eye. On diplopia charting, there was diplopia in superotemporal and downward direction.

Discussion: Serum acetylcholine receptor antibody (AchR Ab) was positive on serum enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA); however, following 4 months of oral pyridostigmine therapy, there were no signs of clinical improvement. Conclusions: Sometimes, CPEO may be difficult to diagnose, especially when the symptoms are asymmetric, lack other systemic signs, have diplopia, or have no family history of CPEO. Thus, practitioners should keep CPEO in their differential diagnosis to avoid unnecessary delay in diagnosis.

Background and Aim: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem immune-mediated disorder characterized by granulomatous inflammation of affected organs. Neurological involvement accounts for 5% to 10% of cases, of which, longitudinal extensive transverse myelitis (LETM) is very rare.

Case report: We present a case of a 53-year-old lady, with leg numbness, slippage of chappals, cotton wool sensation in both feet and swaying while walking. Examination revealed hypertonia in all limbs, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar response. The distal sense of joint position and vibration was impaired in both feet. Laboratory tests showed increased inflammatory markers and a high serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level. The brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was normal. Spine MRI revealed a long segment of T2/ fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity along the posterior portion of the cervicothoracic spinal cord and post-contrast enhancement. A chest X-ray and computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest showed features of sarcoidosis. Bronchoscopy, and bronchoalveolar lavage results were normal. The fine needle aspiration biopsy of the subcarinal lymph node yielded no granulomatous changes.

Discussion: Therefore, elevated serum angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) levels and typical CT chest and MRI spine results led to the diagnosis of neurosarcoidosis, which presented as LETM. We started the patient on steroids and her symptoms completely resolved during the 1-month follow-up. She was then initiated on mycophenolate mofetil.

Conclusions: In neurosarcoidosis, isolated spinal cord involvement is rare and presents significant challenges in diagnosis. Glucocorticoids are the cornerstone of treatment, especially in the acute stage. The most effective steroid-sparing agent is mycophenolate mofetil.

SevenHills Hospital, Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, India

Background and Aim: Cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) affects the smaller caliber vessels of the brain, including arterioles (perforating, diameter < 0.1 mm), capillaries, and venules, and results in chronic and often progressive/accumulating grey and white matter injury in the brain. Small subcortical infarcts (SCI), lacunes, cerebral microbleeds (CMBs), cortical microinfarcts, white matter hyperintensity (WMH), perivascular spaces (PVS), and cortical superficial siderosis are the major neuroimaging markers of cSVD. Our study aims to describe the various clinical phenotypes associated with cSVD.

Methodology: An observational retrospective study was performed between January 2024 and July 2024. In all, 109 patients with cSVD on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain, clinical phenotypes, and neuroimaging markers were studied.

Results: Of the 109 patients, 45 (41.2%) patients had acute ischemic stroke, 25 (22.9%) had hemorrhagic stroke, 10 (9.17%) had cognitive defects, 9 (8.25%) patients had cardiac abnormalities, 7 (6.42%) patients had parkinsonism, 3 (2.75%) patients had bladder disturbances, 5 (4.58%) patients had gait ataxia, 4 (3.66%) patients presented with mood disturbances, 2 (1.8%) patients had obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). WMHs were the most common abnormality- 82%, SCIs- 76%, cortical microinfarcts- 60%, and PVS- 45% cases.

Conclusions: cSVD can present with multiple neurological phenotypes such as stroke, mood disturbances, parkinsonism, gait and bladder disturbances, and cognitive defects. Non-neurological phenotypes such as cardiovascular abnormalities or respiratory (obstructive sleep apnea) have also been associated with cSVD. Tobacco, hypertension, and diabetes are modifiable risk factors for cSVD.

Background and Aim: Niemann–Pick disease type C (NPC) is an uncommon, autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder characterized by progressive neurodegeneration. Case report: A 23-year-old female patient, presented with a history of unsteadiness while walking for 3 years, tremulousness of both upper limbs for 2.5 years, slurred speech for 2 years, and progressive weakness of both lower limbs for 1 year. Background and Aim: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis is a rare disorder characterized by transient attacks of flaccid paralysis of varying intensity and duration. Background and Aim: Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal protein elevation, and skin changes (POEMS) syndrome is a rare paraneoplastic disorder. At the age of 10 years, the patient had a change in seizure semiology, he had abnormal twitching movements in his perioral area and picking movements in both his upper limbs, followed by neck drop and loss of posturing leading to fall. This episode lasted for 20–30 s. The patient had 10–12 episodes per day. Tab valproate 500 mg BD and tab lacoset 100 mg BD were added and dose of clobazam was increased to 10 mg HS. The patient was additionally treated with three courses of methylprednisolone at 10 years old. After three courses, seizures were controlled.

Discussion and conclusions: The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain was done which was normal. The electroencephalogram (EEG) was suggestive of generalized slow-wave activity. Proper history and genetic analysis are essential in neurology.

SEENA V, Gautham Arunachal Udupi, Keerthipriya M S, Saraswati Nashi, Deepak Menon, Atchayaram Nalini

National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease with progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons. In all, 10% of the cases were familial, the rest were sporadic. Common genetic forms are C9ORF72, SOD1, VCP, TDP42, and OPTN. The genetic spectrum of ALS patients in India is unknown and this study was undertaken to know the genetic profile of Indian ALS patients.

Methodology: Retrospective analysis of genetic data of 700 patients with ALS observed in NIMHANS, Bangaluru, from 2015-2022.

Results: In all, 113 patients had a confirmed genetic mutation. The mean age at presentation was 51.9 ±11.2 (19-72) years. The male:female ratio was 71:42. The most common genetic variants identified were - SETX (13) and SOD1 (12). Eight patients, each had mutations in DCTN1, FUS, NEFH, and OPTN. Other less common mutations were in FIG4, UBQLN2, TARDBP, ATXN2, ANXA11, UNC13A and ERBB4. Rarely mutations were found in C9ORF72, MATR3, CHMP2B, VAPB, GRN, SQSTM1 and TBK1. The majority were heterozygous variants, except for two cases of OPTN with homozygous mutations. The majority were missense variants (90.2%), except two in-frame deletions in NEFH, FUS, stop gain mutations in OPTN, FIG4, splice regions in SETX, OPTN, splice acceptor defect in OPTN, splice donor defect in FIG4, initiator codon defect in OPTN, in-frame insertion in NEFH and deletion in SPG11. Novel variants were identified in NEFH, SOD1, OPTN, DCTN1, UNC13A, FUS, TARDBP, UBQLN2, ANXA11, ATXN2, SETX, FIG4, MATR3, ERBB4, and TBK1.

Conclusions: This study unravels the genetic spectrum of patients with ALS from an Indian cohort. SETX and SOD1 mutations were the most common. Missense and heterozygous variants were identified in 90% of the cases.

Background and Aim: Primary headaches, such as migraine and tension-type headaches, are highly prevalent conditions. Sangeetha Nair, Sakthi Velayutham S, Haritha S, Aubin Mathew Varghese, Ramgiri Kamlesh, Mugundhan K

Stanley Medical College Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) is characterized by proximal and distal weakness of all four limbs, progressive over more than 8 weeks, with hypo/areflexia. It is an aberrant immune response directed toward the components of myelin sheath, and occurs in the setting of HIV, as are other immune-mediated neurological disorders.

Case report: A 46-year-old gentleman came with distal followed by proximal lower limb weakness, then distal upper limbs weakness and truncal weakness, associated with the numbness of both lower limbs, gradually progressing over 1 year. Examination revealed hypotonia of all four limbs, distal weakness of both upper limbs and distal more than proximal weakness of both lower limbs, truncal weakness, global areflexia, and graded loss of all sensations over both lower limbs.

Discussion: Routine hematological and biochemical investigations and thyroid profile were normal. The nerve conduction study (NCS) showed demyelinating neuropathy of all four limbs with secondary axonal changes and polyradiculopathy. He was detected to be HIV (+) and his CD4 count was 219. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) study showed albuminocytological dissociation. He was managed with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 0.4 g/kg/d for 5 days with a diagnosis of CIDP associated with HIV.

Conclusions: HIV-infected patients with CIDP have a benign course with a few relapses and respond rapidly to corticosteroids. CSF protein levels are slightly higher in patients with HIV reflecting an immune-mediated disruption of blood–nerve barrier at spinal roots. They have higher CSF lymphocyte counts due to CSF viremia. A decline in T-regulatory-CD4 cells potentiates autoimmune phenomena in HIV. Antiretroviral treatment (ART) results in immune reconstitution and contributes to remission. Some patients with low baseline CD4 and high viral load have CIDP as an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Concomitant use of ART with steroids may curtail IRIS.

Background and Aim: Issac syndrome, is a peripheral nerve hyperexcitability (PNH) disorder marked by muscle twitching, myokymia, neuromyotonia, and dysautonomia. Many patients have voltage-gated potassium channel (VGKC) complex antibodies. It is often considered a paraneoplastic syndrome due to its association with thymoma and small-cell lung cancer. Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi (BHU, Varanasi), Uttar Pradesh, India

Background and Aim: Many conditions mimic seizures. Here, we discuss three cases that were diagnosed as seizures from the periphery but were not true seizures after evaluation.

Case report: We described three cases that mimicked seizures. Case 1: A 42-year-old man presented with a history of multiple episodes of abnormal twitching toward one side along with a brief episode of loss of consciousness lasting for about 30 s. Case 2: A 20-year-girl with right focal seizures in the past presented with multiple episodes of loss of consciousness lasting about 2 to 3 h. Treated as epilepsy elsewhere with levetiracetam 1000 mg/day. History reviewed-abnormal dystonic posturing following sudden getting up from rest. Paroxysmal kinesthetic dyskinesias triggered by the movements. Started on oxcarbamazepine with symptom relief.

Discussion and conclusions: Syncope, psychogenic seizures, and kinesthetic dyskinesias may mimic seizures. Simple clinical assessments such as pulse rate assessment, often omitted in the busy OPDs, may be life-saving. History taking and home video may help in the diagnosis.

Abhinav Ankur

Vardhman Mahavir Medical College (VMMC), New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis accounts for up to 20% of all identified viral encephalitis. A 2014 study showed with acyclovir, mortality has reduced from 38% to around 5.5–11% with the majority of mortality in immunocompromised individuals. We present two immunocompetent patients who presented with gastrointestinal symptoms, developed late neurological symptoms, and despite an adequate dose of acyclovir did not improve.

Case report: Case 1: A 19-year-old immunocompetent female presented with hiccups for 10–15 days. After admission, she developed an altered sensorium. On further questioning, a family member revealed a history of low-grade fever on and off for the past 1 month. Routine cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) parameters were within normal limits. The electroencephalogram (EEG) showed generalized slowing. The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed asymmetrical hyperintensity in the left infero-frontal and insular cortex and thalamus. HSV polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive and despite 21 days of acyclovir therapy, the patient did not improve and died. Case 2: A 15-year-old immunocompetent boy presented with abdominal pain with a low-grade fever for 15 days. Ultrasonography (USG) was suggestive of necrotic lymphadenopathy. CSF parameters were normal. The patient developed new-onset refractory status epilepticus on the 7th day of admission. A repeat CSF study revealed normal routine parameters. EEG showed very low amplitude delta activity. MRI showed symmetrical hyperintensities. HSV PCR was found to be positive and despite 21 days of acyclovir therapy, the patient did not improve and died.

Discussion and conclusions: It emphasizes the possibility of HSV encephalitis even if a patient presents with gastrointestinal symptoms with chronic onset. There should be a low threshold for testing of HSV PCR and consideration for acyclovir therapy even with normal CSF routine parameters if there is either clinical or electroencephalographic finding of seizure.

Results: A total of 19 NORSE patients were included in our study. Mean age of patient is 26.6 ± 12.8 years, male: female= 8:11. Mean duration of hospital stay is 25.6 days. Hospital mortality is 26.3% (n = 5), and total mortality on three-month follow-up is 36.8% (n = 7)

Conclusions: NORSE is rare clinical situation where diagnosis and treatment are challenging. Further research is needed to answer various questions encountered in routine clinical practice.

Background and Aim: Leber’s Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON) is a rare genetic condition caused by mitochondrial DNA mutation. National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Migraine is the second most disabling disease and has a neurovascular basis. Choroid is a vascular layer of retina and can be measured using optical coherence tomography (OCT). This study aims to evaluate the choroid thickness in patients with migraine and compare with that of healthy controls to gain insights regarding migraine pathophysiology.

Methodology: We recruited 16 patients with migraine (as per ICHD3 criteria) (M:F = 3:13) and 16 age and gender-matched controls (M:F =7:9) after written and informed consent. After detailed neurological and ophthalmological evaluation, all underwent OCT. The peripapillary choroid thickness (PPChT) was measured in temporal (T), temporosuperior (TS), temporoinferior (TI), nasal (N), nasal-superior (NS), nasal-inferior (NI) and global (G) segments, while subfoveal choroid (SFChT) was measured beneath fovea manually with calipers. The comparisons were carried out using Student’s t-test.

Results: The mean age of patients was 37.06 (±9.57) years, and the controls were 32.06 (±5.77) years (p = 0.08). The mean duration of illness in patients was 9 (±2.52) years and monthly migraine days were 8 (±4.31). The PPChT (global) in patients (RE-240.88 ± 32.29 µm, LE-239.88 ± 28.07µm) as compared to healthy controls (RE- 295.69 ± 18.47 µm, LE- 307.63 ± 19.61 µm) and SFChT in patients (RE-234.38 ± 28.64 µm, LE-241.81 ± 32.58 µm) as compared to controls (RE-301.56 ± 17.13 µm, LE-305.19 ± 22.48µm) were significantly thinner (p < 0.001).

Conclusions: The findings indicate significant thinning in choroid in patients with migraine as compared to controls. Assessment of choroid thickness may be a potential biomarker in migraine. The same needs to be evaluated by a larger sample size and longitudinal studies.

Background and Aim: Cervical dystonia is the most common focal dystonia in adulthood. Background and Aim: Hyperglycemia-associated seizures with their clinical heterogeneity and atypical brain involvement can complicate diagnosis and management. We present three cases exemplifying the spectrum of hyperglycemia-associated seizures and their radiological profile.

Case report: Case series of three patients with clinical and radiological details taken after informed consent. 1. 62-year-old-known diabetic experienced, intermittent episodes of head turning to right, lasting one minute with intact awareness. Discussion and conclusions: Considering hyperglycemia and associated imaging findings is crucial to avoid unnecessary investigations. The ASL sequence may be a useful marker and can sometimes show early changes even before they appear in other imaging sequences.

Background and Aim: Phospholipase-associated neurodegeneration (PLAN) caused by PLA2G6 mutations is a recessively inherited disorder. We report two siblings with neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA2) in a tertiary care hospital in eastern India.

Case report: A 21-year-old man was asymptomatic until age 10 years, when he begun to drag his left lower limb, gradually developed generalized dystonia over 5 years. At the age of 20, he was bradykinetic with hypomimia, upper extremity myoclonic jerks, dysarthria and dysphagia. He had two episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizure in last 2 months. He was confined to wheelchair since 1 year. He lost his speech since 7 months. His younger brother, 17-year-old male, was asymptomatic until age of 10 years, when he begun to drag his both lower limbs with gait impairment.

On examination both had spastic speech, slow pursuit, vertical gaze restrictions (upward), slow saccade, optic atrophy, increased deep tendon reflex (DTR), bilateral ankle and patellar clonus, extensor plantar, spastic gait. Also, elder brother had masked facies, anterocolis, generalized dystonia and younger brother had cerebellar signs. All laboratory tests including serum biochemistry, liver function test (LFT), thyroid function test (TFT), serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were normal. Kayser–Fleischer rings were not detected. Electroencephalogram (EEG) showed generalized epileptiform discharges in elder brother and normal in younger brother. Discussion and conclusions: NBIA is a very rare case, and it is important to make a diagnosis as early as possible so that patients can get treated. It will also reduce the mortality rate and improve quality of life.

Ragavendar B, Ramkumar Sugumaran, Sunil K Narayan, Rajeswari Aghoram, Sai Kishore

Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research (JIPMER), Puducherry, India

Background and Aim: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuron loss. Accurate diagnosis of PD and differentiation from other Parkinsonian syndromes is challenging but crucial for appropriate management. 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) myocardial scintigraphy has emerged as a promising tool for diagnosing PD due to its ability to detect early cardiac sympathetic denervation, a common feature in PD. Since 123I-MIBG availability is limited in India and costly, we used 131I-MIBG as a viable alternative to detect early cardiac sympathetic denervation.

Case report: A 73-year-old patient exhibited symptoms of orthostatic hypotension, insomnia, urinary urgency and recurrent syncopal episodes. Clinical examination revealed subtle limb rigidity and severe dysautonomia without tremors. He was diagnosed with atypical Parkinsonism. Laboratory tests and imaging studies, including 131I-MIBG myocardial scintigraphy, were conducted to distinguish between Pure autonomic failure (PAF) and multiple system atrophy (MSA) by assessing cardiac sympathetic innervation.

Discussion: 131I-MIBG imaging revealed a reduced Heart/Mediastinum uptake ratio of 1.15 (<1.7), indicating severe postganglionic cardiac sympathetic denervation. This finding confirmed the diagnosis of Pure Autonomic Failure (PAF) over Multiple System Atrophy (MSA). The patient was treated with lifestyle changes, abdominal binders, fludrocortisone and pyridostigmine for orthostatic hypotension and supine hypertension, showed significant improvement in symptoms and is under regular follow-up.

Conclusions: 131I-MIBG myocardial scintigraphy is a feasible and cost-effective method for assessing cardiac sympathetic activity in Parkinsonism, aiding in early and accurate diagnosis. Further studies are needed to validate its clinical utility and establish it as a reliable alternative to 123I-MIBG in PD diagnosis.

All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is an inflammatory disorder of the central nervous system that causes optic neuritis and myelitis. Relapses of NMOSD are severe and lead to residual disability. The current treatment of acute myelitis is intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMPS) for 5 days, followed by plasma exchange (PLEX) if there is no response. This may delay the recovery of the damaged cells. We aim to compare the efficacy of simultaneous PLEX and IVMPS versus IVMPS with add-on PLEX for acute myelitis of NMOSD at 3 months of randomization.

Methodology: We will conduct a prospective, randomized, open-label, blinded endpoint (PROBE) study. We will enroll patients with acute severe myelitis who fulfill the criteria of NMOSD. We will randomly assign them to receive either simultaneous PLEX and IVMPS or IVMPS with add-on PLEX. We will assess the primary outcome of improvement in the Kurtzke Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) at 3 months.

Results: Based on previous studies, we expect a beneficial effect of simultaneous PLEX and IVMPS on the outcome of acute myelitis of NMOSD. We hypothesize that simultaneous PLEX and IVMPS will result in a greater improvement in EDSS than IVMPS with add-on PLEX at 3 months.

Conclusions: This study will provide evidence on the optimal treatment of acute myelitis of NMOSD. It will test the hypothesis that simultaneous PLEX and IVMPS will improve the recovery of the damaged cells and prevent further disability.

Atrikumar Patel, Kumari Archana, Ashish Kumar Duggal, Jyoti Garg

Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, Type III, Connaught Place, New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: GFAP (Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein) is an intermediate filament protein in astrocytes. Antibody to GFAP in Serum/cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) causes a clinical entity known as autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy. Clinical spectrum includes meningitis, encephalitis and myelitis with monophasic or relapsing course. Visual symptoms in GFAP astrocytopathy can occur in the form of papilledema or papillitis. We report a case of GFAP astrocytopathy with asymmetric disc edema.

Case report: A 25-year-old female presented with a complaint of seeing bright visual objects in the visual fields of both eyes, transient visual obscuration for 4 months and subacute onset blurring of vision in the right eye for 2 months. Fundus examination suggested right-side optic disc pallor and left-side optic disc oedema. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain was normal, but there was subtle T2 hyperintensity in the right optic nerve’s intraorbital part. Lumbar puncture revealed normal opening pressure with 2 cells/mm3 and normal protein and sugar. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed increased retinal nerve fiber layer thickness in the left eye and reduced retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) in the right eye. The patient tested negative for Neuromyelitis optica (NMO) and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies, but the serum GFAP antibody was positive. The patient was treated with intravenous (IV) pulse steroids followed by oral steroids in a tapering dose. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) was given after a pulse dose of steroids, with minimal improvement in visual acuity.

Discussion and conclusions: GFAP astrocytopathy is an important cause of optic neuropathy, and GFAP antibody testing should be considered in patients with isolated optic neuropathy, especially when NMO and MOG antibodies are negative.

Mohinish S, Muhammed Shadique, Neeraj Elango, Jered Livingston, Leema Pauline, Sonia Rosalind Martina, Shree Shruthi Badrinath, Neeraj Elango, Jered Livingston, Leema Pauline

Madras Medical College (MMC), Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: In pediatric autoimmune encephalitis (AIE), neurological manifestations are prominent initial presentation as compared to behavioral or psychiatric symptoms. Early diagnosis and prompt treatment lead to improved outcomes with reduced relapses. The aim of this study was to analyze the clinical profile and treatment options in seropositive and seronegative patients and long-term motor and neurocognitive outcomes in both groups.

Methodology: Materials and methods: An ambispective analysis of AIE patients admitted in the center from January 2021 to December 2023.

Results: A total of 36 children were included. 25 (70%) were positive for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) autoimmune panel (NMDAR), in which 5 (20%) were herpes simplex virus (HSV) triggered, 10 (28%) probable, 1 (2%) possible AIE. The mean age of onset was 6.1 years (1.2 years-12 years). The clinical features were seizures (83%), encephalopathy (72%), movement disorders (52%), behavioral disturbances (48%), sleep disturbances and speech disturbances (43%) and autonomic (16%). Mean duration of paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) stay was 23 days. Neuroimaging was normal in 66.7% of cases. Mean time to initiate immunotherapy is 13 days. 23 (96%) seropositive cases and 3 (28%) sero negative cases received 2nd line immunotherapy. Among seropositive cases, 78% received Rituximab, 18% both Rituximab and Cyclophosphamide. Overall mortality was 2 (5.5%). Mean duration of follow-up 18 months (6 – 42 months). Three cases had relapsed during follow-up, and two cases were noted to have autoimmune epilepsy. 60% of seropositive and 18% of seronegative cases had residual deficits in terms of modified Rankin Scale, cognitive and behavior outcome scales. All HSV-triggered cases had residual defects and poor outcomes. No underlying tumor was identified in our cohort.

Conclusions: Though autoimmune encephalitis has a stormy acute phase, it usually remains monophasic in children. Outcomes are favorable in the large majority of affected children. Those with HSV encephalitis and evidence of structural brain lesions fare poorly.

Deenanath Mangeshkar Hospital and Research Center, Pune, Maharashtra, India

Background and Aim: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) occurs due to low cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volume within central nervous system, due to spontaneous leak of CSF into extradural space presenting with varied symptoms. SIH is often misdiagnosed due to vague clinical features and lack of diagnostic consensus among the medical field practitioners. Longer time to diagnosis and treatment can lead to deleterious consequences and delayed recovery. The aim is to study clinico-radiological profile and management of patients diagnosed as SIH.

Case report: A retrospective case series of 13 cases of SIH diagnosed in our hospital from Aug 2020 to April 2024 were included. Demography and clinical characteristics were noted. Imaging findings and treatment given were documented. Functional outcomes in the form of treatment responses and recurrences were noted.

Discussion: A total of 13 cases (males 6; female 7) with diagnosis of SIH were identified. The mean age at onset was 37 years (range: 26-53 years). The most common clinical presentations were postural headache (100%), nausea or vomiting (77%), neck pain (37%) and visual complaints (7%). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated subdural hygroma (61.53%), pachymeningeal enhancement (76.92%), prominent venous sinuses (61.53%). Twelve patients underwent magnetic resonance (MR) myelography which demonstrated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak. Sites of leak were cervical (84.61%), thoracic (15.38%), lumbar leak (7%) while 23% had >1 site of leak. Twelve patients who progressed on conservative treatment were treated with epidural blood patch. Recurrence was 41%.

Conclusions: Timely diagnosis and treatment are required for early functional recovery and to prevent further complications in SIH patients.

Madras Medical College (MMC), Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Hemi facial spasm (HFS) is characterized by paroxysmal, involuntary twitching of facial muscles on one side of the face innervated by the ipsilateral facial nerve. The abnormal involuntary firing of the peripheral facial nerve triggers short or longer contractions of muscles of facial expression. As the name suggests, the disorder is almost always unilateral except in some rare incidences, with a reported prevalence of 2.6% of all HFS cases, during which one can see the bilateral involvement of facial muscles.

Case Report: A 11-year-old male child presented with abnormal twitching movements of both eyelids and twitching movements of left angle of mouth for past 6 months duration which was intermittent in nature, initially less than 10 episodes/day, each episode lasting few seconds. Movement is noted all through the day with no diurnal variation and is noted in sleep also. These movements get aggravated during stress and emotions and not able to suppress it voluntarily. O/E: Eyelid twitching noted with characteristic brow lift associated with twitching around angle of moth on both sides, suggestive of bifacial spasm. Workups for movement disorder including serum ceruloplasmin, antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer, electroencephalogram (EEG) were normal. The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) Axial T1 Spin echo, fast Imaging employing steady-state acquisition (FIESTA) sequence showed bilateral type II AICA loop (vascular loop) is crossing and indenting the 7th nerve at its root exit zone. Diagnosis: Bifacial Spasm: Primary type due to neuro-vascular conflicts at root exit zone. Started on Oral Carbamazepine initially at 10 mg/kg/day, and dose was titrated and monitored closely. During follow-up after 3 weeks, twitching stopped completely.

Discussion and conclusions: Differentials for movement disorders of face include Motor tics, Blepharospasm, Focal seizures and Eyelid myoclonus, which need to be differentiated for appropriate management. “Other Babinski sign” is pathognomonic of HFS and helps distinguish from eye twitching/closure due to blepharospasm, in which brow-lift is characteristically absent.

Background and Aim: Multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN) is a rare immune-mediated motor neuropathy characterized by asymmetric weakness that preferentially affects distal upper limb muscles. The diagnosis of MMN is based on clinical, laboratory and electrophysiological characteristics demonstrating conduction block. Steroids and therapeutic plasma exchange are ineffective in MMN and may lead to worsening of the disease. However, more than 80% of patients with MMN experience improvement after intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). The aim of the study is to emphasize the importance of early recognition and appropriate treatment can have positive impact on quality of life.

Case report: It is a prospective observational case series study of three patients who presented with asymmetrical onset pure motor distal predominant weakness who were investigated and treated. Informed written consent was taken.

Discussion: All three cases were either having conduction block on nerve conduction study (NCS) electromyography (EMG) study or positive IgM ganglioside panel or both. All patients were treated with IV immunoglobulin therapy and 2/3 patients showed significant improvement.

Conclusions: Early intravenous immunoglobulin is the only therapy with proven efficiency in MMN patients by providing improvement of muscle strength.

Santhosh S, Fiju Chacko

Jubilee Mission Medical College, Thrissur, Kerala, India

Background and Aim: Seizure is a medical emergency and about 1 in 10 persons will experience a seizure in their lifetime. There are only few studies on the clinical and etiological profile new-onset seizure. This present study attempted to explore the clinical and etiological profile of new-onset seizure in adults above 18 years of age. Aims and objectives: 1) To determine various clinical type of seizures in adults. 2) To study various causes of new-onset seizures. 3) To find out the most common cause of new-onset seizures in various age groups

Methodology: This cross-sectional observational study was conducted in the department of neurology in a tertiary care hospital between 2022 July and 2023 July after getting Ethical Committee approval. Nature, methodology and risks involved in the study have explained to the patients and their relatives, and informed consent was obtained. The sample size calculated from the parent study was 106. All patients who qualified the inclusion criteria were evaluated following a systematic procedure. They were interviewed as per the proforma, following which, a complete clinical examination was done. Cases of new-onset seizures (first seizure ever experienced by the patient) were diagnosed with clinical history, examination, laboratory, electroencephalogram (EEG) and radiological studies. Seizures were classified according to the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) latest classification. Causes of seizures are evaluated depending upon the clinical history and examination. All patients with new-onset seizure underwent clinical examination, blood investigation, EEG and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain (epilepsy protocol-specific brain MRI with 1-3 mm slices with additional coronal FLAIR sequences). For those patients on whom MRI cannot be performed (in case of any contraindication), computed tomography (CT) scan was performed alternatively. Statistical analysis will be carried out using SPSS version 21.0. Descriptive analyses were reported as mean and standard deviation of continuous variables. Chi-square test and Fischer exact test will be used to establish association, p < 0.05 was considered significant.

Results: A total of 106 patients with new onset seizures were enrolled on our study. Their age ranged from 18 years to 85 years. Highest incidence of new onset seizure was in the age group of 21-30 years followed by 31-40 years. Male to female ratio was 1.3:1. Among the new onset seizures most were generalized tonic-clonic seizures (71%) followed by focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure. All seizure types were common in males except focal aware seizure. In participants with alcohol withdrawal, generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS) was the predominant seizure type. Among the patients studied only 38% had findings on neurological examination. The most common clinical finding was neck stiffness (60) followed by hemiplegia/hemiparesis (30%). 27% new-onset seizures were caused by cerebrovascular accidents, which included ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke. Next common cause was central nervous system infection, which include tuberculous (TB) meningitis 38%, viral (25%), bacterial (11%), 2 cases of neurocysticercosis and one case of cryptococcal meningitis. Sixteen patients with metabolic seizures were seen in our study, among which most common was hypoglycemic seizure. Five cases of seizure due to space occupying lesion were found in our study. Two cases of organophosphorus poisoning and 1 case of camphor poisoning-induced seizures were seen in our study. Among the pregnancy-associated seizure, cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) was the commonest cause, followed by eclampsia. Imaging abnormality was seen in 54%. EEG was done for 49 patients, among 26 were abnormal, 23 were normal.

Conclusions: New-onset seizures had a male predominance with male-to-female ratio of 1.3:1. First episode of seizures was most common in 20-30 years age group. Most common type of seizure in our study was GTCS. Cerebrovascular accidents were the most common etiology followed by central nervous system (CNS) infections. Among cerebrovascular accident, most common was ischemic stroke, while among infections TB meningitis was attributed to maximum cases. In our study, 8.4% of cases no cause have been identified.

Abstract

Background and Aim: Among various causes of secondary headaches, giant cell arteritis should be considered over the age of 50 years particularly in the setting of an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and/or C-Reactive protein (CRP) with visual disturbances especially transient/permanent monocular visual loss, jaw claudication unexplained fever or other constitutional symptoms, temporal artery, tenderness to palpation and a current or prior diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica.

Case report: A 63-year-old female came with complaints of easy fatigability for 2 months, fever for 1 month, headache for 1 month predominantly in bilateral temporal region, associated with tender cord-like swelling in the bilateral temporal region and jaw pain which got aggravated while chewing. On physical examination, both temporal arteries felt thickened, nodular and tender with more pronounced thickening on the left side with diminished pulses on right side and absent pulses on left side. The rest of the general and systemic examinations and basic laboratory investigations were within normal limits. The ESR and CRP levels were elevated. Non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) of the brain was normal. Because of high clinical suspicion of giant cell arteritis (GCA), color doppler ultrasound of bilateral temporal arteries was done which revealed enlargement of both superficial temporal arteries with luminal irregularity, narrowing with hypoechoic wall thickness known as ‘halo sign’. Conventional tomography (CT) angiogram showed left superficial temporal artery attenuation with surrounding cuffing.

Discussion: Provisional diagnosis of GCA was made according to the American College of Rheumatology/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (ACR/EULAR 2022) criteria with score of ≥ 6 points.

Conclusions: If color doppler ultrasound demonstrates halo sign, then the diagnosis is confirmed without need for a biopsy.

Background and Aim: Huntington’s disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant inherited neurodegenerative disease characterized by neuropsychiatric symptoms, a movement disorder (most commonly chorea) and progressive cognitive impairment. Our aim is to present a unique case of HD, which has presented as progressive myoclonic epilepsy with mild cognitive impairment and no mental disorder and fewer CAG repeats.

Case report: A 38-year-old male born of 3rd degree consanguineous parentage with normal birth and developmental history presented with sudden brief jerky movements—myoclonus since 12 years, which were intermittent and brief to start with, they were more in the lower limbs compared to upper limbs, the jerks were present even at rest. Later he developed facial myoclonus, prominent when speaking, leading to unintelligible speech, these movements were absent in sleep, 7 years after the start of illness he developed involuntary, sustained, abnormal posturing of both upper limbs, right more than the left, with no significant behavioral, cognitive, autonomic symptoms, with no significant past history.

Discussion: After the above history, whole exome sequencing was done, which showed no significant gene and analysis showed 37 CAG repeats, confirming the diagnosis of Huntington’s disease and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed caudate atrophy.

Conclusions: Through our case, we would like to impress upon the varied presentations of most common neurodegenerative movement disorder which every clinician has to be aware of in order to avoid misdiagnosis and waste of time and resources.

Aditya Ganguly

Kolkata Medical College, Kolkata, West Bengal, India

Background and Aim: Delirium is a common problem in neurology and is mostly caused by a few common causes. Here we present a case of delirium which developed due to an unusual cause and under unusual circumstances. This will help clinicians make a quicker diagnosis and provide better outcomes.

Case report: Detailed history was taken, general and neurological examination done and neuroimaging performed for this patient admitted under the Department of General Medicine, Medical College Kolkata as a referral case. A 52-year-old lady with a h/o stable ischemic heart disease (SIHD) presented with subacute onset, progressively worsening holocranial headache followed by delirium after traveling to Darjeeling from Kolkata. Her symptoms started within 1 day of reaching her destination. The patient has a history of similar headache and slight drowsiness when she visited Darjeeling around 2 years back. She was advised not to visit the place but she refused to follow that advice. The patient was quickly brought back to Kolkata within 3 days of her symptoms and admitted to our institution. Routine blood investigations were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain showed diffuse T2/ fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensities in the subcortical white matter and corpus callosum with a cytotoxic lesion of the corpus callosum (CLOCC)—these were suggestive of high-altitude cerebral edema. The patient was managed in the ICU with supplemental O2 therapy and dexamethasone and made a complete recovery over several weeks.

Discussion and Conclusions: One should keep a close watch to ensure that high-altitude cerebral edema as a cause of delirium is not missed.

Shailina Ali, Rishikesh Joshi, Mayur Takkar, Neeraj Jain, Dean Sangeeta Ravat

Seth G S Medical College & KEM Hospital, Mumbai, Maharashtra, India

Background and Aim: Lithium, a mood stabilizer, can cause both acute and chronic neurotoxicity. Here, we present an exceptional sequela of lithium toxicity, the Syndrome of Irreversible lithium-effectuated neurotoxicity (SILENT). Usually, full recovery follows lithium discontinuation, but in rare instances, permanent neurological sequelae occur.

Case report: Case description of a patient with subacute onset static cerebellar dysfunction after lithium therapy. A 50-year-old female presented with a four-year history of subacute onset gait and limb ataxia with scanning speech without involvement of pyramidal, extrapyramidal system and cognition. Four years earlier, she was started on lithium therapy for bipolar disorder. After 2 months, she developed fever, gastroenteritis, renal failure and altered sensorium. Her lithium level was 2.6 mmol/L (normal range: 0.6–1.2 mmol/L). She was intubated and underwent hemodialysis. After metabolic parameters normalized, her sensorium improved but developed persistent cerebellar dysfunction. Her recent routine labs, Vitamin B12, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), nerve conduction study (NCS) and whole-body positron emission tomography (PET) study were normal. The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed extensive cerebellar atrophy and normal basal ganglia.

Discussion and conclusions: This case report highlights SILENT as a potential cause of cerebellar ataxia and underscores the need for pretreatment counseling about irreversible toxicity of lithium therapy.

Vydehi Institute of Medical Sciences and Research Centre, Bengaluru (VIMS, Bengaluru), Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: In this poster, we present a case of bilateral facial palsy occurring as first clinical manifestation of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

Case report: A 29-year-old heterosexual male with no significant past medical history presented with a 7-day history of headache with altered behavior, high-grade fever with chills and rigors, 5 days history of bifacial weakness and 1 episode of vomiting the before night. General examination revealed bifacial lower motor neuron (LMN) type of weakness, neck rigidity and drowsiness.

Discussion and conclusions: Peripheral facial palsy can occur at any stage of HIV infection; however, it is more likely to be present in healthy HIV carriers than in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Peripheral palsy can be divided into two types according to etiology; an early stage-related palsy and a late stage-related palsy. In initial stages of HIV infection, patients may develop either Bell’s palsy or Guillain–Barre syndrome.

Vaibhav Bhandari, Animesh Das

All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) is an autosomal recessive heredodegenerative disease caused by a mutation in the PANK 2 gene. It is characterized by progressive neurodegenerative disorder and iron deposition in the central nervous system. PKAN presents with motor symptoms of parkinsonism, dystonia and tremors. The disease has two main phenotypes: typical PKAN, which manifests in the first decade of life with rapid progression leading to loss of ambulation within 10-15 years, and atypical PKAN, which has a later age of onset, slower progression and a better prognosis.

Case report: A 40-year-old female presented with bilateral heel dystonia, bilateral upper limb distal postural tremors and difficulty in walking. Symptoms also included freezing of gait, postural instability, bradykinesia, memory impairment and palilalia. On examination, vertical gaze palsy with slow and hypometric saccades was present. Positive family history, T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in globus pallidus and above symptoms suggested heredodegenerative parkinsonism. Whole exome sequencing suggested PANK2 gene positivity.

Discussion: Given the symptoms, late onset of disease, slow progression, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) finding and positive whole exome sequencing (WES) with PANK 2 gene, the patient was diagnosed with atypical PKAN. Treatment included syndopa, trihexyphenidyl and baclofen for Parkinsonism symptoms. Deferiprone, an iron chelator, was also started.

Conclusions: Atypical PKAN with supranuclear gaze palsy was observed in a patient, contributing to the phenotypic variability of the disease. The report highlights the importance of imaging and genetic studies in diagnosing atypical symptoms and diseases.

Background and Aim: The Russell’s viper is a frequently encountered venomous snake in India, often leading to significant morbidity and mortality. This case report highlights an infrequently observed complication following the treatment of a viper bite.

Case report: A 36-year-old male hotel worker received 20 vials of polyvalent anti-snake venom after a viper bite on his left leg. Patient initially presented with compartment syndrome of left leg managed with fasciotomy. Manvitha G, Johann Christopher, Umesh T, Umesh T, Johann Christopher, Umesh T

Care Hospital Banjara Hills, Hyderabad, Telangana, India

Background and Aim: Left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC) is characterized by a thin, compacted epicardial layer and an extensive non-compacted endocardial layer with prominent trabeculation and deep recesses that communicate with the left ventricular (LV) cavity leading to less ejection fraction which in turn leads to intracardiac thrombus formation and systemic embolization.

Case Report: A 5-year-old child born out of third-degree consanguineous marriage came with chief complaints of sudden onset weakness of right upper and lower limb with deviation of mouth to left side since 1 day. Neurological examination revealed right upper and lower limb pyramidal distribution of weakness with right upper motor neuron facial palsy. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain was done which showed acute infarct in the left middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory and cerebral angiogram revealed abrupt cut off of left M1 segment suggestive of thrombotic occlusion. 2D echo showed left ventricular (LV) non-compaction with dilated left ventricle and left ventricular dysfunction, left atrial appendage (LAA) aneurysm with thrombus and spontaneous echo contrast. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) which showed aneurysmal Left atrial appendage with one-third thrombotic occlusion. N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-pro BNP) was elevated. She was treated with anticoagulants. 2D-ECHO at the end of 1 year revealed complete resolution of the thrombus from the left atrial appendage. Cardiac MRI was done for quantification of the non-compaction and thrombus evaluation which revealed non-compaction volume equal to 82 ml, non-compaction mass equal to 86 grams and resolution of the thrombus. Family screening revealed a younger sister having 2D echo which revealed LV non-compaction with left atrial appendage aneurysm with no thrombus and a first cousin sister who succumbed 8 years ago. Genetic evaluation was unremarkable.

Discussion and Conclusions: Coexisting of left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC) and left atrial appendage (LAA) aneurysm is accompanied by a high risk of thrombosis, and anticoagulation needs to be instituted. Comprehensive workup for the etiology of stroke is warranted as it modifies the treatment.
