Background and Aim: Spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA) type 12 is the most common SCA reported from India. It is particularly reported in North Indian Agarwal community. Being autosomal dominant in inheritance, it presents with strong family history. The presenting features are postural hand tremor to start with and followed by cerebellar ataxia of variable severity. More than 43 CAG/CTG repeat expansion in PPP2R2B gene in chromosome 5q32 is needed for clinical manifestations. Here, two cases of SCA 12 will be reported from a Bengali family who presented with some unusual clinical features.

Case report: We examined two sisters of a Bengali Hindu family from Murshidabad district of West Bengal. Both are symptomatic for more than 10 years with abnormal speech quality, postural hand tremor and gait imbalance. The elder sister aged 57 years also had significant fidgetiness of limbs and forgetfulness. Younger of them aged 50 years was wheelchair bound out of severe gait imbalance. Onsets were before 50 years of age in both. Family history was positive for tremor and gait imbalance.

Discussion: In either case, gross features of cerebellar ataxia including ataxic speech were found. The elder sister had generalized choreiform movements. Younger sister showed wing-beating tremor in both proximal upper limbs. In both cases, recent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain showed mild cerebellar atrophy. Wilson’s disease and previous cerebrovascular event were excluded. We did a comprehensive SCA panel with a future plan of targeted exome sequencing. The report was positive for SCA 12 with > 51 CAG repeat sequences.

Conclusions: SCA 12 is more ubiquitous than it was previously thought, and it can present with much different movement phenomenology.

Background and Aim: Morvan’s syndrome is an autoimmune disorder of peripheral and central nervous system mediated by voltage-gated potassium channel (VGKC) antibody. It is characterized by peripheral nerve hyperexcitability, dysautonomia, insomnia and fluctuating delirium. We report a case of 36-year-old male with neuromyotonia-like presentation, with anti-contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR-2 ab) positive after Ayurvedha drug intake.

Case report: A 36-year-old male presented with complaints of muscle cramps, twitching’s, mood and sleep disturbances with fatigability of 1-month duration. He had H/o intake of Ayurvedha medicine for 1 month for his complaint of gastritis, before the onset of his present symptoms. On examination, he was found to have postural hypotension and myokymic rippling muscle movements over his bilateral chest, arms and thighs.

Discussion: Electromyography (EMG) showed spontaneous activity and motor unit action potential (MUAPs) in the form of doublets and triplets. Morvan’s syndrome was thought of, and test for VGKC antibody was done. CASPR-2 antibody turned out to be positive in high titer. He was treated with high-dose pulse steroids for 5 days, and there was inadequate response for which he was treated with intravenous (IV) immunoglobulins at a dose of 0.4g/kg/day for 5 days followed by slow steroid taper over 2 months.

Conclusions: A rare association of Ayurvedha drug intake with Morvan’s syndrome has been established in this case report. This highlights the importance of recognizing this entity, in a country like India where Siddha and ayurvedic drugs are used in abundance.

Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI), Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Amyloid light chain or primary amyloidosis (AL amyloidosis) is the most common form of systemic amyloidosis; AL amyloidosis is caused by disorders of plasma cells, or rarely B cells that produce light chain immunoglobulins with the potential for misfolding and deposition as amyloid fibrils. Peripheral neuropathy occurs in 17% to 36% of patients with AL amyloidosis

Case report: A 47-year-old male was referred with a diagnosis of alcoholic peripheral neuropathy. He had a 10 years history of progressive paresthesia of bilateral lower limbs distal weakness in form of slippage of footwear. He did not have any autonomic symptoms. He was a chronic alcoholic for 20 years. The general examination was unremarkable with no autonomic dysfunction, neurologic examination demonstrated distal leg weakness; his patellar reflexes were reduced, and ankle reflexes were absent. Sensory examination showed reduced pin-prick and temperature sensation up to mid-shin and a decreased vibration sensation and proprioception in toes. His gait revealed sensory ataxia with positive Rhomberg sign. Electrodiagnostic (EDX) studies demonstrated demyelinating pattern.

Discussion: His serum protein electrophoresis showed a positive M Spike, serum immunofixation assay showed IgG lambda monoclonal gammopathy, and sural nerve biopsy was done which showed congophilic and eosinophilic deposits in the walls of the capillaries which exhibited apple green birefringence on polarizing, he is being initiated on chemotherapy.

Conclusions: Serum protein electrophoresis should be a part of routine workup to prevent missing paraproteinemic neuropathies which are often underdiagnosed. The mainstay of treatment is to address the underlying plasma cell dyscrasia.

Background and Aim: We present the case of an 11-year-old boy from Pune, belonging to an upper-middle socio-economic class, currently in the 3rd standard with a good academic performance. The patient presented with acute neurological symptoms, including jerky movements, increased sleepiness, decreased appetite and irrelevant talk over the past 4-5 days, with a prior history of fever and parotitis.

Case report: A detailed clinical evaluation was conducted, including patient history, physical examination and various diagnostic tests. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, electroencephalography (EEG), visual evoked potential (VEP), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis and specific serological tests for measles antibodies were performed. VEP results indicated anterior optic nerve pathway inconsistent responses. Discussion: The patient was diagnosed with subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), confirmed by the presence of high anti-measles antibody titers in both serum and CSF, with a CSF/serum ratio of 8.65 and a total CSF IgG index of 4.2.

Conclusions: This case highlights the importance of considering SSPE in pediatric patients presenting with new-onset myoclonic jerks and behavioral changes, especially in the context of a recent measles infection. Background and Aim: Superficial siderosis is a chronic progressive neurological disorder characterized by triad of symptoms—sensorineural hearing loss, cerebellar ataxia and myelopathy. Hemanga K. Dhing, Masaraf Hussain, Chandan Nath

All India institute of Medical Sciences, Guwahati, Assam

Background and Aim: Migraine constitutes a complex disabling disease with a multifactorial background. Dietary habits and nutrients have been associated with migraine. The aim of the study was to correlate serum vitamin D3 levels with the severity, disability and chronicity of Migraine.

Methodology: Patients fulfilling international classification of headache disorders (ICHD 3) criteria were retrospectively enrolled between December 2023 and May 2024. Severity was determined by visual analog scale (VAS). Migraine Disability Assessment (MIDAS) was calculated to evaluate the migraine-related disability over the previous 3 months. Serum concentrations of vitamin D3 were determined by enhanced chemiluminescence method.

Results: A total of 172 patients were included in the study. Majority (77%) of patients were females. Mean age was 33.3 (±11.4) years. Mean duration was 5.5 (±7.35) years. Hemicranial headache was present in half (51%) of patients. Headache was pulsatile in nature in 55% of patients. Photophobia and phonophobia were most common associated features (78%). Migraine was transformed to chronic in 46 (26.7%) patients. Mean vitamin D levels were 26 (±8.8) ng/dl. Vitamin D levels were insufficient (<30 ng/dl) in 65% of patients. Vitamin D3 levels were correlated negatively with severity of Migraine pain as determined by VAS score (Pearson’s r=-0.308, p < 0.01) and disability as determined by MIDAS score (Pearson’s r=-0.162, p = 0.03). However, the level was not found significantly higher in case of chronic Migraine (P = 0.384).

Conclusions: Vitamin D deficiency is associated with the severity and disability of Migraine patients. Adequate supplementation of Vitamin D is necessary to ameliorate the severity and disability of Migraine patients.

Background and Aim: Measles is a highly contagious disease caused by a virus of the paramyxovirus family. Various measles-related neurological syndromes include primary measles encephalitis, acute post-measles encephalitis, measles inclusion body encephalitis and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). SSPE is a rare slowly progressive fatal inflammatory disease of the central nervous system characterized by seizures, myoclonic jerks, progressive deterioration of cognitive and motor functions, sometimes associated with pyramidal and extrapyramidal symptoms including chorea, dystonia and parkinsonism. Here, I am reporting a case of young male presenting with slow myoclonic jerks, cognitive decline and characteristic electroencephalogram (EEG) findings suggestive of SSPE.

Case report: A 17-year-old male with normal perinatal period and development with history of meningoencephalitis at the age of 6 months and another separate history of fever with rashes at 8 years of age presented with abnormal body movements for the past 1 year. He also had gradual decline in scholastic performance. On examination, he had an mini mental state examination (MMSE) score of 18/30 and found to have slow myoclonic jerks affecting the entire body, involving proximal and distal parts of limbs which disappeared in sleep. His EEG showed generalized periodic epileptiform discharges with inter-burst interval of 5-6 seconds. His measles IgG was elevated in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood.

Discussion: So, with the above characteristic findings, he was diagnosed as probable SSPE and treated with antiepileptics and other supportive measures for which he showed symptomatic improvement.

Conclusions: The purpose of this case report is to have awareness regarding the presentations of SSPE, especially in a developing country.

Sharanya Raj, Archana N B, Janardhan DC, Praveen Kumar S, Pramod K

Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute, Bengaluru (BMCRI Bengaluru), Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: SCAR8 (Spinocerebellar ataxia recessive type 8), also known as ARCA1 (Autosomal Recessive Cerebellar Ataxia type 1), is a rare genetic cause of autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia. While it typically presents with pure cerebellar symptoms, it can occasionally involve other systems, as well. It is caused by mutations in the SYNE1 gene.

Case report: We report the clinical and radiological features and genetic analysis of a sixteen-year-old female patient with SCAR8. Our patient had delayed attainment of gross motor milestones, slurred speech since two years of age, imbalance while walking and tremors of all four limbs since the age of 5 years, which has been slowly progressive. On examination, she exhibited scanning speech, broken pursuits, end gaze nystagmus, cerebellar ataxia, brisk deep tendon reflexes, focal dystonia of the right great toe and mild intellectual disability. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed mild cerebellar atrophy with corticospinal tract and optic radiation hyperintensities, a finding not previously reported. Whole exome sequencing identified a pathogenic heterozygous nonsense variation in exon 35 of the SYNE1 gene resulting in a premature stop codon and truncation of the protein at codon 1521 (p.Arg1521Ter). Additionally, a novel heterozygous missense variation in exon 143 of the SYNE1 gene leading to the amino acid substitution of Histidine for Arginine at codon 8651 (p.Arg8651His) was also detected.

Discussion and Conclusions: SCAR8 may present with various neurological features beyond cerebellar involvement. Furthermore, in the appropriate clinical context, it should be considered as a differential diagnosis for corticospinal tract and optic radiation hyperintensities observed on magnetic resonance imaging.

Background and Aim: Spinal dysraphism refers to a group of congenital anomalies of the spine which results in a defective neural arch through which meninges and/or neural elements are herniated leading to a variety of clinical manifestations. The aim is to study the incidence, clinical presentations and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings in spinal dysraphism patients.

Methodology: This was a retrospective observational study among 35 patients conducted in KAPV Government Medical college, Trichy over a period of 1 year from April 2023 to May 2024. All OPD as well as IPD patients were screened.

Results: The incidence was high in males (60%) compared to females (40%). Most of the cases were reported to hospital during the first one month of life (51.4%). Spina bifida Aperta was present in 22 patients (62.86%) compared to Spina bifida occulta in only 13 patients (37.1%). The commonest site was the lumbosacral region in 14 patients (40.0%). Most common finding was myelomeningocele in 17 (46.87%) cases. Lipomyelomeningocele was seen in 4 cases which was most common finding in closed type. Diastematomyelia was seen in 1 case (6.25%). The most common associated anomaly was hydrocephalus in 12 (34.28%) patients and next common was Arnold Chiari malformation type 2 in 8 (22.8%) cases. Eight cases didn’t have any proper anti-natal checkups and no folic acid supplementations were taken in the antenatal period. Mothers of 4 patients were on anti-epileptic drugs (AED) during the time of conception.

Conclusions: Spinal dysraphism patients should be referred to a higher center where all the facilities including surgery are available. Patients should be given proper awareness in the ground level mainly in the primary health centres (PHCs) regarding intake of folic acid supplementation during antenatal period.

Stanley Medical College Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Elseberg syndrome is a rare, mostly self-limiting condition characterized by acute to subacute onset lumbosacral radiculitis, with or without myelitis confined to lower spinal cord. Herpes simplex virus- 2 (HSV-2), reactivation or occasionally primary infection is the most commonly reported cause of Elseberg syndrome; varicella-zoster virus (VZV), West Nile and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV) being the other infectious causes. We report a case of clinically definite Elseberg syndrome, caused by VZV reactivation.

Case report: A 70-year-old lady presented with vesicular skin lesions in the perineal region, right buttock, right foot dorsal and plantar aspect. Four days later she developed severe burning pain in the same regions, due to which she was unable to walk. She also developed urinary disturbances in the form of urgency and frequency. After two days, she lost sensation of bladder fullness and developed retention of urine. On examination, she had grouped vesicles in L5, S1, S2 and S3 dermatomes. She had spasticity in both lower limbs, with normal power and bilateral brisk knee and ankle jerk, with anal reflex absent in the right side. All the modalities of sensations are reduced in the right L5 to S5 distribution. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) lumbosacral spine was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed elevated protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis. CSF serology is normal.

Discussion: The above case is fitting into the diagnosis of clinically definite Elseberg syndrome, as per the Salvodi diagnostic criteria, based on the signs and symptoms of cauda equina involvement, subacute onset and progression less than three months, coexisting herpes zoster and CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis.

Conclusions: Elsberg syndrome may progress to a very severe neurological illness which could be avoided by prompt diagnosis and effective management.

Background and Aim: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) is a rare non-inflammatory central nervous system (CNS) demyelinating disease. It is reported commonly with rapid correction of hyponatremia but can also occur with other conditions causing rapid changes in serum osmolarity.

Case report: A 45-year-old diabetic male presented with complaints of sudden onset unsteadiness of gait and slurring of speech of 7 days duration. Examination showed dysarthria, nystagmus, bilateral impairment of finger nose and heel knee tests, dysdiadochokinesia and impaired tandem gait. Vital signs were normal.

Discussion: Random blood sugar (RBS) :610, HbA1C : 8.6, Na+ : 136, K+: 3.6, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) : Normal, magnetic resonance imagin (MRI) brain: T2 and fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintense signal with T1 hypointensity showing facilitated diffusion restriction in pons, middle and inferior cerebellar peduncles.

Conclusions: Not only rapid correction of hyponatremia, but also sudden rapid change in extracellular fluid osmolarity due to diabetes mellitus can cause ODS. The exact mechanism for the development of ODS and appropriate glycemic correction rate needs further evaluation. ODS can be missed in clinical setting; as it can be fatal and debilitating, it must be considered in any kind of disorder associated with change in osmolarity.

Continental Hospital Plot no 3, Financial district Gachibowli, Nanakramguda, Hyderabad, Telangana, India

Background and Aim: Bell’s palsy is a common cranial neuropathy causing acute unilateral lower motor neuron facial paralysis. Though Bell’s palsy is common, recurrent Bell’s palsy is an unusual occurrence and reported in only 0.3-2% of Bell’s palsy cases and recognizes very few identifiable causes. Here, we present a case of recurrent Bell’s palsy with prolonged intervals between episodes, where she developed lymphadenopathy in the later stages leading to the diagnosis of sarcoidosis.

Case report: A 44-year-old woman presented with right lower motor neuron (LMN) facial palsy in February 2021. She was started on steroids and her facial weakness improved within a few weeks. Four months later, she developed left LMN facial palsy. This time, she was evaluated in detail for causes of recurrent Bell’s palsy. Tests including antinuclear antibodies- immunofluorescence assay (ANA-IFA), serum- angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) levels, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), COVID-19, IgG Lyme and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain were done, and all reports were negative. Considering idiopathic Bell’s palsy steroids and valganciclovir were given and showed improvement. She developed a third episode of facial palsy on the left side on December 23. Upon examination, she also had a cervical lymph node. Investigations were repeated to assess the cause of recurrent Bell’s palsy, and the lymph nodes fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed. Contrast enhanced computed tomography (CECT) chest also showed mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

Discussion: Serum ACE levels were elevated and the FNAC showed non-caseating granuloma confirming the diagnosis of Sarcoidosis and confirming it as the cause for recurrent Bell’s palsy. The patient was started on mycophenolate mofetil with bridging steroids and is doing well.

Conclusions: Sarcoidosis can cause recurrent Bell’s palsy, often before other symptoms appear. Thus, clinicians should suspect sarcoidosis in recurrent cases to ensure early diagnosis and treatment, preventing complications and improving outcomes.

Madurai Medical College, Madurai, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: The boomerang sign refers to a boomerang-shaped region of cytotoxic edema in the splenium of the corpus callosum typically seen in cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum. Transient signal alteration in the splenium of corpus callosum on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain has been reported in a variety of neurologic and non-neurologic conditions such as epilepsy, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), hypoglycemia, encephalitis/encephalopathy. We describe 2 cases here.

Case report: Case 1— A 25 year/Female P2L2, post- lower segment caesarean section (LSCS), postoperative day (POD)- 24 presented with C/o fever, headache and vomiting for 2 days with altered mental status and got admitted. On examination, vitals stable, disoriented. MRI of the brain showed hyperintensity of the splenium of corpus callosum (“Boomerang sign”) on diffusion-weighted image (DWI). Total leukocytes increased and other routine biochemical parameters normal. Treated with I.V. antibiotics and clinically improved. Follow-up MRI brain done after 1 month showed normal study. Case 2— A 33 year/Male presented with C/o fever for 2 days followed by loss of consciousness and got admitted. On examination, vitals stable patient is drowsy and on day 2 sensorium improved and bilateral cerebellar signs present and MRI brain showed diffusion restriction of splenium of corpus callosum and no post-contrast enhancement. Total WBC count increased, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood culture normal, blood urea–96 mg/dl, serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dl. The patient was treated with IV antibiotics. Thereafter, patient clinically improved and the repeat MRI done after a week showed normal study.

Discussion and Conclusions: Apart from epilepsy, the transient signal alterations in splenium of corpus callosum have been described in patients with encephalitis/encephalopathy due to various organisms, hypertensive encephalopathy, preeclampsia, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) and toxic effects of cyclosporine. It is a self-limiting phenomenon, which subsides over a period once the underlying disease gets controlled.

Background and Aim: Neurosarcoidosis is one of the common causes of chronic myelopathy. Classically a trident sign involving the posterior cord is a pathognomonic finding. Diagnosis is confirmed by histological evidence from any affected tissue.

Case report: A 28-year-old gentleman presented with history of chronic progressive lower limb spasticity beginning from the right lower limb later involving the left lower limb with some history of cotton wool sensation involving the lower limbs. Jayavardhan Reddy Katam, Haritha S, Subbaraj Devaraj, Lakshmanan S, Mugundhan Krishnan, Sowmini P. R, Sakthi Velayudham, Malcolm Jeyaraj K, Viveka Sarvanan, Kannan V, Tino Baby

Stanley Medical College and Hospital Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Cerebral proliferative angiopathy (CPA) is a distinct entity from cerebral arterio-venous malformations; characterized by multiple small arterial feeders and draining veins with normal brain parenchyma seen in between the abnormal vessels. It is usually seen in younger age group. Here, we report a case of diffuse CPA in a 57-year-old female patient, with characteristic imaging findings.

Case report: A 57-year-old, diabetic and hypertensive, presented with headache, vomiting, seizure, altered sensorium. Physical examination was normal, except for b/l papilledema. No skin lesions were present.

Discussion: Non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) of brain showed left occipital lobe intraparenchymal hemorrhage, and left parieto-occipital lobe subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Since this is not a common site for hypertensive bleed, and her blood pressure levels were normal, we proceeded with CT angiogram, which showed dilated tortuous vessels in left temporoparietal lobe with no prominent arterial feeder or venous drainage, showing puddling of contrast in delayed venous imaging, suggestive of cerebral proliferative angiopathy.

Conclusions: Cerebral proliferative angiopathy should be considered as a separate entity from “classical” brain arteriovenous malformation (AVMs). It is important to recognize this entity to avoid aggressive surgery or intervention and thus prevent permanent damage to the normal intermingled brain tissue.

We herein report a case of Scrub Typhus pneumonia with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) that later developed into Parsonage-Turner syndrome.

Case report: A 57-year-old male with no comorbidities presented with a 1-week history of fever and headache. On examination, he was found to be dyspnoeic, tachypnoeic, and hypoxic, with respiratory failure. General examination revealed the presence of a skin eschar. Due to respiratory failure, he was intubated and placed on mechanical ventilator. IgM antibody for Scrub Typhus was positive at a high titer. A diagnosis of Scrub Typhus pneumonia with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) was made. He was treated with parenteral antibiotics: doxycycline, piperacillin–tazobactam, and levofloxacin. He recovered from his illness. A week later, while recuperating, he developed severe pain in his left shoulder and arm. Subsequently, he experienced weakness in the left shoulder girdle and left elbow muscles. On examination, he exhibited wasting and weakness of the left shoulder girdle and left elbow muscles, including the trapezius, deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and biceps. There was also patchy sensory involvement from the left C5 to C8/T1 segment. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left brachial plexus revealed short-tau inversion recovery (STIR) hyperintensity of the left C4-C5 to C7-D1 nerve roots, trunk, division, and cords up to the axilla, with clumping and contrast enhancement. Denervation changes in the left supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles were evidenced by hyperintensity. Nerve conduction studies of the brachial plexus were suggestive of left brachial plexopathy.

Discussion: A diagnosis of Parsonage–Turner syndrome was made. The patient was treated with pulse methyl prednisolone followed by oral prednisolone, leading to remarkable improvement.

Conclusions: We herein present this case for its rarity and to highlight the occurrence of Parsonage–Turner syndrome as a late complication of Scrub Typhus pneumonia.

Background and Aim: Cerebral amoebiasis is a rare form of invasive amebiasis with a fatal outcome. It is uncommon to observe cerebral involvement without any lung or liver infestation.

Background and Aim: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS) is a rare idiopathic vasculitis that affects small and medium-sized vessels, confined to the brain, leptomeninges, and spinal cord.

Conclusions: Diagnosing PACNS is challenging not only due to its rarity but also because of its variable and often nonspecific presentations. A high index of clinical suspicion and rigorous investigations are necessary to confirm the diagnosis and exclude other mimicking conditions.

Background and Aim: Ptotic tongue (PT) or tongue paresis—whether unilateral or bilateral—is one of the less acknowledged clinical features found in routine practice. PT can result from lesions involving the supranuclear, nuclear, infranuclear pathways, or the tongue musculature itself. Although the segmental approach for diagnosing infranuclear lesions has been well described in the literature, the supranuclear pathway is often overlooked. In this case series, we present various etiologies of both supranuclear and infranuclear PT.

Discussion and Conclusions: A segmental approach for the tongue paresis helps in evaluation of the supranuclear, nuclear, and infranuclear causes of ptotic tongue.

Background and Aim: Isolated interhemispheric subdural hematoma (IHSDH) represents one of the rarest forms of intracranial hemorrhage. Case report: A 60-year-old male presented with an acute onset of severe holocranial throbbing headache and vomiting. The patient had no history of seizures or weakness. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable, with a blood pressure (BP) of 140/90 mmHg and a Glasgow coma scale (GCS) score of 15/15. His pupils were normal, muscle tone and power were intact. Discussion: The CT angiogram showed no evidence of an aneurysm or cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT). The coagulation profile, complete blood count, bleeding time, peripheral smear, D-dimer, and cancer screening results were all normal. His sensorium remained stable, and he was treated conservatively.

Conclusions: Isolated spontaneous IHSDH is rare. We carefully excluded all potential causes, and the patient was observed for any expansion of the hematoma or rapidly deteriorating levels of consciousness. Nonsurgical treatment was chosen, as his neurological condition remained stable.

Suman S. Khushwaha, Pratik Pravin Babel, Aldrin Anthony, Rachana Agarwal, Monali Chaturvedi, Mohammmed Faruq, Rajinder Dhamija, Chandra Tripathi

Institute of Human Behaviour and allied sciences, New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Wilsons disease (WD) is associated with a variety of movement disorders. Although dystonia and dysarthria are the most common neurological signs, cognitive changes have been reported since 1912. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is abnormal in the majority of neurological WD cases. India has been a geographical hotspot for WD. Cognitive changes reported in WD include frontal syndrome and subcortical dementia. This study provides insight into detailed cognitive functions.

Methodology: We recruited 30 patients with WD. The unified WD rating Scale (UWDRS) and global assessment scale (GAS) were used to determine the severity of neurological involvement. Detailed cognitive testing was performed, and MRI of the brain was conducted to study the pattern of involvement and its correlation with the severity of neurological involvement.

Results: Interim analysis yielded the following findings: 1. The mean duration from disease onset to diagnosis was 2.5 years. 2. Among the 30 patients, 19 (63.3%) had cognitive impairment at presentation. 3. Frontal cognitive dysfunction was found in 16 (53.3%) patients. 4. Baseline MRI of the brain showed abnormal findings in 27 (90%) of the patients in the form of T2 hyperintensities and atrophy, which correlated with the severity of functional disability.

Conclusions: Although WD typically presents as various movement disorders, cognitive dysfunction—predominantly involving frontal circuitry—should not be overlooked. This includes executive function, memory dysfunction, and behavioral changes. Neuro-rehabilitation for patients with WD should also include cognitive rehabilitation to maximize independence and quality of life. The degree of neurological impairment in WD correlates with the time gap from disease onset to diagnosis, as well as the extent of atrophy and T2 hyperintensity in MRI of the brain. Further studies are required to guage the reversibility of cognitive symptoms with conventional treatment.

Background and Aim: Headache disorders are among the most disabling conditions causing significant morbidity both worldwide and within the Indian population. Background and Aim: This case report aims to highlight the importance of early clinical findings that can precede the onset of alopecia in the rarely diagnosed condition of thallium poisoning.

He was initially treated with oral steroids for suspected acute neuritis at another facility. Due to persistent severe symptoms, he presented to our hospital. On examination, he was unable to walk but had retained reflexes in the lower limbs with no demonstrable weakness or sensory deficits. He developed a perioral rash soon after starting gabapentin, which was considered an allergic reaction to the drug. Nerve conduction studies indicated demyelinating radiculoneuropathy. Vasculitic workup and porphyria screening was negative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed albuminocytologic dissociation. Suspecting early Gullian–Barre syndrome, the patient was treated with IVIG at total dose of 2 g/kg, which led to significant improvement in neuropathic pain and the resumption of normal walking. The patient was asymptomatic at discharge, except for persistent abdominal pain with a normal computed tomography (CT) Abdomen. One week later, he returned with the sudden onset of lower limb weakness and repeated episodes of vomiting black coloured fluid. Heavy metal toxicity, porphyria, vasculitis, atypical infections, and autoimmune neuropathies were considered. Significant alopecia was noted, leading to the consideration of thallium toxicity. Although the patient initially denied any exposure to heavy metals, 24-h urinary and blood thallium levels were found to be over 400 ug/L (normal values: 24-h urine < 10, blood < 2).

Discussion: The patient was treated with oral Prussian blue and underwent repeated hemoperfusion until his serum thallium levels normalized.

Conclusions: Thallium poisoning should be proactively considered in cases of acute neuropathy.

Narayana Health City, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: The Foix–Chavany–Marie syndrome (FCMS), also known as anterior opercular syndrome, is characterized by the loss of voluntary movement in the orofacial and pharyngeal muscles, while automatic and reflex movements remain preserved. This syndrome arises from bilateral lesions in the anterior opercular cortex. The most frequent etiology is vascular, but the causes can be heterogenous. Clinically, FCMS can be divided into three categories—developmental, acute/subacute, and transient. The developmental form is commonly associated with congenital bilateral anterior opercular dysplasia, while the acute/subacute form is often caused by central nervous system (CNS) infections or cerebrovascular accident.

Case report: We herein report two cases of FCMS with etiologies of stroke and herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis presented to our hospital. 1) A 56-year-old female with a history of right hemispheric stroke presented with complaints of swallowing difficulty and slurred speech for the past 5 months, with no limb involvement. On examination, she had buccal apraxia and oro-facial weakness, but no limb deficits were noted. Evaluation revealed a cardioembolic stroke with a new infarct in the left MCA and left ventricular (LV) clot. Due to her prolonged need for a nasogastric tube (NG) tube for over 6 months, she was given the option of a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube placement. 2) A 51-year male presented with a 3-day history of headache followed by altered behavior for 1 day, diagnosed with HSV encephalitis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed encephalitis features involving the bilateral opercular region. He gradually recovered after a course of IV antivirals, but he experienced minimal residual cognitive impairment and swallowing difficulties, necessitating an NG tube. However, these symptoms improved gradually with aggressive therapy within 1 month.

Discussion and Conclusions: This report highlights two varied etiologies of the FCMS and their different outcomes. Increased awareness of this syndrome among clinicians is essential, especially from a clinical localization perspective.

Background and Aim: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) is an inflammatory disorder of the central nervous system characterized by immune-mediated demyelination predominantly targeting the optic nerves, brain, and spinal cord. Rohit Kushwah, Samhita Panda, Sarbesh Tiwari, Swati Chhabra, Suryanarayanan Bhaskar, Simran Bhalla

All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Jodhpur, Rajasthan, India

Background and Aim: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) is a clinical condition caused by low cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volume or pressure, which may result from a spinal or cranial CSF leak. Various diagnostic modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computer tomography (CT), magnetic resonance (MR) myelography, digital subtraction myelography (DSM), and radioisotope cisternography (RIC) may be employed, depending on the complexity of the case.

Case report: A 44-year-old male, with a history of head trauma followed by cranioplasty and post-traumatic sequelae of left facial palsy, developed an insidious onset of a slowly progressive headache and intermittent drowsiness 10 years after the injury. After a further diagnostic delay of 6 years, he presented with a persistent headache, dysphagia, and an unsteady gait. SIH was confirmed by MRI and CT myelogram. Cisternography and DSM in different positions, including lateral decubitus and prone, revealed no CSF leak, and an epidural blood patch (EDBP) was performed. After the first EDBP, he experienced significant clinical improvement, but this was transient, lasting only 20 days. Over the course of a year, three subsequent digital subtraction myelography (DSMs) failed to detect a CSF leak, and additional EDBPs were unsuccessful. On reviewing imaging, the cranioplasty site was suspected, despite no leak being demonstrated. Re-exploration revealed the dissolution of the previous graft with multiple defects, and cranioplasty reconstruction was performed. This led to a gradual resolution of symptoms over 3 months.

Discussion and Conclusions: In cases where the patient remains negative for spinal longitudinal epidural collection (SLEC), those with a history of cranial site surgical intervention should be investigated for both spinal and cranial CSF leaks. Additionally, the cranioplasty implant should be thoroughly investigated for defects and managed accordingly.

Background and Aim: Eight-and-a-half syndrome is a rare neuro-ophthalmological condition characterized by conjugate horizontal gaze palsy, ipsilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and ipsilateral lower motor neuron-type facial palsy. Background and Aim: Hypernatremia is a potentially lethal condition that can cause encephalopathy, rhabdomyolysis, and osmotic demyelination. Extrapontine myelinolysis, a fairly common metabolic disorder, is associated with neurological complications.

Ranjini Metta, Salil Uppal, Ashok Uppal, Ashok Uppal, Salil Uppal

Uppal Neuro Hospital & Multispeciality Centre, Amritsar, Punjab, India

Background and Aim: Post-stroke recrudescence syndrome is a rare syndrome defined as the transient worsening of post-stroke neurological deficits or the reemergence of previous stroke-related deficits in the absence of an acute stroke. The study aims to investigate the triggers and risk factors for post stroke recrudescence (PSR).

Methodology: This observational study was conducted from July 2022 to January 2024. Both OPD and IPD patients were included. Informed consent and Institutional Ethics Committee clearance has been taken. Patients aged 18 years or older and those suspected of having an acute stroke within 72 h of symptom onset were included. Patients who did not undergo magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) after admission or who had new infarctions were excluded. Data collected included duration of stay, prognosis, comorbidities, treatment details, premorbid modified Rankin scale scores, and National institutes of health stroke scale (NIHSS) scores at admission. The criteria proposed by Topcuoglu et al. were used for the diagnosis of PSR. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 21.0 software, employing mean and SD or median and interquartile, as well as percentages.

Results: In this study of 26 patients with PSR, the most common triggering factor identified was infections (38.4%), with pneumonia being the major contributor. Other triggers included hyponatremia (26.9%), benzodiazepines usage (15.3%), hyperglycemia (11.5%), hypoglycemia (7.69%), and hypernatremia (7.69%).

Conclusions: This study highlights the importance of considering possible triggers such as infections, hyponatremia, benzodiazepine usage, hyperglycemia/hypoglycemia when a patient with a history of stroke presents with similar symptoms and MRI shows no new findings. When the triggering factors are addressed, the neurological impairments in patients with PSR typically resolve within a few days.

Further, he exhibited resting tremors in both upper limbs, slowness in initiating and performing voluntary movements, and slurred speech during activities.

Discussion: The autoimmune panel, including dopamine receptor basal ganglia antibodies, was negative. Serum IgM antibody for measles was positive. A diagnosis of seronegative basal ganglia encephalitis secondary to post-measles infection was made, and the patient was started on injectable methylprednisolone, followed by an oral prednisolone taper. There was almost complete recovery of symptoms related to speech and behavioral disturbances; however, residual deficits in the form of tremors were present.

Conclusions: Acute post-infectious measles encephalitis is a rare immune-mediated complication of measles infection that can present as basal ganglia encephalitis. Early diagnosis and treatment with immunosuppressive agents help prevent long-term sequelae.

Background and Aim: The spinal arachnoid web is a rare entity characterized by a band of arachnoid tissue extending to the pial surface, resulting in indentation of the spinal cord. The index case highlights the importance of diagnosing the arachnoid web as a correctable cause of paraparesis.

All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Raipur, Chhattisgarh, India

Background and Aim: Hemiballismus is an abnormal involuntary hyperkinetic movement disorder affecting the ipsilateral hemibody due to a lesion in the contralateral basal ganglia and its inhibitory connections. The etiology includes stroke, infections, dyselectrolytemia, and malignancy. We report three cases of hemiballismus with varied etiologies.

Case report: Case I: An apparently healthy 56-year-old female presented with an abrupt onset of abnormal involuntary movement involving the left hemibody for 2 days. Examination revealed a Glasgow coma scale (GCS) score of 15/15, with chorea-ballismus of the left hemibody. Investigations showed a fasting blood sugar level of 345 mg/dL and an HbA1c of 12.6%. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed T1 hyperintensity involving the bilateral globus pallidus, suggestive of diabetic striatopathy. Her symptoms improved with blood sugar control and treatment with tetrabenazine. Case II: A 67-year-old male with uncontrolled diabetes presented with an acute onset of involuntary movement involving the right hemi-body for 3 days. Examination revealed a GCS score of 15/15, with choreo-ballismus of the right hemibody. Investigations showed elevated blood sugars levels of 308 mg/dL and an HbA1c of 13.1%. MRI of the brain showed T1 hyperintensity involving the bilateral globus pallidus, suggestive of diabetic striatopathy. He was started on insulin, tetrabenazine, and risperidone. Over 5 months, he developed features of parkinsonism, including bradykinesia, rigidity, and incomplete resolution of choreoballistic movements. Tetrabenazine and risperidone were gradually tapered, and he was started on levodopa-carbidopa, resulting in symptomatic improvement.

Discussion and Conclusions: Hemichorea-ballismus usually carries a good prognosis with the correction of the underlying pathology. Supportive treatment with antidopaminergic drugs, benzodiazepines, antiepileptics, and in rare cases, pallidotomy is indicated.

Background and Aim: Acute encephalopathy with biphasic seizures and restricted diffusion (AESD) is an uncommon parainfectious disease in the Indian subcontinent, though it is quite common in Japan. This condition typically affects children aged 1 to 2 years. The illness follows a biphasic pattern; the first phase presents as a febrile seizure on day 1, followed by a recurrence of seizure clusters on days 4 to 6 of the illness. This study aimed to promote awareness of AESD and its management to avoid disastrous sequalae.

Case report: A fifteen-month-old male infant was referred to our hospital on day 5 of illness, initially diagnosed with viral encephalitis and treated for febrile seizures. Due to the prolonged nature of the seizures, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain were conducted, both of which were normal. Discussion: The child was admitted to the paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) and started on appropriate antiseizure medications. An electroencephalogram (EEG) suggested bitemporal sharp waves. The seizures were successfully brought under control. A repeat magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) suggested extensive bilateral and asymmetrical subcortical diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) bright signal changes, leading to a “bright tree” appearance. In view of the biphasic illness and characteristic MRI changes, AESD was considered. Intravenous (IV) methylprednisolone was administered due to persistent lethargy and head lag, despite control of seizures. The child showed gradual improvement.

Conclusions: Early control of seizures and immunosuppression is associated with better outcomes.

Background and Aim: Nonaka myopathy, also known as hereditary inclusion body myopathy (HIMB) or Glucosamine (UDP-N-acetyl)-2-epimerase/N-acetyl mannosamine kinase (GNE) myopathy, is an extremely rare form of autosomal recessive myopathy characterized by adult-onset distal skeletal muscle weakness. Its prevalence is estimated to be around 1 to 9 per 1000000 individuals. A distinctive feature of this condition is the sparing of the quadriceps muscle, which is the specific topographic feature of this myopathy.

Case report: The current study is a case report of a 33-year-old male who presented with distal-onset muscle weakness characterized by sparing of the quadriceps muscle to the neurology clinic. He underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thigh muscles, bilateral legs, arms, and forearms. Additionally, tests for total creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels, electromyography, nerve conduction studies, and genetic testing were performed. A 33-year-old male presented with an insidious onset and gradually progressive motor quadriparesis lasting 11 years duration, characterized by distal onset and sparing of bowel and bladder functions. On examination, he exhibited weakness in all four limbs, with notable sparing of the quadriceps muscles. Considering this sparing of quadriceps muscles, GNE myopathy was suspected. MRI of the thigh showed sparing of the quadriceps muscles, while predominantly involving the tibialis anterior muscle. Electromyography (EMG) revealed a myopathic pattern in the affected muscles, and nerve conduction study (NCS) indicated reduced compound muscle action potential (CMAP) in the tested nerves. Creatine phosphokinase - N acetyl cysteine (CPK NAC) levels were elevated at 554 U/L. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous missense mutation in the GNE gene.

Discussion and Conclusions: The diagnosis of GNE myopathy is primarily based on clinical features, muscle pathology findings, and confirmation through the identification of mutations in the GNE gene. While there is currently no specific treatment available for this myopathy, early diagnosis is crucial as it helps in avoiding unnecessary interventions and provides valuable insights into the prognosis regarding disease progression.

Background and Aim: A wide spectrum of congenital abnormalities of the pons has been demonstrated, including both malformations and disruptions. Results: A total of 30 participants were included in the study. All patients presented with headache and seizures, while additional symptoms included focal neurological deficits and altered sensorium. MRI revealed superior sagittal and transverse sinus thrombosis accompanied by focal cortical edema in most cases. The majority of patients experienced complete recovery following anticoagulant therapy.

Conclusions: CVST is a complex and challenging condition with significant implications for patient outcomes. Early recognition and prompt, targeted treatment are essential for improving prognosis and reducing the risk of complications.

Government Mohan Kumaramangalam Medical College Salem, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Nonaka distal myopathy, also known as GNE myopathy, with or without rimmed vacuoles, is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by predominant distal weakness and atrophy of lower limbs.

Case report: We present a case of 20-year-old male admitted to our hospital with complaints of difficulty in walking for the past 5 months, which was gradual in onset and progressive in nature. There was no reported fasciculations, cramps, pain, or myotonia. There was no involvement of higher mental function (HMF), cranial nerves, sensory pathways, or autonomic systems. The family history was not significant. On examination, the patient exhibited bilateral calf muscle wasting and distal predominant weakness, especially in the dorsiflexors, with retained reflexes and bilateral flexor plantar.

Discussion: Laboratory evaluations, including complete blood count, renal function test (RFT), liver function test (LFT), serum electrolytes, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and other blood parameters, yielded normal results. However, serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels were significantly elevated at 2896 IU/L. An echocardiogram was normal. Electromyography indicated myopathic features in the tibialis anterior and calf muscles. A muscle biopsy from the affected muscles showed variations in fiber size, atrophic fibers, and fibrosis, with no significant inflammatory cells present. MRI of the bilateral thigh and leg muscles showed atrophy primarily in the anterior tibialis muscle, calf muscles, and posterior thigh muscles. Genetic analysis identified a mutation in the GNE gene (Transcript GNE NM_005476.7 variant c.1124A>C P.Lys375T) in exon 7, which is suggestive of Nonaka myopathy.

Conclusions: Several features of this disorder have not yet been fully explained, including the reasons for sparing of the quadriceps and other organs despite the widespread expression of the GNE gene, as well as a full understanding of the role of sialic acid in the disease’s pathophysiology. Atri Chatterjee, Ankur Abhinav Arvind, Sanghamitra Laskar, Sonali Aggarwal, Sundeep Singh Saluja, Aathira NS, Arun Kumar, Nimisha, Abhay Kumar Sharma

Vardhman Mahavir Medical College (VMMC), New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: The APOE e4 allele (ApoE4) is a risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Lewy body dementia (DLB) and vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) and is associated with faster cognitive decline and an increased burden of neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) in both AD and DLB. This study aimed to investigate the differences in cognitive impairment and neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) between ApoE4 carriers and noncarriers in patients with all-cause dementia.

Methodology: This cross-sectional, observational study was conducted at the Cognitive Neurology Clinic at VMMC, Safdarjung Hospital, and GIPMER, New Delhi. Patients underwent clinical assessment at the clinic, including the collection of a detailed history of symptoms, clinical diagnosis, and the completion of the Montreal cognitive assessment (MoCA) and the neuropsychiatric inventory questionnaire (NPI-Q), following informed consent. Blood samples from 24 patients were subjected to polymerase chain reaction- restriction fragment length polymorphism (PCR-RFLP) and genetic sequencing to detect the ApoE4 allele (rs429358) and E2 allele (rs7412). Patients who were homozygous or heterozygous for the ApoE4 allele were considered as carriers. We compared the age of onset, clinical diagnosis, MoCA scores, and NPI-Q scores between the two groups. NPI-Q scores were further grouped into sub-syndromes representing mood, psychosis, and frontal lobe dysfunction, and these were compared between the groups. Continuous variables were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test, while categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test.

Results: The study included 8 carriers and 16 non-carriers as participants. There was no significant difference in the age at the onset of symptoms or the age at presentation to the clinic. Diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) were found in 37.5% of carriers and 31.5% of noncarriers (P > 0.05). MoCA scores were not significantly different between carriers (10.4 ± 4.1) and noncarriers (6.1 ± 5.7). Carriers and noncarriers did not demonstrate any significant difference in the total NPI-Q scores (8.7 ± 8.1 vs 11.7 ± 8.6, P = 0.28). There was no significant difference in the severity of any NPI-Q sub-syndromes.

Conclusions: ApoE4 was not associated with worse cognition or NPS burden.

Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences, Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Cluster headaches, a type of trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias, are thought to involve both peripheral and central pathophysiology, leading to trigeminal autonomic symptoms and a distinctive rhythmic pattern.

Case report: We herein present a unique case of “cluster-like headache” that developed following a tooth extraction and endodontic procedure, shedding light on the potential mechanism of cluster headache. This case discussed a patient who developed cluster-like headaches following a tooth extraction. A 43-year-old male with no prior history of craniofacial pain presented with severe pain following tooth extraction. The pain originated approximately 4–5 cm lateral to his right lips and radiated from below his right ear to the right temporal region. Kamalesh Nataraju, Archana B. Netto, Praveen Kumar Kumar S, Pramod K, Janardhan DC, Thejus B, Divyashree Katti

Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI), Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Thrombolysis using tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) for acute ischemic stroke is widely accepted, though it is commonly associated with bleeding complications. However, paradoxical thrombosis is a rare and lesser-known complication. A review of the literature reveals two case reports of paradoxical thromboembolism following tenecteplase for acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), but no such complications have been reported in stroke thrombolysis.

Case report: This case study involves a 50-year-old man who experienced a stroke. A 50-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus and systemic hypertension presented with acute onset right hemiparesis lasting 20 min. He was conscious, oriented, and had a National Institutes of health stroke scale (NIHSS) score of 6. His blood pressure (BP) was 170/100 mmHg, and his random blood sugar (RBS) was 314 mg/dl without ketoacidosis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-brain showed an acute infarct in the left middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory, without corresponding T2 FLAIR changes. His BP was reduced to 142/92 mmHg with intravenous (IV) labetalol. The patient was given insulin for hyperglycemia and had no contraindications for thrombolysis. IV tenecteplase at a dose of 0.25 mg/kg body-weight was administered. After 30 min, the hemiparesis improved, and the NIHSS scale dropped to 3. The patient developed acute breathlessness with wheezing, initially suspected as an allergic reaction to tenecteplase. He was treated with bronchodilators, IV antihistamines, and hydrocortisone. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) with strain, but cardiac biomarkers were normal. Within 12 h, he developed right lower limb ischemia with absent femoral and distal arterial pulses. Arterial doppler confirmed complete occlusion of the right femoral artery. A computed tomography (CT) brain scan taken 12 h post-thrombolysis showed no signs of intracerebral hemorrhage. Before intervention for limb ischemia could take place, the patient succumbed to cardiac arrhythmia and cardiogenic shock.

Discussion and Conclusions: This case represents the first reported instance of paradoxical thrombosis following thrombolysis with tenecteplase for acute ischemic stroke. The occurrence of such a complication poses a significant management challenge and can be life-threatening.

Background and Aim: The term “Young onset dementia” (YOD) refers to dementia with onset below the age of 65 years. While dementia is largely a disease of the elderly population, the prevalence of YOD is increasing. The differential diagnosis for YOD encompasses a wide range of disorders, including degenerative, vascular, toxic, metabolic, infectious, autoimmune, neoplastic, and traumatic causes. This study aimed to explore the clinical presentation and etiological spectrum of YOD.

Methodology: This institution-based, cross-sectional, observational study included 64 cases of YOD (age < 65 y) over a period of 12 months (October 2021–September 2022). Cognitive functions were assessed using standard tools, including the Montreal cognitive assessment, mini-mental status examination, and detailed lobar function tests. Relevant investigations were conducted as per individual clinical needs.

Results: The majority (72%) of cases had irreversible causes of dementia, with degenerative and vascular etiologies together comprising 79% of patients. Alzheimer’s disease (48%) was the most prevalent degenerative cause, followed by frontotemporal dementia (41%). The most common infectious causes included tuberculosis, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and neurocysticercosis. Autoimmune encephalitis contributed to 33% of the reversible causes.

Conclusions: The diagnosis of dementia is profoundly impactful for both young and elderly individuals. However, early identification of the potential reversible causes is crucial, as prompt treatment can help restore cognitive functions. Recognizing potential genetic factors in inherited cases may help in family planning and prevention of future cases.

Background and Aim: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) poses significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges and is associated with a high mortality rate. TBM predominantly affects the basal parts of the brain. A rare complication of TMB is optochiasmatic arachnoiditis (OCA), which involves inflammation of the arachnoid matter surrounding the optic nerve and chiasmatic cisterns. OCA is infrequently encountered and may arise as a paradoxical reaction during anti-TB treatment. It is hypothesized that this occurs due to a massive release of mycobacterial proteins upon treatment, provoking an intense delayed -type hypersensitivity reaction and leading to the development of the characteristic lesions of OCA.

Case report: A 22-year-old female patient presented with a 2-month history of fever, neck stiffness, and vomiting, accompanied by frequent headaches and constitutional symptoms. She was admitted to the medical ward, where cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies showed a neutrophilic picture with elevated protein levels and a significant sugar drop in glucose (21% of venous blood sugar). A clinical diagnosis of TB meningitis was made, and treatment with standard anti-TB chemotherapy and IV dexametnasone was commenced.

Discussion: One month later, the patient reported persistent headaches and deteriorating visual acuity in her right eye, along with a temporal field defect in his left eye. At the time of admission, vision in her right eye was limited to PL only. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed a large cluster of ring-enhancing lesions in the suprasellar region, compressing the optic chiasm, which was compatible with the diagnosis of OCA. Given the suspicion of a paradoxical reaction, the patient was treated with a pulse dose of IV methyl prednisolone (500 mg) for 5 days, resulting in an improvement of her vision to 20/200 and subsequently to 6/9 at discharge. Multidisciplinary team discussions lead to the consideration of a second-line antituberculous treatment (ATT) regimen, which was initiated alongside prednisolone. The patient is currently under follow-up care.

Conclusions: This case highlights OCA as a complication of TBM and underscores the therapeutic challenges associated with its management.

Background and Aim: Paroxysmal dyskinesias (PDs) are a rare group of hyperkinetic movement disorders characterized by their episodic nature. Diagnosis may be missed unless the episodes are witnessed or video-recorded.

St. Johns Medical College, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Autoimmune nodopathies (AN), first described in the acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) variant of Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), have now been distinguished from chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) and are recognized as a distinct entity. This classification transcends traditional dichotomies such as acute vs chronic presentation, peripheral vs central demyelination, and axonal vs demyelinating electrophysiology. The absence of overt inflammation and macrophage-mediated demyelination along with a favorable response to rituximab compared to IvIg underscores the pathophysiological and practical relevance of this categorization. In AN, antibodies target node and paranode proteins, including NF155, nodal neurofascin (186 and 140), contactin-1, and Caspr-1, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of nodal architecture. This study aimed to demonstrate the need of considering ANs as a differential diagnosis in clinical cases of GBS and CIDP.

Neurological examination revealed hyporeflexic proximal-distal weakness, predominantly in the lower limbs, postural tremor, and sensory ataxia. Nerve conduction study (NCS) indicated a sensorimotor demyelinating neuropathy with axonal features, showing conduction blocks and prolonged F-waves. Background and Aim: Epilepsy is one of the common presentations in methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) mutation, and metabolic therapy is found to reduce the seizure frequency in these patients.

Background and Aim: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is characterized by symptoms such as gait disturbances, cognitive impairment, and urinary incontinence. There are limited case reports that discuss patients diagnosed with concomitant iNPH and bvFTD.

Background and Aim: Gitelman syndrome (GS) is a rare renal disorder resulting from a mutation in the SCL12A3 gene that encodes the thiazide-sensitive sodium chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. It is characterized by hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalciuria, metabolic alkalosis, and normal blood pressure. Many symptoms of this rare renal disorder are related to these electrolyte abnormalities and adversely affect the patient’s quality of life. Moreover, rarely patients with GS may present with hypokalemic paralysis, mimicking Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), and cause diagnostic and therapeutic delay.

Case report: A 59-year-old male patient presented with paresthesias of four limbs for one month with progressive weakness of four limbs in an asymmetrical fashion and proximal more than distal weakness over eight days and without sphincter involvement, with recurrent spasms of limbs. The patient was admitted in the hospital in view of progressive asymmetrical weakness of all four limbs with suspicion of demyelinating polyneuropathy. He did not have any respiratory insufficiency or any bulbar symptoms.

Discussion: Acute neuromuscular paralysis is one of the common neurological emergencies. Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) and hypokalemic paralysis are the most common differentials of acute flaccid quadriparesis, and therapeutic interventions greatly differ in both electrolyte disturbances are not a part of the syndrome; however, autonomic dysfunction in GBS can lead to cardiac disturbances that may be aggravated by the coexistence of dyselectrolytemia such as hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. This can be perplexing and pose diagnostic as well as therapeutic challenges.

Conclusions: Gitelman’s syndrome is an autosomal recessive tubular disorder caused by mutations of the genes encoding the sodium, chloride, and magnesium carriers in the apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) and hypokalemic paralysis are the most common differentials of acute flaccid quadriparesis and therapeutic interventions greatly differ in both.

Raj Gokul Prabhakar, Velusamy S, Nithyanandam A, Aravind Visweswaran

Madras Medical College (MMC), Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Docking Protein 7 (DOK-7) is a postsynaptic cytoplasmic protein that activates muscle-specific tyrosine kinase, leading to Rapsyn-associated endplate acetylcholine receptor (AChR) clustering and normal folding of the postsynaptic membrane. Key differentiating features are onset after infancy, normal walking milestones, limb-girdle phenotype, normal eye movements, stridor, tongue-wasting, associated nonspecific myopathy, and poor response to pyridostigmine and 3,4-diaminopyridine.

Case report: We present a case of a 35-year-old female with a DOK-7 mutation, consistent with congenital myasthenia. The patient had normal developmental milestones and experienced difficulty using proximal upper limbs and getting up from a squatting position for 13 years. She also noted bilateral eyelid drooping for 12 years, and, for the past three months, experienced breathing difficulties and worsening limb weakness. Examination revealed bilateral ptosis, restricted extraocular movements, no tongue-wasting, normal tone, and 3/5 power in all limbs. The patient was tachypneic, and required continuous positive airway pressure therapy (CPAP) support. Routine investigations and serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) were normal. Whole exome sequencing identified a DOK-7 mutation. Treatment with oral salbutamol led to improvement.

Discussion: This case report describes a 35-year-old female with bilateral ptosis, limb-girdle weakness progressing to distal muscles, and respiratory involvement. Differential diagnoses included congenital myopathy, congenital myasthenia, and mitochondrial myopathy. Whole exome sequencing confirmed a DOK-7 mutation. Favorable features for DOK-7 congenital myasthenic syndrome include onset after infancy, normal walking milestones, limb-girdle phenotype, and good response to salbutamol. Contradictory features include complete ophthalmoparesis and the absence of tongue-wasting.

Conclusions: DOK-7 congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS) should be suspected in patients with long-standing limb-girdle weakness, ptosis, and nonspecific myopathy. High clinical suspicion is essential for diagnosis and appropriate management.

Background and Aim: Converging evidence suggests that migraine patients frequently experience difficulties in various executive functions such as attention, information processing speed, visuo-spatial attention, and memory. Additionally, migraine is often associated with psychiatric comorbidities, most commonly depression and anxiety. This clinic-based study investigated specific cognitive functions and psychiatric comorbidities among episodic and chronic migraine patients without aura, compared to a normal subject group.

Methodology: Among 59 adult migraine patients, migraine was assessed using the International Classification of Headache Disorders- 3 (ICHD-3) classification. Participants were classified into three groups: episodic migraine patients (n = 30), chronic migraine patients (n = 29), and control subjects (n = 30). Migraine characteristics were determined using a proforma. Cognition assessment was conducted using mini mental state examination (MMSE), frontal assessment battery (FAB), and other standardized cognitive tests. Psychiatric comorbidities were assessed using patient health questionnaire (PHQ), mood disorder questionnaire (MDQ), and Yale-Brown obsessive-compulsive scale (Y-BOCS). Only patients detected with psychiatric abnormalities on the PHQ were further assessed for depression and anxiety. Data on cognitive performance and psychiatric comorbidities among the three groups were analyzed.

Results: The mean age of presentation in episodic migraine patients was 31.1 ± 11.2 years, and in chronic migraine patients, it was 30.5 ± 9.5 years. Chronic migraine patients experienced greater activity restriction, sleep disturbance, and premonitory and postdrome symptoms. Both migraine groups showed lower performance on tests assessing attention, lexical fluency, language, and color recognition compared to controls. Cognitive performance in chronic migraine patients was partially influenced by psychiatric comorbidities.

Conclusions: This study provides evidence of deficits in specific cognitive domains among migraine patients and highlights the partial influence of psychiatric comorbidities on these neuropsychological findings.

Background and Aim: Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis (NCL) comprises lysosomal storage disorders marked by progressive neurodegeneration due to ceroid lipopigment accumulation, leading to cognitive decline, vision loss, and refractory seizures. NCL manifests from birth to adulthood, showing genetic and phenotypic diversity based on the gene involved. The most common subtypes are CLN1, CLN2, CLN3, and CLN6. In India, the prevalent subtype is NCL2, caused by a tripeptidyl peptidase one mutation, presenting with seizures, ataxia, progressive dementia, and motor and visual deterioration. Case Report: Case 1: An eight-year-old female, born to consanguineous parents, presented with progressive vision loss, seizures, and cognitive decline starting at age 5. Symptoms included drop attacks, myoclonic jerks, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, progressive vision loss, and increasing motor and cognitive impairment. Examination showed optic atrophy, pigmentary retinopathy, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy on neuroimaging. Case 2: The proband’s 10-year-old brother experienced progressive vision loss, myoclonic seizures, and cognitive decline starting at age 5, leading to total dependence in three years. He exhibited optic atrophy, pigmentary retinopathy, exaggerated reflexes, and bilateral clonus. Neuroimaging revealed cerebral and cerebellar atrophy. Case 3: The proband’s six-year-old sister, symptomatic for one year, presented with progressive vision loss and myoclonic seizures. Examination revealed pigmentary retinopathy and normal motor strength.

Discussion and Conclusions: We described one of the first NCL5 families from India. NCL should be considered in children with cognitive impairment, epilepsy, and vision loss. Early diagnosis can facilitate enrollment in gene therapy trials, potentially providing a cure.

Background and Aim: Stroke is rapidly developing clinical signs of focal (or global) disturbance of cerebral function, with symptoms lasting 24 h or longer, or leading to death, with no apparent cause other than vascular origin. Numerous studies have revealed that risk factors have variable correlations with different stroke subtypes. Currently, there is no data regarding this in North-East India. The aim is to study the TOAST subtypes of ischemic stroke and its risk factors.

Methodology: An observational study was carried out in the Department of Neurology, from November 2022 to April 2024. All patients underwent thorough clinical examination, routine blood tests, electrocardiogram (ECG), 2D echo, and neuroimaging. Results: The study had 579 cases of acute ischemic stroke. When classified according to TOAST criteria, there were 229 (39.5%) cases of large artery atherosclerosis (LAA), 205 (35.4%) cases of small artery occlusion (SAO), 62 (10.7%) cases of cardio-embolism, 12 (2.07%) cases of stroke of other determined etiology, and 71 (12.26%) cases of stroke of undetermined etiology.

Conclusions: Large artery atherosclerosis was the most common ischemic stroke subtype. The most common risk factor in large artery atherosclerosis and small vessel occlusion was systemic hypertension, which was more prevalent in small artery occlusion. Non-valvular atrial fibrillation was the most common cause of cardioembolic stroke.

Background and Aim: Monoclonal gammopathies consist of a spectrum of clonal plasma cell disorders, including monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), multiple myeloma (MM), and Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (WM). Peripheral neuropathy is a well-recognized complication of monoclonal gammopathies and a difficult clinical problem in terms of diagnosis and treatment.

Case report: A 54-year-old male presented with symmetrical chronic progressive lower motor neuron (LMN) type quadriparesis (distal > proximal) lower limb predominant with wasting, fasciculations, hypotonia, and hyporeflexia, with both small and large fiber sensory involvement with skin changes, with cachexia, with no cranial nerve involvement with no cerebellar or autonomic involvement with no cognitive or extrapyramidal signs with no signs of raised intracranial tension. Advised immunotyping revealed a very faint, non-discrete protein band in the gamma globulin region of the IgG and kappa lane, corresponding to M spike.

Discussion: Final diagnosis: Paraproteinemic neuropathy – monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS).

Background and Aim: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), a devastating stroke subtype with high mortality, necessitates novel therapeutic approaches. Background and Aim: Recurrent painful ophthalmoplegic neuropathy (RPON), known historically as ophthalmoplegic migraine, is characterized by recurrent episodes of unilateral headache associated with one or more ipsilateral cranial nerve palsies (most commonly being third nerve). It predominantly affects children and young adults. Diagnosis of RPON is primarily of exclusion, necessitating a thorough investigation to rule out orbital, parasellar, or posterior fossa lesions and vascular or other cerebral causes.

Case report: We present a unique case of RPON in an 18-year-old female with bilateral ophthalmoparesis. An 18-year-old female presented with throbbing, bifrontal headache, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia, followed by double vision after 10–12 h. She had a history of two similar episodes in the past that resolved spontaneously over two to three weeks with a family history of migraine in her mother. On examination, she exhibited binocular diplopia and restricted abduction in both eyes, with no ptosis and normal pupil reactivity. Other cranial nerves, motor, sensory, speech, and cerebellar exams were normal. There were no meningeal signs. Investigations, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), blood glucose, and other metabolic profiles were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal, with no oligoclonal bands or elevated IgG index. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels, anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO), antinuclear antibodies (ANA) profile, and Lyme serology were negative. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain, visual evoked potential (VEP), and electroencephalogram (EEG) were also normal. After exclusion, a diagnosis of bilateral RPON was made. She was treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and tapering oral steroids, leading to headache improvement within 72 h and resolution of ocular symptoms within two weeks.

Discussion and Conclusions: Further research is warranted to explore the cause and optimal preventive strategies for RPON episodes.

Madras Medical College (MMC), Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Biotin thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease (BTBGD) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder due to a mutation in the SLC19A3 gene encoding thiamine transporter 2, which allows thiamine to cross the blood-brain barrier. It is a treatable disorder if identified and treated early.

Case report: We present a case of infantile BTBGD missed as hypoxic ischemic sequelae. A six-month-old female child first born of third-degree consanguineous parents was brought with recurrent seizures and regression. Her neonatal period was uneventful. She achieved a social smile at two months and partial head control by three months. At four months, she developed fever, recurrent seizures, and altered sensorium. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain showed bilateral symmetrical hyperintensities in the caudate, putamen, and cerebral cortex reported as hypoxic ischemic changes. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal. Examination revealed an awake child with microcephaly and spastic quadriparesis. She was neither recognizing her mother nor following the light. Fundi were normal. There were no dysmorphic features, neurocutaneous markers, or organomegaly. MRI findings were suggestive of BTBGD and was started on biotin 5 mg/kg/day and thiamine 15 mg/kg/day. Repeat MRI showed striatal and cerebral atrophy. Seizures were controlled, and she made developmental gains. Whole exome sequencing revealed a pathogenic mutation in the SLC19A3 gene confirming the diagnosis of BTBGD. Genetic counseling regarding the risk of recurrence and prenatal screening was advised.

Discussion and Conclusions: There should be a high index of suspicion to diagnose BTBGD, and thiamine and biotin should be started early to have a better outcome.

National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Resting motor threshold (RMT), measured using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), is believed to reflect the trans-synaptic excitability of cortico-spinal neurons. The pathogenesis of idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) is associated with neuronal hyperexcitability. Hence, studying RMT in patients with IGE and the effect of anti-seizure medications (ASM) can offer significant insights into epileptogenesis in IGE.

Methodology: In this study, 31 patients with IGE were analyzed along with 31 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Among these, eight patients with IGE were drug-naïve. A 32-channel electroencephalogram (EEG) system was utilized to record EEG signals connected to a TMS-compatible EEG amplifier. Magnetic stimuli were delivered using a figure-of-eight coil connected to a Magstim 200 stimulator. The target areas of the motor cortex were localized through neuronavigational techniques. Surface electromyography (EMG) measurements were made on the abductor pollicis brevis muscle. The RMT was calculated in patients and controls.

Results: The mean age of the patients was 23.56 years (7.89), ranging from 18 to 50 years. An age- and sex-matched group of 31 healthy controls, comprising 15 women and 16 men, was also included. The mean age of the control group was 26.02 years (6.13), ranging from 18 to 47 years. The mean RMT in patients with IGE was higher compared to control subjects (50.06 ± 9.53 vs. 44.52 ± 12.69; P = 0.003). However, there was no difference in RMT between controls and drug-naïve patients with IGE (44.75 ± 12.96; P > 0.05). Patients with IGE on Levetiracetam had a lower RMT (48 ± 4.5) compared to patients on valproate (55.73 ± 8.2).

Conclusions: Levetiracetam had a lesser impact on RMT compared to valproate. We could not demonstrate significant differences in RMT between drug-naïve patients with IGE and those on ASM.
