Background and Aim: Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula is a common vascular anomaly, affecting the spinal cord. The early clinical features are nonspecific with low back pain and paresthesia, and patients develop weakness of limbs, bladder, and bowel disturbances eventually. The diagnosis is often overlooked resulting in morbidity. We report two such cases diagnosed later into illness.

Case report: Case I: A 48-year-old male presented with a one-year duration of low back pain radiating to bilateral lower limbs. It was associated with progressive weakness and numbness of the right followed by the left lower limb. Subsequently, he developed bladder disturbances with urinary incontinence. Examination revealed hypotonia, MRC 1/5 bilateral lower limbs with brisk deep tendon reflex (biceps, supinator, triceps, knee), absent ankle jerk, mute plantar, sensory level around T6 suggestive of myeloradiculopathy. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed longitudinally extensive myelitis from D6 to conus with dilated perimedullary vessels (flow voids). Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) showed fistulous communication between the left sacral artery and filum terminale vein and he underwent ethylene-venyl-alcohol embolization. Two months later, power had improved to MRC 2/5 bilateral lower limbs. Case II: A 50-year-old male presented with four months duration of low back pain followed by progressive weakness and paresthesia of the left followed by the right lower limb. Examination revealed wasting, hypotonia, power MRC 4/5 bilateral hip, right knee and ankle, 3/5 in left knee, 2/5 in the left ankle with sluggish knee and ankle jerk, and sensory level around L2.

Discussion and Conclusions: Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula is often an underdiagnosed cause of myelopathy. Spinal angiogram is the gold standard in the diagnosis. Early identification and timely intervention prevent disability and morbidity.

All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of small and non-coding RNA molecules that play a crucial role in gene regulation. Studies have shown that miRNAs can be involved in the pathogenesis of many diseases, including stroke. Stroke is a major public health problem and a leading cause of death and disability worldwide. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we aimed to investigate the role of miRNAs in stroke.

Methodology: We conducted a comprehensive search of several databases, including PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library, from inception to April 2024. We included studies that reported miRNA expression in stroke patients compared to healthy controls or in stroke patients with different stroke subtypes. We performed a meta-analysis using a random-effects model to estimate the pooled effect size.

Results: A total of 34 studies were included in this systematic review and meta-analysis. The meta-analysis showed that the expression of miR-21 was significantly upregulated in stroke patients compared to healthy controls (standardized mean difference [SMD] = 1.35, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.99–1.71, P < 0.001). In addition, the expression of miR-145 was significantly downregulated in stroke patients compared to healthy controls (SMD = −1.09, 95% CI: −1.47 to −0.71, P < 0.001). Furthermore, the expression of miR-221 was significantly upregulated in ischemic stroke patients compared to hemorrhagic stroke patients (SMD = 1.13, 95% CI: 0.57–1.68, P < 0.001).

Conclusions: Future research should focus on the mechanisms of miRNA dysregulation in stroke and the development of miRNA-based diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for stroke management.

Background and Aim: Paroxysmal movement disorders are characterized by episodic and brief involuntary movements that can be inherited or acquired. Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia (PKD), an autosomal-dominant disorder, manifests as recurrent episodes triggered by sudden movements, presenting with symptoms like chorea, dystonia, and ballismus. PKD’s prevalence is approximately 1 in 150,000.

Case report: A 17-year-old boy from Thiruvannamalai, with no consanguinity in his family, presented with a one-year history of abnormal posturing of limbs and face. The episodes, triggered by sudden movement, involved painless, asymmetric posturing of all four limbs and face, lasting less than 1 min and occurring 10–20 times daily. These episodes, accompanied by slurred speech, were exacerbated by cold environments and preceded by a premonitory sensation described as tightness.

Discussion: Considering stereotypical movements on getting up after prolonged sitting, short duration < 1 min, 10–20 episodes per day, associated with right lower limb dystonia. The patient was diagnosed with PKD. Extensive neurological workup, including serum electrolytes, creatine kinase levels, electromyography (EMG), electroencephalogram (EEG), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), was normal. Whole exome sequencing sent for further evaluation. The reports are awaited. The initiation of carbamazepine at a dosage of 200 mg BD led to symptomatic improvement within one week, with a significant reduction in episode frequency at one-month follow-up, and the dose was gradually titrated.

Conclusions: The patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by sudden, stereotypical, short-duration episodes of involuntary movements triggered by sudden movement, aligns with PKD. Continuous follow-up is crucial for differentiating PKD from other similar conditions and understanding the full spectrum of the disease.

Bharat Sahu, Pranay Gupta, Swapan Gupta, Swapan Gupta

Govind Ballabh Pant Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education (GBPIPMER, New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive motor neuron degenerative disorder. Edaravone was approved by the FDA to be used in this condition in 2017. This study aims to assess the efficacy of edaravone in ALS patients.

Methodology: ALS patients attending neurology OPD from March 2022 to September 2023 diagnosed using the gold coast criteria were screened for eligibility to receive edaravone injection. Those patients who had scores of at least two points on all 12 items of ALS functional rating scale (ALSFRS)- R score was administered edaravone infusion for six cycles with a first cycle of 14 days with a subsequent cycle of 10 days per month. Intravenous edaravone infusion was given at the dose of 60 mg/day. The primary outcome was an improvement in the ALS-FRS R score by three points from the baseline score after 6 cycles of edaravone therapy.

Results: Out of a total 21 patients screened, seven patients received edaravone injections. Age range was 49–75 years with six males and one female. Three patients had limb onset ALS, and one each had bulbar onset ALS, progressive bulbar palsy, flail arm syndrome, and progressive muscular atrophy, respectively. Three patients completed six cycles of edaravone, while two patients succumbed to their illness during therapy, while two patients dropped out during the study period due to the progressive nature of the disease despite therapy. A single patient with the diagnosis of progressive muscular atrophy had significant improvement with edaravone therapy.

Conclusions: Inj. Edaravone was not found efficacious in the majority of the patients with ALS. More studies are needed to define its role.

Chebolu Harshika, Randhi Venkata Venkata Narayana, Amarapu Sravanthi, Puvvada Srikar

Sevenhills Hospital, Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, India

Background and Aim: Bee stings are commonly associated with local reactions like erythema which are self-limiting while systemic effects like anaphylaxis, rhabdomyolysis, intravascular coagulation, cerebral hemorrhage, acute pulmonary edema, acute renal failure, heart block, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, and death rarely.

Case report: A 53-year-old woman, known epileptic, presented with a history of being stung by a massive attack of honey bees followed by swelling and itching of face and one episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She was treated with antiepileptics and supportive measures. After 10 h, she presented with weakness of the right upper limb and lower limbs. On examination, the patient was conscious and coherent with stable vitals with erythematous papules on the face and back, Broca’s aphasia, upper motor neuron (UMN) right facial palsy, and right hemiparesis.

Discussion: Routine blood investigations were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed acute infarcts in the bilateral fronto-parieto-occipital lobes and basal ganglia, possibly embolic or related to hypoxia. Carotid arterial Doppler studies revealed a floating thrombus in the right common carotid artery. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) testing was negative. Serum homocysteine levels were at normal limits. A 2D echocardiography revealed no abnormality.

Conclusions: A stroke following a bee sting is very rare but is still a possibility. In cases of multiple bee stings, the patient often becomes unconscious and may not be able to provide a history. In such cases, careful general examination would reveal insect bite marks which would lead to the diagnosis. Awareness of this rare entity can lead to appropriate diagnosis and prevent unnecessary evaluation for the cause of stroke.

Sonia Martina, Shree Shruthi Badrinath, Muhammed Shadique, Mohinish S, Jered Livingston, Neeraj Elango, Leema Pauline

Madras Medical College (MMC), Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Rabies is a fatal zoonotic encephalomyelitis transmitted by the saliva of a rabid animal. Two-thirds of human rabies present as furious rabies with agitation, hallucinations, and autonomic hyperactivity, with in-between lucid periods being calm and cooperative. One-third develop paralytic or dumb rabies. Here, we report a case of rabies presenting as new onset refractory seizures being undiagnosed by reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RTPCR) and requiring next-generation sequencing for diagnosis.

Case report: A six-year-old male child who had been scratched over the ear by a stray dog was without bleeding and was diagnosed as category 2 bite for which no immunoglobulin was given and was in the course of anti-rabies vaccine with the fourth dose being given on the day of presentation which is one month after the bite when at 30 min of vaccination child developed generalized seizures and was admitted. The seizures were recurrent requiring multiple anti-seizure medications and were completely normal in between the episodes. On the fifth day of admission, he had behavioral disturbances in the form of sleeplessness and tactile hallucinations. On the sixth day, he developed fever, refractory status epilepticus, and shock. There was no aerophobia or hydrophobia throughout the period. He had a stormy course there on with septic shock and multi-organ dysfunction. He developed liver dysfunction with elevated transaminases and coagulopathy, acute kidney injury, and hemolytic uremic syndrome He had bicytopenia, coagulopathy, hemolysis, and hyper-ferritinemia.

Discussion: His initial computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain were normal. On the eighth day of admission, after the worsening started repeat image showed T2/ fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensities in bilateral centrum semiovale, corona radiata, bilateral thalamus, lentiform nucleus, dorsal pons, bilateral cerebellar peduncles with restricted diffusion suggestive of brainstem encephalitis/demyelination. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal with normal protein and no pleocytosis, viral markers were negative, and CSF and blood culture were negative. Rabies work up with samples from the nape of the neck, and buccal smear and CSF for reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RTPCR) were negative. Milwaukee protocol was followed for treating this child in the PICU. He required multiple blood products, IV immunoglobulins, hemodialysis, and plasmapheresis. The child expired after 20 days of admission. Postmortem brain biopsy RTPCR was also negative for rabies as its detection limit is 100 picograms of viral load. Hence, the sample was further subjected to next-generation sequencing. The complete genome of the sequence finally revealed the rabies virus.

Conclusions: Rabies is a fatal zoonotic disease requiring early detection and complete post-exposure prophylaxis where vaccine alone is not sufficient, but immunoglobulin should also be administered based on the category of bite. Apart from usual presentations like aerophobia and hydrophobia, rabies can also present with refractory seizures. The metagenomic next-generation sequencing, a novel option in the diagnosis, is seldom reported, and if the viral load is less than 100 pg, next-generation sequencing may help to diagnose rabies.

St. Johns Medical College, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: A 68-year-old woman with a medical history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with the sudden onset of dizziness, characterized by a spinning sensation, along with slurred speech and swaying while sitting, standing, or walking. She also noticed weakness and incoordination in her right hand in the form of hand grip weakness and smearing food over her face. There was no history of diplopia, dysphagia, facial deviation or numbness, hearing difficulty, or manipulating food bolus in her mouth.

Case report: Upon examination, her higher mental functions and cranial nerve function, including eye movements, were normal. However, there was generalized hypotonia in all four limbs, with reduced power in the right hand. Sensory examination revealed no abnormalities. Cerebellar function testing demonstrated bilaterally impaired finger-nose and heel-shin tests, with dysdiadokokinesia more pronounced on the right side without any evidence of nystagmus. Truncal ataxia was evident as swaying of the head and body while seated. Her speech exhibited a scanning and spastic quality. MRI of the brain revealed an acute, non-hemorrhagic infarct in the paramedian midbrain tegmentum, more pronounced on the right side.

Discussion: The patient was diagnosed with Wernekink commissure syndrome (WCS), characterized by damage to fibers involved in the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles following a caudal midbrain infarction.

Conclusions: This case is noteworthy for presenting only the core features of WCS, namely, dysarthria and bilateral ataxia without any associated eye movement abnormalities, posing a challenge for clinical localization.

Background and Aim: Mitochondrial disorders may resemble vascular, infectious, or autoimmune conditions and are especially challenging when the onset of symptoms is beyond childhood. Case report: The data has been collected and compiled after taking due patient consent. Background and Aim: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) manifests as acute onset neurologic symptoms in the form of encephalopathy, headache, and visual disturbances. This is a rare case of atypical presentation of spinal PRES with retinal detachment and brainstem involvement.

Case report: Case discussion of a rare presentation of PRES. A 34-year-old male presented with headache and blurring of vision for six days and altered sensorium for one day. The headache was bifrontal, continuous with the associated progressive blurring of vision. On presenting to the hospital, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was E3V4M6 with a blood pressure of 230/130 mmHg with visual acuity limited to hand movement perception. Computed tomography (CT) Brain showed bilateral symmetrical parieto-occipital hypodensities. The possibility of PRES and cerebral venous thrombosis was considered. Retinal detachment was confirmed by ocular ultrasound and optical coherence tomography (OCT). The autoimmune profile was positive. Dramatic improvement in visual acuity was seen within three days with the resolution of findings on MRI.

Discussion and Conclusions: This highlights the fact that conditions as common as PRES can have uncommon manifestations, and a high index of suspicion helps in identifying the same. In this case, fundus examination was the key to identifying non-cortical visual loss.

Subhra Sen, Uddalak Chakraborty, Soumik Das, Biman Kanti Ray, Atanu Biswas

Institute of Post Graduate Medical Education and Research (IPGMER), Kolkata, West Bengal, India

Background and Aim: Intracranial atherosclerotic disease (ICAD) affects 33–50% of Asians and is the leading cause of stroke globally. Contrast-enhanced vessel wall imaging is almost equivalent to plaque activity, which correlates to ischemic episodes. This study aims to characterize vessel wall architecture and assess plaque activity in intracranial stenosis.

Methodology: This cross-sectional observational study included 20 patients over a period of three months.

Results: The median age of our population was 55, with hypertension (65%) and diabetes (50%) as primary comorbidities. A total of 75% were addiction-free, and tobacco (20%) was the most prevalent addiction. Subcortical involvement was observed in the majority (50%) of patients, while 35% were associated with cortical, internal, and exterior watershed infarcts. The median magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) Alberta stroke program early CT score (ASPECTS) score was 7. Patients exhibited a median of two plaques, with a median occlusion of 70%. The anterior circulation contributed to 95% of plaques, with the internal carotid artery (ICA) contributing to 70% and the middle cerebral artery (MCA) contributing to 55%. The median plaque length measured 7 mm. Post-contrast enhancement was seen in 80% of plaques, while 20% showed signs of intraplaque hemorrhage.

Conclusions: Our findings suggest that contrast-enhancing plaque indicates instability when imaged promptly after a stroke. The findings are consistent with extracranial atherosclerotic plaques, linking contrast enhancement with inflammation and instability. Based on plaque morphology, this model and other similar prospective model might predict culprit plaque, plaque activity, and stroke recurrence risk.

Background and Aim: PPP2R5D spectrum disorder typically manifests in children and is characterized by a range of clinical features, including intellectual disability, neurodevelopmental delay, behavioral disturbances, and autism spectrum disorder. PPP2R5D encodes the delta isoform of the regulatory subunit B56, which is part of the protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) enzyme complex. PP2A is a serine/threonine phosphatase that plays a crucial role in various cellular processes, including cell growth, division, and signaling pathways. We report a case of adult-onset dystonia-parkinsonism as a clinical phenotype associated with PPP2R5D mutation.

Case report: A 26-year-old male with a history of delayed motor milestones and mild intellectual disability presented with an insidious onset of gradually progressive slowness and stiffness in his left upper and lower limbs over the past two years. It was associated with intermittent posturing and tremulousness of the left hand, with mirror movements in the right upper limb. On examination, he exhibited axial rigidity and asymmetrical appendicular rigidity, left more than right. Action dystonia with dystonic tremor was noted in the left upper limb with mirror movements on the right. Subtle frontal lobe involvement was present on cognitive examination. The rest of the neurological examination was normal. The levodopa challenge resulted in a 10% improvement in the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) motor III score without any dyskinesia.

Discussion and Conclusions: Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism can be a phenotypic presentation of a PPP2R5D mutation, which is often levodopa responsive as suggested by various case reports (although not seen in our patient). Subtle developmental delay in childhood may provide a clue toward this etiology.

Background and Aim: Motor band sign refers to a linear hyperintensity in susceptibility weighted imaging (SWI) sequences in the primary motor cortex. Case report: A 68-year-old lady presented with progressive spasticity of the left upper and lower limbs for two years. There was no evidence of apraxia, cortical sensory loss, alien limb phenomenon, or hemineglect on examination. A detailed cognitive examination was normal. The differential diagnoses considered at this point were as follows: 1. hemiplegic variant of primary lateral sclerosis (Mills syndrome), 2. Upper motor neuron (UMN) predominant ALS, 3. corticobasal syndrome.

Discussion: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain showed subtle atrophy of the motor cortex on the right side with SWI sequences showing linear hyperintensity in the right motor cortex. ASL imaging was normal. The serum paraneoplastic profile showed ZIC4 strong positivity. Background and Aim: Peripheral nerve hyperexcitability (PNH) syndrome is a group of disorders ranging from cramp fasciculation syndrome to neuromyotonia. Neuromyotonia is the syndrome of continuous muscle fiber activity that was first described by Isaacs in 1961 (1). Recently, a strong association between S. aureus infections has been linked to PNH (2).

Case report: A 35-year-old male presented with generalized cramps and neuropathic pain, along with abnormal undulating movements of muscles all over his body which present continuously, over large muscles in all four limbs which developed after a week of surgical drainage of pyocele from the left scrotum. These symptoms were not associated with stiffness or any encephalopathy.

Discussion: All routine investigations were normal, with mildly raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)/ C-Reactive protein (CRP) levels. Routine nerve conduction study (NCS) was normal, but there were after-discharges noted on electrical stimulation of the tibial nerve. Electromyography (EMG) shows the presence of spontaneous discharges in the form of continuous, irregular doublet, triplet, or multiple motor unit discharges [Figures 2 and 3]. Serum samples were positive for both voltage-gated potassium channel (VGKC) (CASPER2/LGI1) antibodies which is very rare. The patient was managed with carbamazepine, pulse steroid, and plasmapheresis, following that his symptoms improved after 4–5 cycles of plasma exchange (PLEX).

Kamineni hospital, Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh, India

Background and Aim: Phenytoin is the most common antiepileptic used in the treatment of seizures. Sodium valproate is an antiepileptic known to cause hyperammonemia alone or in combination with other anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) like topiramate, zonisamide, carbamazepine, and phenobarbitone. Phenytoin alone producing hyperammonemia and presenting as T1 hyperintensities on neuroimaging is a rare entity.

Case report: A 58-year-old female patient presented to our hospital with complaints of sudden onset confusion for one week. The confusion was associated with a sense of imbalance while walking and a reeling sensation. The patient had a K/C/O seizure disorder since childhood and used to get generalized tonic-clonic seizures once in 15 days and was treated with phenytoin at a dose of 100 mg thrice a day and phenobarbitone 30 mg twice a day but had poor control of seizures with one active seizure in every 20 days for that dose of phenytoin was escalated to 300 mg twice a day. On examination, the patient was awake, following simple commands (Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)-13-14), and had gaze-evoked nystagmus on both sides, and ataxic gait was present. No meningeal or other lateralizing signs are present. Examination of other systems was normal.

Discussion: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain showed bilateral basal ganglia hyperintensities on T1-weighted images with no post-contrast enhancement with discrete T2 and flair hyperintensities. Electroencephalogram (EEG) showed predominant theta activity with a frequency of 5–6 Hz and amplitude of 30–50 mV which is symmetrical. Blood investigations such as complete Blood Picture (CBP), liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, blood sugars, chest X-ray, and electrocardiogram (ECG) were normal. Both serum ammonia (200 mcg/mL) and phenytoin (35.65 mcg/mL) levels were found to be high. Serum calcium, parathyroid hormone (PTH), and ceruloplasmin are normal. Based on the above reports, phenytoin and phenobarbitone were stopped and observed. After four days, serum ammonia levels came to normal, patient’s sensorium improved and was clinically better. Based on clinical history and investigations, a final diagnosis of phenytoin toxicity was performed.

Conclusions: To conclude, any patient presenting with altered sensorium, especially with associated recent initiation or escalation of AEDs, should lead to suspicion of AED toxicity.

KAPV Government Medical College, Trichy, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Ataxia with oculo-motor apraxia type 2 (AOA2) is an autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia with an age of onset between 10 and 28 years. Patients have associated oculomotor apraxia, neuropathy, head tremor, cerebellar atrophy on imaging, and an elevated α-foetoprotein (AFP) serum level.

Case report: Here, we discuss the clinical, electrophysiological, and genetic findings of two siblings who presented with a clinical picture of AOA type 2.

Discussion: The mean age at disease onset of the elder sister was 21 years, and the younger brother was 19 years. Both of them had gait ataxia initially which progressed slowly over two years, and at the time of presentation, both of them were unable to walk independently. Both had limb ataxia and truncal ataxia, scanning speech. Oculomotor apraxia was present, and gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus, saccadic pursuit, and slow inaccurate saccades were present in both. Both patients had areflexia and impaired vibration and position sense distally. Head tremor was present in the brother. Cognition was normal. Pes cavus was present in both patients. No telangiectasia was observed. Both of their parents and elder sister had normal neurological examinations. Routine laboratory findings were normal. AFP was raised in both patients. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain showed cerebellar atrophy in both patients, and nerve conduction study (NCS) showed sensorimotor axonal neuropathy in both patients. Whole exome sequencing showed homozygous SETX mutations in both patients.

Conclusions: Both of these patients represent a classical phenotype of AOA2 with one sibling presenting with head tremor as the first symptom. In autosomal recessive ataxia apart from ataxia with vitamin E deficiency (AVED), AOA2 is also considered in the differential diagnosis of patients presenting with head tremors and juvenile-onset ataxia, as well as sensorimotor neuropathy.

Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS), Hyderabad, Telangana, India

Background and Aim: Histopathological analysis of muscle biopsies is a cornerstone of diagnosis of muscle disorders. However, sampling error is a common problem. In inflammatory myopathies, false negative results occur in 10–20% of all biopsies due to focal disease activity. A sampling of early or end-stage muscle may result in the absence of disease-specific abnormalities impeding correct diagnosis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) triage can be performed to reduce sampling error by selecting the appropriate muscle.

Case report: A 57-year-old female presented with weakness of both upper limbs and lower limbs for eight months. Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) was elevated, electro neuro-myography (ENMG) showed myogenic potentials, and myositis profile was negative. A muscle biopsy done from the left quadriceps showed lipid inclusions with no evidence of inflammation or myophagocytosis. Workup for metabolic myopathy and mitochondrial genetics sent. The patient was given intravenous immnuoglobulin (IVIg), and she showed improvement. One month later, the patient presented with worsening weakness. Metabolic workup and mitochondrial genetics were negative. MRI muscles showed T2/STIR hyperintensities in the subscapularis and bilateral biceps. A repeat biopsy was performed on the biceps. It showed features suggestive of inclusion body myositis. She was treated with immunosuppressants and is doing well currently.

Discussion: CPK: 10,000 U/L; Myositis panel: negative; ENMG: muscle disease; First biopsy: lipid inclusions with no evidence of inflammation and myophagocytosis; MRI muscles: T2/STIR hyperintensities involving bilateral biceps and subscapularis; Repeat biopsy: S/o endomysial and perivascular inflammation around non-necrotic fibers. Many fibers with single-to-multiple-rimmed vacuoles. Features s/o inclusion body myositis.

Conclusions: MRI has high diagnostic accuracy in diagnosing subacute onset idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM), in particular as an add-on test to the muscle biopsy.

Background and Aim: IgG4-related disease (RD) is a multisystemic, fibroinflammatory, and lymphoproliferative disease that is characterized as a polyclonal IgG4-infiltration, leading to storiform fibrosis and obliterating phlebitis. Central neurologic manifestations are rare with reports of mostly HP. Elevated serum IgG4 levels are consistent with IgG4-RD and are present in 70% to 90% of patients. Biopsy material from meninges is the gold standard for diagnosis. There are currently no guidelines about treatment for IgG4- related hypertrophic pachymeningitis (IgG4-RHP). Case report: A 50-year-old female presented with complaints of bilateral progressive hearing loss, headache, and deviation of the mouth toward the right side for the last three years, and difficulty in swallowing for the last one year. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain reveals pachymeningeal thickening and enhancement in the posterior fossa, causing a mass effect. Two doses of I/v rituximab 1 gm were given 14 days apart and were discharged with six monthly follow-ups for I/v rituximab. Discussion and Conclusions: By early treatment with rituximab, we can achieve better neurological outcomes with a lesser relapse rate.

Background and Aim: Rhino-orbitocerebral mucormycosis associated with COVID-19 (C-ROCM) was rampant in India during the COVID-19 pandemic. Methodology: This retrospective study was conducted between March 2020 and June 2021 at a tertiary referral care center in Hyderabad. Results: Of the 31 subjects, eight were excluded due to nonavailability of imaging. Background and Aim: Myotonia congenita (MC) is a rare hereditary muscle disease caused by CLCN1 gene variants, with limited data on its clinico-genetic spectrum, especially from India. This study aims to elucidate the clinico-genetic spectrum of MC in an Indian cohort.

Methodology: Clinical and investigation data from 2006–2024 were collected for 19 MC patients who underwent whole exome sequencing.

Results: There was a male predominance (89.5%) with a mean age at presentation and onset of 14.4 ± 8.6 and 8.6 ± 6.7 years, respectively. Developmental delay, consanguinity, and positive family history were observed in 31.6%, 42.1%, and 47.4% of patients. Initial symptoms included climbing difficulty (63.2%), limb stiffness (47.4%), walking difficulty (47.4%), and other motor difficulties. Warm-up phenomena were noted in 94.7% and cold-induced exacerbations in 31.6%. Common signs included delayed muscle relaxation (78.9%), muscle hypertrophy (68.4%), Herculean appearance (63.2%), and percussion myotonia (52.6%). Median creatine kinase (CK) was 159.0 U/L (IQR: 106.0-291.0), elevated in 47.4%. Electromyography showed myotonic discharges in all tested patients (7/7,100%). The majority of cases showed autosomal recessive inheritance (AR) (89.5%), with predominantly homozygous (63.2%) and less commonly heterozygous (26.3%) or compound heterozygous (10.5%) mutations. 63.2% of mutations were pathogenic, and 36.8% were likely pathogenic. The mutations were most frequently located in exon 15 (21.1%), followed by exons 16 (15.8%) and 17 (10.5%), among others. The most frequent variants were c.1667T>A, c.1876C>T, and c.2083G>T (p.Glu695Ter), each occurring in 10.5% of cases. Except for muscle hypertrophy and Herculean appearance, more common in AR inheritance (P < 0.05), other clinical features showed no significant variation between AD and AR inheritances. Most received carbamazepine (52.6%), followed by phenytoin (31.6%); 36.8% had a good response.

Conclusions: This study, being the largest Indian cohort on MC, offers crucial insights for clinicians, enriching their understanding and improving the diagnosis and management of this disease.

Background and Aim: Anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) is an autoimmune-mediated central nervous system (CNS) demyelinating disorder with a broad spectrum of clinical presentation that is often difficult to distinguish from other demyelinating disorders, such as multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders. Background and Aim: Syphilis is an infectious disease caused by the spirochete bacteria Treponema pallidum (T. pallidum). Five types of neurosyphilis exist, which range from 1. the early forms – asymptomatic, 2. meningeal (presenting <1 year from infection), 3. meningovascular (presenting at 5 to 12 years from infection), 4. the late or tertiary forms – general syphilitic paresis, 5. tabes dorsalis (presenting at >10 years from infection). Conclusions: The discovery of a novel mutation in the STUB1 gene associated with SCA 48 in this Indian case adds valuable knowledge to the field, emphasizing the need for genetic diversity considerations in the diagnostic process and offering a new avenue for research into the pathophysiology and management of SCAs.

Gonaboyina Srinivas, Vipin Venugopalan, Santosh Kumar Dash, Pragateshnu Das

Kalinga Institute of Medical Sciences (KIMS), Bhubaneswar, Odisha, India

Background and Aim: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), valued for its antimicrobial properties, is commonly used in households for wound cleansing, oral hygiene, etc. While low concentrations are safe, higher concentrations—industrial – grade (33–35%), and recently, “food grade hydrogen peroxide” (33–35%) marketed for “hyper-oxygenation therapy”—increased its availability, leading to accidental and intentional ingestions. High-concentration ingestion can cause severe complications, including gastric rupture, enteric necrosis, and central nervous system (CNS) acute gas embolism.

Case report: A 48-year-old male poultry worker with no known comorbidities presented to the emergency, following the accidental ingestion of 60 mL of 50% w/w H2O2 (floor disinfectant). The patient was admitted to the Department of General Medicine and treated symptomatically. Twelve h post-admission, a neurology consultation was sought due to deteriorating sensorium. On examination, he was lethargic with asymmetric quadriparesis.

Discussion: An immediate non contrast computed tomography (NCCT) brain revealed acute bilateral high frontal hyperintensities, leading to the diagnosis of acute embolic stroke. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and computed tomography (CT) angiography confirmed the same with no evidence of thrombus. The final diagnosis of ischemic stroke – hydrogen peroxide-induced acute air embolism was made. The patient received symptomatic care due to nonavailability of hyperbaric oxygen. Sensorium improved within three days and motor strength improved from 0/5 on the right side and 2/5 on the left side to 4/5 bilaterally over the following 3 weeks.

Conclusions: This case underscores the importance of considering gas embolism in cases presenting with acute bilateral embolic phenomena, particularly in patients without traditional risk factors and negative diagnostic workups as a widespread increase in its availability and use.

Arunav Garg, Akhil Sahib, Astha Bansal, Deepti Grover, Debashish Chowdhury

Govind Ballabh Pant Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education (GBPIPMER), New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Ross syndrome is a rare disorder characterized by a triad of segmental anhidrosis, areflexia, and tonic pupil. Acute cerebellar syndrome (ACS) can arise from various etiologies, including vascular events, infections, metabolic imbalances, and toxins. This case report describes an unusual presentation of ACS in a patient with Ross syndrome triggered by heat stroke, highlighting diagnostic challenges and management strategies.

Case report: A 54-year-old female with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with acute onset of slurred speech, imbalance while walking, and transient loss of consciousness after exposure to extreme heat during a religious visit. Detailed history, clinical examination, and investigations were conducted.

Discussion: The patient was diagnosed with heat stroke leading to ACS. Diagnostic criteria included elevated body temperature (>40°C/105°F), central nervous system (CNS) dysfunction, and a history of extreme heat exposure. This diagnosis was supported by exposure to extreme heat, high-grade fever, and acute cerebellar features. Predisposing factors included uncontrolled diabetes, obesity, and sweat gland dysfunction secondary to newly diagnosed Ross syndrome. Ross syndrome was confirmed by sweat testing (starch iodine test) revealing segmental anhidrosis, dilute pilocarpine test showing tonic pupils, and demonstration of areflexia. Various investigations, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain, vitamin B12, thyroid function test (TFT), toxin screening, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, ruled out other causes of ACS. Treatment included rehydration, cooling, and thiamine supplementation. The patient showed significant improvement, was discharged healthy, and was advised to avoid excessive heat exposure.

Conclusions: This case underscores the importance of recognizing heat stroke as a potential cause of ACS, particularly in patients with conditions like Ross syndrome that impair thermoregulation. Awareness and preventive strategies are essential to avoid heat-induced neurological emergencies. Early diagnosis and prompt treatment are crucial for recovery.

Background and Aim: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) is an immune-mediated disorder affecting the peripheral nerves, characterized by progressive weakness and sensory dysfunction in the limbs. Only 1–2% of all CIDP cases can be attributed to the spectrum of nodopathy or paranodopathy with specific autoantibodies, such as those against Contactin-1 and Neurofascin-155.

Case report: A 62-year-old female patient presented with symptoms of acute-onset areflexic, flaccid quadriparesis (proximal more than distal weakness in both upper limb (UL) and lower limb (LL)), pins, and needle-like sensations in both UL and LL with severe sensory ataxia, reaching nadir over 10–15 days. Discussion: She was initially suspected of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and received intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). The patient was having significant nephrotic range proteinuria. Despite the initial response with methylprednisolone (MPS) pulse therapy, it was not well sustained on oral steroids, and she was given rituximab with maintenance pulse steroid at progressively increasing intervals. Nephrotic range proteinuria resolved completely with improvement in the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scale from 4 to 1.

Conclusions: This case underscores the importance of considering rare subtypes like nodopathy/paranodopathy in the differential diagnosis of CIDP, particularly in patients presenting with atypical features. Background and Aim: Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy (AAG) is a rare disorder characterized by autoantibodies targeting the autonomic ganglia, leading to widespread autonomic dysfunction. Patients typically present with symptoms such as orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, dry eyes, urinary retention, gastrointestinal dysmotility, and anhidrosis. The condition is often associated with antibodies against the ganglionic acetylcholine receptor (AChR). Diagnosis can be challenging, requiring a combination of clinical evaluation and specialized antibody testing.

Case report: A 65-year-old male patient presented with progressive autonomic dysfunction over 3–4 months. Discussion: The patient was investigated thoroughly, including all routine blood investigations and specific tests for autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibodies (antinuclear antibody (ANA)/ extractable nuclear antigen (ENA), vasculitis profile, paraneoplastic antibody panel), all which returned negative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal. Imaging studies, including chest x-ray (CXR), abdominal ultrasound, and positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT), were performed to rule out malignancy. The patient underwent detailed autonomic function tests which confirmed the extent of autonomic dysfunction (Parasympathetic >> Sympathetic). Given the clinical presentation and nonavailability of antibody testing, the diagnosis of AAG was considered, and the patient was treated with IVIG. Conclusions: This case underscores the importance of a thorough diagnostic workup and the potential effectiveness of immunotherapy in managing suspected AAG.

All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Takayasu arteritis (TAK) is a systemic vasculitis involving large arteries. This occlusive thrombus aortopathy lacks pathognomonic features, often resulting in a diagnostic dilemma leading to its under-recognition, misdiagnosis, and delayed management. Reports of direct central nervous system (CNS) involvement are not uncommon in TA, altered sensorium as an initial clinical presentation is extremely rare in the literature. Herein, we describe a case of altered sensorium in a TAK patient that mimicked meningitis.

Case report: A 29-year-old female presented to us with an altered sensorium and headache to emergency with a background history of epistaxis, hemoptysis, polyarthralgia, and eye pain for 2 years. She was intubated in the ward i/v/o poor Glasgow coma scale (GCS) for airway protection. Non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) head showed diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement with sulcal effacement. The initial working diagnosis was infective vs inflammatory meningitis. She was treated on the same lines with anti-tubercular therapy, antibiotics, and steroids empirically. Further examination revealed absent left-sided radial pulse and brachial pulse, and there was discordance in blood pressures in bilateral upper limbs, bruit present over left-sided carotid. Computed tomography (CT) aortogram revealed diffuse stenosis of the left proximal subclavian artery, with the bilateral common carotid artery and the pulmonary artery. Based on physical and radiological findings, we reached a diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed which showed a minor infarct in the left centrum semiovale. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination was normal for infective workup. CT abdomen revealed hepatosplenomegaly, which is also a rare finding in Takayasu arteritis. The diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement was due to diffuse leptomeningeal collaterals causing sulcal effacement.

Discussion: She was started on steroids, intravenous (IV) dexamethasone 0.4 mg /kg, with treatment patient improved clinically and symptoms resolved over 3 weeks, and she was started on mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 3g for long-term immunosuppression and is currently doing well on treatment.

Conclusions: In view of this, physicians should strive to take a detailed history and perform thorough physical examinations to timely pick the characteristic signs of TA, especially in patients presenting with unanticipated symptoms, to also consider diffuse collaterals which can radiologically mimic leptomeningeal enhancement, in patients often presenting with altered behavior with headache.

Background and Aim: Hirayama disease is a rare, nonfamiliar, monomelic amyotrophy originally described in 1959. The classical findings are pure motor lower motor neuron (LMN) weakness involving unilateral or asymmetric bilateral forearms and hands. This plateaus after a few years. It causes significant disability in some patients who can benefit from timely surgical intervention. Aim – To assess the frequency of Hirayama in patients presenting with focal upper limb amyotrophy and to assess factors contributing to progression.

Methodology: It is a single-center prospective observational study planned between November 2022 to November 2024. All patients presenting to OPD fulfilling the inclusion criteria will be enrolled and assessed every 6 months. Motor system examination with modified MRC scale and dynamometry and functional scales like overall neuropathy limitations scale (ONLS), Rasch-built overall disability scale for multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN RODS), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis functional rating scale (ALS FRS) are applied to assess patients periodically every 6 months. A total of 28 patients were followed up till 1 year.

Results: A total of 88 patients were screened. Out of these, 75 patients (85%) met the diagnostic criteria. Males were 96%. The mean age was 22.5 years (SD: 7.634). The average age at symptom onset was 17.8 years (SD: 7.23). The symptoms started in the left upper limb in 44% and the right upper limb in 42% with eventual asymmetric bilateral involvement in 68.5%. Family history was positive in two patients. A total of 79% of the patients were found to be historical progressors at the time of enrolling. Baseline ONLS, MMN RODS, and ALS FRS were 1.772 (SD 0.784), 33.4 (SD 7.231), and 44.8 (SD 1.22). The average power in the worst limb by manual and digital dynamometry was 29.58 (SD: 23.5) and 32.153 (SD: 26.42) pounds, respectively. A total of 77% had MRC grade 4 in the worst limb. The disability is mild in 78.5% and severe in 3.2%.

Conclusions: Timely diagnosis based on clinical criteria and dynamic MRI and surgical intervention when needed can halt progression.

Methodology: A retrospective chart analysis of children less than 18 years of age presenting to our department with CCM was performed. A total of 40 children were enrolled. Results: A total of 40 children were enrolled. Male: female ratio is 1.1:1. Fifteen children were diagnosed during the antenatal period, and mean gestational age at diagnosis was 31.8 weeks. Twenty-five were diagnosed after birth, and mean age at diagnosis was 13 months. Twenty-six children had complete agenesis of CC, of whom nine had isolated CC agenesis. Nine had hypoplasia, and five had hypoplasia with dysplasia. Epilepsy was seen in 67%, global developmental delay in 65%, behavioral issues in 40%. Facial dysmorphism was seen in 95%, and extra-cerebral malformations in 37.5%. Genetic testing was performed in 24, with a positive result in ten children. One child succumbed to refractory epilepsy.

Conclusions: Prospective and long-term multi-center studies, with cohesive inter-departmental cooperation, are required for further characterization and prognostication of malformations of corpus callosum.

Background and Aim: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a progressive brain disorder caused by the persistent mutant measles virus. Aim: To study the movement disorders in patients with subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE).

Methodology: A prospective observational study conducted in a tertiary care center. SSPE patients were diagnosed by modified Dyken criteria, and Jabbour staging was performed. We assessed their clinical profile and examined for movement disorders.

Conclusions: Our study concludes that movement disorders are important clinical findings of SSPE in the form of myoclonus and non-myoclonic disorders, including dystonia, repetitive motor behavior, tremor, and parkinsonism. Background and Aim: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) localized to the unilateral cerebral convexity is a rare presentation often associated with distinct etiologies such as trauma or vascular abnormalities. Background and Aim: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is characterized by increased intracranial pressure (ICP) occurring predominantly in women with obesity without an identifiable etiology. Methodology: The patients presenting at PGIMER (Chandigarh) and fulfilling the revised diagnostic criteria (modified Friedman criteria, 2013) for IIH were included in this prospective pilot study. They were assessed for neurological, visual, and radiological outcomes. The demographic and clinical findings, including the lipid profile (cholesterol, low-density lipoproteins (LDL), very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL), and triacylglycerols [TAGs]) in these patients, were explored.

Results: Thirty-six female IIH patients with a mean age of 35.22 ± 10.6 were assessed. The mean body mass index (BMI) (kg/m2) of disease onset was 29.2 ± 4.8. The median cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure reported was 280 mm (150, 400). The median cholesterol, triglyceride, LDL, high density lipoprotein (HDL), and VLDL reported were 169 mg/dL (119, 354), 134 mg/dL (58,309), 96 mg/dL (37, 257), 46.7 mg/dL (29.7, 116), and 27 mg/dL (11.6, 51), respectively. Background and Aim: Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) can lead to several electrocardiogram (ECG) changes. The Tpeak–Tend (Tpe) interval, a transmyocardial repolarization parameter, is associated with sudden cardiac death in AIS patients. However, its relationship with functional outcomes has not yet been studied. The aim of this study is to determine if Tpe interval predicts the short and long-term outcome in AIS patients without any known cardiac comorbidities.

Methodology: Tpe interval was calculated in ECG obtained from 100 patients who were assessed for stroke severity by national institutes of health stroke scale (NIHSS) and disability scores with modified rankin scale (mRS) at admission, discharge, and 3-month follow-up.

Results: The mean Tpe interval at admission was 104.6 ± 18.8 ms. Tpe interval was prolonged in 74% of patients at admission and 51% at 48 hpost-admissionn and 8% at 3 months. Among patients with insular involvement, 91.17% had prolonged Tpe interval (P value = 0.005). At admission, those with NIHSS >5 (82.5%) and mRS >4 (79.7%) had significant Tpe prolongation (P value < 0.01). Independent of stroke severity and disability at admission, those with persistently prolonged Tpe after 48 h had worse NIHSS and mRS scores (P value < 0.05), at discharge and 3 months. Of those with normalization of Tpe at 48 h, 74% had improvement of mRS score at discharge (P value < 0.001), and 52% at 3 months (P value = 0.684).

Conclusions: Our data sheds light on those patients who must be keenly observed for Tpe prolongation, as this may imply selecting medication as well as avoiding electrolyte disturbances that predispose them to arrhythmias.

Electroencephalogram (EEG) at this point was suggestive of generalized rhythmic delta activity, and the midazolam challenge showed significant clinical and EEG improvement, confirming nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) as per modified Salzburg criteria. MRI brain was suggestive of cerebral cortical encephalitis (CCE) with bilateral cortical cytotoxic edema. Based on the high suspicion and severity of the clinical condition, an empirical steroid pulse with antivirals was started. Infectious encephalitis and autoimmune panel, including neuromyelitis optica (NMO)/ myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG), were sent.

Discussion: Cell-based immunoassay for MOGAD was strongly positive, while other panels were negative. Antivirals were stopped and immunotherapy continued. The patient had a dramatic response to treatment.

Conclusions: New-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE) could be the initial manifestation of MOGAD. The diagnostic algorithm for NORSE should include testing for MOG antibodies especially when there are features suggestive of cerebral cortical encephalitis (CCE) with bilateral cortical cytotoxic edema on neuroimaging.

Govind Ballabh Pant Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education (GBPIPMER), New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a recognized independent risk factor for stroke, and it is associated with higher morbidity and mortality. Moreover, the onset of DM may preceded by a prolonged period of insulin resistance (IR). The true prevalence of DM in acute stroke is often underestimated because of this it goes unrecognized.

Methodology: This was a prospective observational study conducted over 18 months at the Department of Neurology, Safdarjung Hospital, and included 100 patients of AIS with no previous history of DM. Along with daily fasting plasma glucose (FPG) levels; HbA1C, oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), and insulin levels were also measured during the hospital stay. They were followed up, and OGTT was repeated at the end of 3 months.

Results: Unrecognized DM was more prevalent than recognized DM in acute ischemic stroke (AIS) patients. The reactionary hyperglycemia at stroke presentation was found only in a few subjects, while the majority had a persistent abnormal glucose metabolism at 3 months follow-up. In our patients, IR also increased progressively with the impairment of glucose metabolism.

Conclusions: Unrecognized DM was more prevalent than recognized DM in acute stroke patients. It is advisable for clinicians to screen every ischemic stroke patient for impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and IR to reduce their long-term morbidity and mortality.

Background and Aim: Dyke–Davidoff–Masson syndrome (DDMS) is a rare syndrome characterized by typical manifestations including drugs resistant epilepsy, intellectual disability, hemiparesis, skull bone thickening associated with cerebral hemi atrophy, and hyper-pneumatization of paranasal and frontal sinuses on neuroimaging. Some patients may present with additional symptoms like cerebellar and basal ganglia atrophy and neuropsychiatric disorders. Congenital causes of DDMS include intrauterine vascular injury and cerebral hemispheric hypoperfusion. Acquired causes mostly derive from birth trauma, periventricular leukomalacia, cerebral hemorrhage, cerebral infarction, cerebral infection, radiation, postictal cerebral hemi atrophy, and prolonged seizures.

Case report: A 21-year-old male presented to the Department of Neurology with a 7-year history of seizures and violent antisocial behavior. He was thoroughly examined and investigated. Injectable antiepileptic drugs and antipsychotic tablets were given to the patient to control seizures and antisocial aggressive behavior. After that, the disease course remarkably changed to fewer seizures. Then, we added oral valproic acid (500 mg twice a day) which drastically improved the seizures to a maximum of two seizures daily.

Discussion: Examination of the patient revealed drug-resistant epilepsy, intellectual disability, hemiparesis, skull bone thickening, and ankylosis of the right wrist associated with cerebral hemi atrophy and hyperpneumatization. Electroencephalogram (EEG) showed a slowed background with delta wave activities in hyperpnea and continued focal to diffuse pseudo-periodic activities.

Conclusions: This case is presented as the Dyke–Davidoff–Masson syndrome. It highlights the challenges of an early diagnosis and the treatment of this rare condition. We suggest that in the presence of pharmaco-resistant epilepsy in childhood and body deformities, further investigations should be undertaken to establish an evidence-based diagnosis.

Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS), Hyderabad, Telangana, India

Background and Aim: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is a condition characterized by headache, altered mental status, seizures, and visual disturbances, with white matter changes in the posterior cerebral hemispheres. Lead poisoning, a rare but serious condition, presents with a variety of neurological symptoms, complicating its diagnosis. This case is of lead poisoning presenting with clinical features and imaging suggestive of PRES.

Case report: A 61-year-old male, diabetic, hypertensive with past history of coronary artery disease (CAD), presented to our emergency with a history of altered sensorium for 1 week in the form of excessive drowsiness but was arousable and a history of one episode of generalized tonic–clonic seizure (GTCS) seizure. Past history of recurrent abdominal pain for 2 months, extensively worked up, proved unfruitful. On examination, he was drowsy, arousable, obeying stage 1 commands, with stable vitals. Pallor was present. Rest central nervous system (CNS) examination was unremarkable.

Discussion: Routine blood investigations were normal except for iron deficiency anemia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain revealed ill-defined T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the medial occipital lobes bilaterally which were hypointense on T1, no diffusion restriction, negative susceptibility weighted imaging (SWI), and no contrast enhancement. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, normal glucose, elevated protein 224 mg/dL, nine cells, and 100% lymphocytes. Further history disclosed the patient’s chronic usage of herbal medication for diabetic control, raising suspicion of heavy metal exposure. Serum lead levels were significantly elevated, >100 mcg/dL. The patient was treated with intravenous chelation therapy using ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) and supportive care. The patient improved symptomatically and blood lead levels returned to normal levels post-treatment.

Background and Aim: Moyamoya angiopathy is characterized by progressive stenosis of the terminal portion of the internal carotid arteries and the development of a network of abnormal collateral vessels. Discussion: A 20-year-old boy presented to our institution with 1-year history of recurrent headaches. Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST), Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, India

Background and Aim: Autonomic dysfunction which affects about 2/3 of patients with GBS is frequently unnoticed despite its significant impact. This study aims to estimate the prevalence of autonomic dysfunction in the acute phase of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and to look for any association between the presence of specific antiganglioside antibodies with autonomic dysfunction in GBS.

Methodology: All consecutive patients diagnosed with GBS between November 2022 and May 2024 have been enrolled. Standard investigations, including nerve conduction study (NCS), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and antiganglioside antibody panel, were conducted. Sympathetic function was evaluated with postural hypotension and a cold immersion test. The parasympathetic function was assessed via heart rate variability to posture and deep respiration using a surface electrocardiogram (ECG) rhythm strip.

Results: A total of 32 patients were recruited, of which 21 were male, and 11 were female. Respiratory tract infection is the most common antecedent factor. The mean time gap between the antecedent event and the onset of symptoms is 3.87 days (6.99). A total of 90% patients presented to the hospital within 2 weeks of symptom onset. The most common subtype is AIDP (46.9%), followed by acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) (15.6%). The prevalence of autonomic dysfunction was estimated to be 40.6%. Association with antiganglioside panel could not be established due to low positivity (9.3%). The cold immersion test is the best performer with the highest area under the curve (AUC) (0.820) with a decent sensitivity (69.2%) and low false positive rate (5.3%). Sympathetic skin responses (SSR) performed moderately well with an AUC of 0.743, moderate sensitivity (53.8%), and low false positive rate (5.3%).

Conclusions: The prevalence of autonomic dysfunction and the presence of antiganglioside antibodies could not be correlated due to the low sample size and low positivity rate. SSR and cold immersion tests were found to be sensitive bedside tests in detecting autonomic dysfunction.

All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Myofibrillar myopathy is an umbrella term for a group of inherited neuromuscular disorders that share a common histopathological phenotype. It is characterized by the disintegration of networks of intermyofibrillar protein around the Z-disk followed by their intra-sarcoplasmic accumulation leading to a myopathy.

Case report: In this case, a 49-year-old male presented with a 7-month history of insidious onset, asymmetric, progressive quadriparesis with wasting, spasticity, and hyper-reflexia. Clinical presentation was consistent with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

Discussion: Electromyography revealed spontaneous activity (fasciculation, fibrillation, and positive sharp waves) and large amplitude long duration motor unit action potentials in cervical, thoracic, lumbo-sacral, and bulbar segments supplementing diagnosis of ALS. However, he had elevated muscle enzymes. Exome sequencing revealed two heterozygous autosomal dominant mis-sense variants in TTN (c.820222G>A) and FLNC (c.2560G>A) genes. Electron microscopy of the muscle biopsy specimen showed destruction of the Z band and disorganization of the myofibrillary network. Biopsy was hence compatible with a diagnosis of myofibrillar myopathy.

Conclusions: Elevated creatine kinase more than five times in patients with clinical presentation of Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis should always prompt further investigation and can be part of the myofibrillar myopathy spectrum.

All India Institute of Medical Sciences Delhi, India

Background and Aim: Acute stroke comprises 80% of ischemic strokes out of which approximately 30% of ischemic strokes are due to large vessel occlusions. Nearly 25% of these patients develop rapid infarct growth in the first few hours of anterior circulation large vessel occlusion (LVO) and are known as fast progressors. The temporal expansion of the ischemic core after large vessel occlusion (LVOS) is highly variable among individuals where some have rapid infarct growth rates (IGRs) known as fast progressors. Hence, determining factors associated with infarct growth rate (IGR) in the setting of LVO over 24 h will help in early patient triaging for an appropriate course of action. To address this hypothesis, we present here a case report of fast progress in our hospital setting.

Case report: This is a case report of an observational study approved from the Institute’s ethics committee. A 65-year-old male patient with past history of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) developed right middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory stroke 3 h 5 min from last known well. His admission national institutes of health stroke scale (NIHSS) score was eight. Hence, he was thrombolyzed with an injection of tenecteplase 15 mg. His computed tomography (CTA) was also s/o large vessel occlusion hence taken up for mechanical thrombectomy. Post-thrombolysis and post-thrombectomy patient’s NIHSS improved to 5 and 4, respectively. Following post-thrombectomy, he reported to have persistent hypotension for which inotropes were started. Later, inotropes tapered off, and the patient was discharged in hemodynamically stable condition with modified rankin scale (mRS) 1.

Discussion and Conclusions: Infarct growth rate is a critical determinant of tissue damage and functional outcome in acute ischemic stroke. Early intervention is essential to prevent further infarct growth for better patient’s outcomes. In hospital settings where magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) imaging is not available, the determination of infarct growth rate (IGR) in acute ischemic stroke (AIS) patients can still be estimated based on clinical and other factors.

Sevenhills Hospital, Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, India

Background and Aim: Unilateral calf swelling can occur due to various causes like Iliac vein compression, deep vein thrombosis superficial thrombophlebitis, ruptured Baker’s cyst, ruptured leg muscle, sprain/strain, fracture, lymphedema, intramuscular hematoma, muscular infarction (particularly in diabetes), etc.

Case report: A 45-year-old man, known diabetic, no addictions, history of left lower limb poliomyelitis, and thinned out limb since the age of 8 years, presented with a sudden increase in the size of the calf muscle on the left side since 1 month and occasional paresthesias in left foot and sole. There was no history of low back ache, neck pain, tingling, paresthesias, and numbness over other limbs, visible swellings over lower limbs, or trauma. There is the history of lifting heavy weights. On examination, the left thigh circumference was 2 cm more, and the left calf circumference was 0.5 cm less compared to the right side. The ankle jerk was depressed on the left side.

Discussion: Routine blood investigations were normal. Color doppler of the arterial and venous systems of the left lower limb revealed no abnormality. A nerve conduction study of the left lower limb revealed an axonal neuropathy pattern with reduced amplitudes in the left peroneal and tibial nerves. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study of lumbosacral spine was performed which revealed slight midline protrusion of the L3-4 intervertebral disc with no significant compression of nerves, the L4/L5 and L5-S1 intervertebral discs protruding toward the back moderately asymmetrically, more on the left side, with thecal sac and left nerve root indentation without cord compression.

Conclusions: Neurogenic muscle hypertrophy, referred to as “denervation hypertrophy,” is caused mainly by compression of the nerve root, most commonly the S1 root affecting the calf muscles. The pathomechanism of muscle hypertrophy is not completely clear and is certainly multifactorial.

Background and Aim: Thyroid-related ophthalmopathy can present with various ocular manifestations. An interesting case of ocular neuromyotonia associated with thyroid-related ophthalmopathy is discussed here.

There is no h/o difficulty in swallowing or weakness in the limbs.

Discussion: He was seen in the outpatient service. In the resting position, the right eye was normal. The left eyeball was deviating upwards, and it was corrected in 2–3 min. Ashwini Hiremath

BLDE (DU) Medical College, Bijapur, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Emamectin benzoate poisoning is a broad-spectrum insecticide used to treat vegetables. It is a semisynthetic derivative of avertmectin. There is a significant paucity of literature due to its uncommon consumption and underreporting of cases. It interacts with the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors. Patients predominantly present with severe abdominal pain, gastritis, and vomiting in the initial stages. Later, they have central nervous depression, agitation, and seizures. Unfortunately, no specific antidotes exist, and most times, it has proven fatal despite thorough symptomatic treatment. This study aims to raise awareness about uncommon yet fatal poisoning caused by emamectin benzoate, a broad-spectrum insecticide.

Case report: Records of two patients were retrieved with emamectin benzoate poisoning. There were two male patients with emamectin benzoate poisoning in the last 2 years. Case 1: a 28-year-old presented with acute abdomen. On day 3, he developed severe aggression and status epilepticus and was intubated. Until then, it was assumed to be unknown compound poisoning. He also received Inj Midazolam. We realized it to be emamectin only after they got the can. Case 2 presented with severe breathlessness and drowsiness only 2 h after consumption of 500 mL of the above poison. Pupils in case 1 were unequal and sluggishly reactive whereas normal in case 2. Extensive investigations included a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies, toxic screening, USG abdomen, and blood reports were normal. Case 1 was managed for 15 days but finally succumbed. Case 2 expired on day 3 due to severe respiratory acidosis. Both were given gastric lavage with charcoal, antiepileptics, antibiotics, and thorough supportive care.

Discussion and Conclusions: There is a paucity of literature. Hence, awareness of its effects and treatment is essential among physicians/neurologists.

Aare Sidhartha, Varun Reddy Gundluru, Sanket Kulkarni, Ravikanth J, Shashidhar Matam

Yashoda Hospital, Malakpet, Hyderabad, Telangana, India

Background and Aim: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) is caused by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage without a history of trauma or dural puncture. It is common in middle-aged people. Incidence is estimated to be 5 per 100, 000 persons per year. Postural headache is the main presenting symptom.

Case report: A 45-year-old gentleman presented with a history of headache for the last 3 months that worsened in the last 1 week. The headache was holo-cranial, throbbing type which worsened in an upright position and subsided when he lay down. Due to this, he was unable to do his daily activities comfortably and could not discharge his duties at his workplace.

Discussion: In view of this positional variation of headache, an magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain was performed that showed bilateral subdural collections with features suggestive of intracranial hypotension. The patient was advised rest in lying down position and hydrated well. To identify any leak of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), an MR Myelogram was performed. It showed a CSF leak on the left side at the C1–C2 level extending into adjacent posterior paraspinal soft tissues. Targeted epidural blood patching was performed in consultation with an interventional radiologist. A total of 5 mL of the patient’s autologous blood was drawn from peripheral access and injected slowly into the epidural space under computed tomography (CT) guidance. Gradually, the patient improved and experienced a reduction in his postural headaches, along with the ability to sit and mobilize for a long duration. He was also able to resume his daily activities. His review of CT brain at follow-up showed a significant reduction in subdural collections along with other changes related to spontaneous intracranial hypotension.

Conclusions: MR myelogram is an important diagnostic tool for identifying CSF leak. Epidural blood patching is an important treatment modality.

Dhanya Sureddy, Vijaya Shankar P, Muthukani S, Vijayashankar P

Apollo hospitals Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

Background and Aim: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by varying degrees of skeletal muscle weakness. While the condition is typically associated with antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) or muscle-specific kinase (MuSK), less commonly, antibodies against low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 (LRP4) are implicated. MG with LRP4 antibodies can present with atypical symptoms, complicating diagnosis and management.

Case report: 1. Case 1: A 65-year-old male k/c/o T2 diabetes mellitus (DM), hypertension (HTN), chronic kidney disease (CKD) on hemodialysis presented with acute, unexplained respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Initial evaluations, including imaging and standard neurological examinations, were inconclusive. Neostigmine test was performed when he was intubated which showed improvement in spontaneous breaths. Serological tests revealed elevated anti-LRP4 antibodies. Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and corticosteroids resulted in marked clinical improvement. 2. Case 2: A 35-year-old male was admitted with progressive dyspnea and episodes of respiratory failure for 6 months. Extensive workup, including pulmonary function tests and chest computed tomography (CT) scans, failed to identify a primary respiratory pathology. Repetitive nerve stimulation showed a decremental pattern making a diagnosis of MG. The serological analysis identified high titers of anti-LRP4 antibodies. The patient responded positively to plasmapheresis, with significant improvement in respiratory function.

Discussion: These patients responded positively to immunomodulation, IVIG, plasmapheresis, and corticosteroids with significant improvement in respiratory function.

Conclusions: Although LRP4-positive myasthenia gravis is generally described in the literature as a mild disease, it can present with atypical and severe manifestations such as unexplained respiratory failure. Recognizing this potential for atypical presentations is essential for early diagnosis and effective treatment.

Manipal Academy of Higher Education (MAHE), Manipal, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Asymmetric weakness as a presenting feature in acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculopathy (AIDP).

Case report: It is a rare case report. Here is a gentleman in his late of 50s with nil comorbidities presented to neurology OPD with complaints of right upper and right lower limb weakness (proximal and distal) and difficulty in walking which was gradual in onset and progressive in nature since 20 days, also complains of left-sided facial deviation, difficulty in holding water in mouth since 20 days. At the time of presentation, vitals were stable with a blood pressure (BP) of 120/80 mmHg, pulse was 84 bpm, and regular and general physical examination was grossly normal. Treatment initially comprised of intravenous (IV) immunoglobulin of 2 g/kg over 5 days and other supportive measures. Physiotherapy was also initiated immediately.

Discussion and Conclusions: Asymmetric weakness is rarely demonstrated in AIDP. Our case highlights the importance of clinical examination in the current AI era.

Yashoda Hospital, Malakpet, Hyderabad, Telangana, India

Background and Aim: Hypertrophic cranial pachymeningitis (HCP) is a rare chronic fibrosing inflammatory disease characterized by marked diffuse thickening of cranial dura matter, resulting in progressive neurological deficits. Chronic headaches and multiple cranial palsies are most common clinical manifestations. Various clinicopathological entities produce HCP, and idiopathic HCP is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Case report: A 45-year-old female, with no prior comorbid illnesses or addictions, presented initially with complaints of headache, hoarseness of voice, and mild facial deviation to the right. She was diagnosed clinically with Left lower motor neuron (LMN) VII, VIII, and X cranial nerve palsies.

Discussion: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain (plain/contrast) showed T2 FLAIR hyperintensity (with post-contrast enhancement) posterior to the nasopharynx, involving clivus and extending to bilateral adjacent parapharayngeal space. Pachymeningeal enhancement was noted along the right anterior temporal lobe. Vasculitic workup was negative transnasal endoscopic biopsy, serum. IgG4 levels and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis were normal. She was treated with oral steroids and immunosuppressants (MMF). Patient symptoms gradually improved but any attempts to gradually taper and stop steroids (as the patient developed chronic steroid usage-related complications like cushingoid features, and pathological vertebral body fractures) resulted in a flare of HCP and multiple cranial nerve palsies (subsequently, she developed bilateral LMN VII, VIII, and X, Left XII; Left III and VI, Right II, V1, III, IV, VI cranial nerve palsies). Later, she developed pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) and was started on antituberculous treatment (ATT) (rituximab is planned in review).

Conclusions: Idiopathic HCP is very rare and very difficult to diagnose, and treatment modalities steroids, immunosuppressive drugs, and other supportive treatments are required.
