Neerupaka Venkatachalam, pooja Mailankody, Girish Baburao Kulkarni, Sivakumar P T, Seshagiri D V

National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: The migraine types, presentation, and treatment options change with advancing age. Depression, anxiety, sleep issues, medication overuse, and co-existing medical comorbidities make the elderly migraine different from that in the younger age. We aimed to compare the clinical profile of migraine, associated symptoms, treatment profile, and comorbidities like depression, anxiety, and sleep issues in migraine between younger age and older age groups.

Methodology: The prospective cross-sectional study was conducted in the Department of Neurology at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru, India, after approval by the Institute Ethics Committee. We included 154 patients, fulfilling the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3) criteria for migraine. They were assessed with history, clinical examination, severity of migraine (Migraine Disability Assessment Scale, MIDAS), headache impact test-6 (HIT-6), depression (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, HAM-D), anxiety (Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A), and sleep disturbances (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, PSQI).

Results: In the old age group (age > 60 years, n = 81), females constituted 46 (56.8%), and males were 35 (42%). In the young age group (age 20–40 years, n = 73), 50 (68.5%) were females, and 23 (31%) were males. In the old age group, throbbing (P value = 0.009) and vomiting (P value = 0.003) are less common compared to the young age group. Depression was seen in 65.4% of the old age group compared to 42% seen in the young age group (P value = 0.004). Anxiety was seen in 63% of the old age group and 78% of the young age group (P value of 0.041).

Conclusions: Older patients with migraine have more frequent headaches, higher depression, and sleep disturbances along with less disability, anxiety, throbbing, and vomiting compared to young migraine patients. Our findings have implications for the management of migraine in the elderly, both from diagnostic and therapeutic perspectives.

Om Prasad, Francisco J. Cidral

Gobind Ballabh Pant Hospital, Delhi University, New Delhi, India

Background and Aim: In this study, we aimed to investigate the impact of a 20 min audiovisual brainwave entrainment session on alpha brainwave activity using continuous real-time Electroencephalogram (EEG) monitoring.

Methodology: The study was conducted at the Electrophysiology Laboratory of Sri Sri Neuro Center in Warangal, Telangana. The research included 30 healthy participants aged 18 to 65 (male and female), with no neurological or psychiatric conditions. The BrainTap headset was used for audiovisual brain entrainment targeting alpha waves, and wave activity was measured before, during (EEG recording began 2 min after the beginning of the session), and after the session. The EEG data, recorded with a Nihon Kohden EEG machine, was preprocessed to ensure quality by removing artifacts and applying a notch filter. We used power spectral analysis and density spectral array (DSA) to evaluate the power spectrum within a frequency band of 8 to 13 Hz over time. Statistical analysis, including ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis followed by multiple comparison tests, was conducted to compare alpha wave activity across the three phases.

Results: A significant increase in alpha amplitude was observed during (P ≤ 0.0001) and after (P ≤ 0.0001) the session with large effect sizes (1.52 and 1.73, respectively), as well as a significant increase in alpha power during (P ≤ 0.0001) and after (P ≤ 0.0001) the session also with large effect sizes (1.72 and 1.91, respectively).

Conclusions: The findings of this study demonstrate that a 20 min audiovisual brainwave entrainment session significantly enhances alpha brainwave activity in healthy adults. Both alpha amplitude and alpha power showed substantial increases during and after the session, as evidenced by the highly significant P values and large effect sizes. These results suggest that audiovisual brainwave entrainment is an effective method for increasing alpha brainwave activity, which could have implications for relaxation, mental clarity, and overall cognitive function. Further research may explore the long-term benefits and potential applications of this technique in various clinical and non-clinical settings.

Kasturba Medical College (KMC), Manipal, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Rabies is transmitted through the rabies-infected animal bite, primarily dogs. Furious type and paralytic type of rabies are the two clinically recognized forms. Paralytic rabies should be considered as a potential differential diagnosis in patients presenting with acute flaccid paralysis with atypical features. Rabies needs to be considered even in patients with acute progressive asymmetrical quadriparesis; despite receiving prior vaccination.

Case report: A 38-year-old male presented with h/o acute-onset progressive quadriparesis with bulbar involvement was treated initially as Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and h/odog bite 2 months ago surfaced 3 days before death. A 25-year-old male, with h/o dog bite 1 month ago, completed five doses of rabies vaccination, now presented with acute progressive asymmetrical quadriparesis since 1 week. The diagnostic dilemma of vaccination-induced myelitis vs GBS was considered.

Discussion: In the first case, a nuchal biopsy was positive for rabies polymerase chain reaction (PCR). In the second case due to the rapid downhill course associated with delirium, an altered sensorium repeat magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed which progressed to encephalomyelitis; repeat rabies PCR was sent and showed rising titers, and hence, rabies infection was considered and both patients succumbed to their illness.

Conclusions: In a rabies endemic region, any patient presenting with acute-onset quadriparesis with atypical features, paralytic rabies should be considered as a potential differential diagnosis. A patient with H/O of rabid animal bite should receive adequate post-exposure prophylaxis as stated by world health organization (WHO). Early diagnosis of paralytic rabies is crucial to prevent unnecessary treatment along the lines of GBS.

Kasturba Medical College (KMC), Manipal, Karnataka, India

Background and Aim: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is usually a disease of the elderly but a small percentage of the population develops young-onset Parkinson’s disease (below 50 years). Patients can be divided into several subtypes, and one of them is depending on the age of symptom onset. There is a heterogeneity in clinical presentation and prognosis between young onset PD (YOPD) and late-onset PD (LOPD). To compare clinical characteristics in YOPD and LOPD cases.

Methodology: This prospective study was conducted from September 2023 to May 2024 at the Neurology Department of Kasturba Medical College, Manipal. To evaluate motor and non-motor symptoms, we used Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale III (UPDRS III), non-motor symptoms questionnaire (NMSQ), and for the disease stage, we used the Hoehn and Yahr Scale.

Results: A total of 40 patients were studied. The median age in YOPD was 43. 3 years, and in LOPD, it was 61. 9 years with a higher prevalence in males. Tremor and bradykinesia were the most frequent predominant initial symptoms in both groups, while gait instability was more frequent in LOPD. The average UPDRS III score was lower in YOPD. The average Hoehn and Yahr Scale are lower in YOPD. The predominant non-motor clinical features in YOPD were depression and low mood, and in LOPD, predominant non-motor clinical features were urinary symptoms and constipation; fatigability is equal in both groups.

Conclusions: In our study, tremors and bradykinesia were the most frequent predominant initial presenting symptoms in both YOPD and LOPD, while gait instability was frequent in LOPD, and non-motor features constipation followed by sleep disturbance was more frequent in LOPD, while restless leg was the least reported in our study.

Nishal Thellakula, Sunil K Narayan1, Sulochana Shaktivel2, Vinod A Chaudhari3, Nagarajan L4, Rajeswari Aghoram1, Pawan Sabale5

Departments of, 1Neurology, 2Anatomy, 3Forensic Medicine and Toxicology and 4Radiodiagnosis, JIPMER, Pondicherry, 5Department of Forensic Medicine, B.Y.L Nayar Charitable Hospital, Mumbai, Maharashtra, India

Background and Aim: Tamil is arguably the oldest surviving classical language in the world and is considered to be the mother of all the Dravidian languages. Hindi is the most common language among most of the population of North India. Few studies are available on the topographical anatomy of speech areas and none on the cytoarchitectonic histology of speech areas. The present study focused on exploring any differences between the persons with Tamil and Hindi as their mother tongue.

Methodology: This was a single-blinded and single-center study that was conducted in Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research (JIPMER). The study tried to standardize brain autopsy and histopathological techniques for language areas using standard stains and to identify and distinguish the topographical and cytotechtonic differences in the language areas between two major linguistic and subracial ethnic groups. Tamil-speaking and non-Tamil-speaking (Hindi) groups were chosen for this pilot study. JIPMER: The ethics committee (Human) had approved study No. JIP/IEC/2021/187 dated 21/7/21. Based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, brain samples from patients who were cognitively intact at death and died from clearly non-neurological causes were collected from the Department of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, JIPMER, Puducherry, and the samples were transferred to the Department of Anatomy, JIPMER where the later part of the processing of the brain tissues, histology (Luxol fast blue and Toluidine blue stains were used), and images of the slides were taken. Written informed consent was taken from the legally accepted representative of the deceased before the start of the autopsy for the study. The brain weight was measured before fixation by using an electronic weighing machine and the volume of the brain was measured using the Archimedes principle (by immersing the brain in a measuring glass jar filled with water to measure the displaced volume of water before and after the immersing of the brain into the glass jar). The brain was put in a plastic jar containing 10% formalin in an upside-down position suspended on the basilar artery with the other end of the thread tied to the rod kept on the jar for carrying out the later processes on the brains. Gross morphology parameters like fronto-occipital length, lengths of lateral sulci, the distance between the Anterior Sylvian point and inferior Rolandic point, length of the posterior rami, anterior ascending, anterior horizontal rami of the lateral sulci, presence of diagonal and triangular sulcus, and the shapes of the rami of lateral sulcus were measured, and intra and intercomparisons of the measurements were performed. Using Image J software, the histology slides were analyzed, and statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software v.20. For the radiological part of the study, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans were performed on a different set of samples with an equal representation of Tamil and non-Tamil (Hindi) speaking individuals. The volume of the Broca’s area was calculated using Syngovia Neuro 3D software and the vertical and horizontal lengths of the cerebellum were compared between the samples.

Results: Males had more neuronal density than females in the motor speech area. In contrast, the females had more neuronal density when both the motor and sensory speech areas were considered. The fronto-occipital length showed a significant difference between the left and right hemispheres with the left side being longer than the right. U/V-shaped configuration was more commonly observed on the hemispheres than the Y-shaped configuration. Hindi-speaking individuals exhibited a higher average neuronal count of 9.2 million neurons while Tamil-speaking individuals showed a lower average count of 8.1 million neurons, and this finding is possibly due to the share of participants among Tamil-speaking and non-Tamil-speaking cadavers. The imaging studies failed to show the differences between the language-speaking groups.

Conclusions: Dravidian languages remained relatively insulated for centuries due to geographical peculiarities of the region and are considered to have evolved from the proto-Dravidian roots and are relatively independent of influences from Sanskrit/Prakrit believed to have evolved from the Aryan languages Tamil-speaking individuals had insignificantly lesser number of neurons in relevant brain regions. However, neuronal density count alone does not correlate with functional efficiency, and more important are factors like synaptic density, synaptic arborization density, and neurohumoral receptor/channel density. Our study did not look into those finer differences. In this preliminary study, with limited study samples, there were only statistically insignificant differences in the neuronal density and neuronal count between the brains of Tamil and non-Tamil-speaking persons.
